View image in fullscreen Michael Carrick looks on from the touchline during the Manchester derby. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

City now have 12 points, second only to Arsenal on goal difference, while United have only four points and are 13th. “We will get there, I’m convinced of that,” Carrick said.

“We haven’t got as many points as we wanted and we should have. We’ve got to accept that and take that. It doesn’t change us moving forward and our hopes for the season and what we can achieve as a team. We’ve made really good strides over a period of time and we will continue to do that.”

Carrick was asked about the pre-game protest against the club’s move to eradicate ticket touts that some believe to be draconian. United said on Friday that 685 accounts had been subject to a ban and 464 supporters had received a reduced sanction or final warning.

Carrick said: “The details in terms of all what goes behind it, I’m not always in line to get to the bottom of it, but I definitely appreciate the supporters.

“If they do feel [unhappy] in certain ways then, of course, we want to try everything to make them happy. That’s part of performances on the pitch and off the pitch. That’s obvious. They’re a huge part of this football club. They’re everything for this football club.”

Inside the stadium The Red Army hung a banner over the tunnel that said, “The Way You Treat Us Is A Disgrace.” All usual banners were removed from the Stretford End.

Sports.title: Arteta embraces perfect storm to play the victim in game of his own making | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
A gentleman is never rude unintentionally, only by design. Nobody really knows who said this first. But it could easily be a line from the Elite Football Manager’s Guide to Press Conferences (Premier League edition). Because nothing happens by accident in these spaces.

Every word spoken in front of the board covered in adverts is metered and planned. A manager is never angry, or concerned, or even charming unintentionally. The game is the game, but so are all the other bits spilling out either side of it.

It was hard not to think about this while listening to Mikel Arteta talk about the penalty awarded to Sunderland at the Stadium of Light for a perceived act of grappling on Dan Ballard by Ezri Konsa. This is said with genuine professional respect. As everyone who has ever done a podcast knows – and this is, let’s be clear, everyone – there are lost Amazonian tribes discussing Girls season three in their own dark corner of Spotify – there are moments when you just have to flip the switch, up the energy and turn on full clip‑this‑bit‑up‑please‑Dave sincerity mode.

Arteta did this beautifully in the moment, appearing genuinely struck by what he was saying, radiating wounded integrity, like a disappointed junior headmaster appealing for the return of the school minibus keys.

Let’s be clear though. Arteta is not “very worried” about all this. He’s not “sad” or indeed, as he later emphasised for good measure, “really sad”. He’s not concerned solely with “protecting the game”, speaking here for all of us, just a fan of football.

Come off it. This is a manager we know to be obsessed with the most marginal of gains, to micro-plan the micro-details. As is all elite sport now. There has been talk of rowing coaches installing fibreglass toilet seats at their training hubs having calculated the average athlete spends 20 minutes in there and this is all key glute management time. Arteta loves this stuff. There’s no way Ben White isn’t sat fiddling with his phone at the training ground on a gold-standard Easy‑Cup Mega-Soft Evacu-Throne.

So it is with his public statements. This will have all been gamed and contingency‑planned in advance. And for hard, rational, tactical reasons, because this is how the game is played and run now. So what does it mean?

View image in fullscreen Ezri Konsa is penalised for a contentious foul on Dan Ballard in the box. Photograph: MI News/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

There are three things we know for sure. First, Arteta was right. This was a bad refereeing decision. Most obviously it was factually wrong. Ballard very skilfully pulled Konsa down on top of him, while simultaneously feigning shock that such a thing could happen.

It was doubly bad because the referee’s response was pre-planned, flagged by the early-season chat about refereeing in a more interventionist fashion. Go into any situation with a voice in your head, a vaguely worded mission to fulfil: this will skew your judgment.

The second thing is that referees are not biased. They’re just not very good. Two things have happened to them. First, the barrage of information to be absorbed in real time during a game is now utterly mind-boggling.

Most referees are not from a high-pressure data-processing background. These are not military pilots or traders on a currency floor. Less than a quarter have an academic degree. The task is beyond them. This is not a slur or an insult. It’s a simple description of what is happening, as supported by the evidence.

This is doubly annoying because referees have become fundamentally confused about their role. Referees are not ringmasters, or curators of the spectacle. They don’t get to decide what our sport should look like. Pro Ref is a private company with no locus standi to rule on the aesthetics of football. A referee should exist at the very edge of the spectacle. You’re not a local government planning officer with a mandate to decide which double-glazed French doors are or aren’t in character with the neighbourhood. Stop getting football not just wrong, but wrong.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Arteta has a word with the fourth official, Elliot Bell, at Sunderland. Photograph: Scott Heppell/Reuters

But Arteta was also ready for this. Arsenal’s coaches will have known this would happen at some point. That press conference response was already in the chamber. Arteta may even have practised his sad-not-angry face, his key lines.

And this would be the correct thing to do. None of this is breaking the rules, just as Arsenal are not a dirty team or a bunch of cheats. They play the game that is being presented to us, a sport that is being made to operate at the edge of its own ludicrously micro‑analysed rules on small issues of physical contact.

Arteta’s Arsenal have been masterful at finding advantages in this. Defenders are very good at playing with the ball at their feet now. Defenders are not selected for their ability to resist physical challenges. It is logical to exploit this, just as it is logical to seek to protect your ability to do so by speaking in public about how the rules are applied. This is why Arteta is good, and why he wins.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It is also true that this has created a strange environment. The tone of the wider Arsenal fanbase is another element here. There is no one type of football fan. All human life is here. But the fact remains, the loudest voices in the online Arsenal hive mind, even the atmosphere in the stadium is unique in its absolute conviction of victimhood, of conspiracy, of a galvanising sense of adversity.

There is no other ground where every single refereeing decision, even the who-knows 50-50s, is so violently and eloquently disputed. There are supporters who seem to spend most of the game up on their feet in a state of performative, weaponised indignation, whose entire interaction with the spectacle is an attitude of aggrieved injustice.

This makes sense, too. It speaks directly to the game we have created. Aggrieved middle-aged rule pedantry. This is the new cauldron of hate.

View image in fullscreen Set-piece grappling was a theme once more in Arsenal’s win at Sunderland. Photograph: Ian Hodgson/AP

Is it based in reality? Not perhaps on the outline numbers. Arsenal have been awarded more fouls than any other team this season. Only six teams last season had more fouls awarded against them, and the same the year before. They had the fewest yellow cards last season. They haven’t had a single red since they had six of them in 2024‑25.

Still, certain key incidents continue to grate and fester. There was the incorrectly denied penalty claim for Bruno Guimarães at Aston Villa. The balls-up with VAR lines against Brentford in 2023, which, if it really was deliberate conspiracy-cheating, was the worst, most public attempt at deliberate conspiracy-cheating ever conceived.

There is discontent at the way some rules seem to be applied more severely to Arsenal, the silly little stuff like delaying or fiddling about with restarts. But then again, if you make the game about that, if you plan to play on the margins, and successfully so, more stuff might happen in that place while you’re doing it.

Arteta has also played the role of arms-length rage conjurer expertly, has gone from rarely commenting on referees to heartfelt and carefully targeted critic. The Sunderland penalty award was a first opportunity to unload on the refereeing backlash to Arsenal’s tactics, to launch his pre-prepared defence; and to point out something demonstrably true. Referees have lost control of this, because the game has got beyond them.

In many ways this was a perfect storm for Arteta. Not just a decision that didn’t matter, because the penalty was saved. But a decision that was clearly incorrect too, a chance to get your lobbying in while very obviously in the right.

There will be more of this as the season plays out, as Arsenal work to preserve the advantages they have made for themselves in close quarters, tactical attack and defence. Factor in that masterful turn at a press conference j’accuse, and Saturday was a significant win in more ways than one.

Sports.title: Lewis Dunk’s showstopper helps five-star Brighton to rout 10-man Coventry
Sports.content:
The bare facts are bleak: Coventry City are only the second team in Premier League history to lose their first four games of the season ­without scoring a goal. “And yet …” will be the enduring message from Frank ­Lampard to his players.

And yet they have caused prob­lems for opposition teams. And yet they have already faced three of the top flight’s European contingent. And yet they are not altogether playing that badly – the Brighton goalkeeper Bart ­Verbruggen being named player of the match can attest to that. But Coventry des­perately need a point, or even a goal, to give their ­confidence a much-needed boost. It does not take long for a promoted club’s relegation fears to turn to reality.

Goals from Charalampos Kostoulas, Malick Yalcouyé, Lewis Dunk – especially – and Yasin Ayari were all moments of individual brilliance. But there was also a sense of Coventry self-destruction, with no complaints from Lampard over Taiwo Awoniyi’s red card for an elbow into Maxim De Cuyper’s face, nor the penalty conceded by Bobby Thomas for Pascal Gross to score the ­visitors’ third. There are also legitimate questions to be asked of Lampard’s decision to maintain an attacking approach even after the sending off.

“It’s a difficult scoreline and it’s not easy at home,” Lampard said. “The first half was pretty good, we created some chances, better chances and we had them under a lot of pressure. Then a mistake to make it 2-0 and the red card makes it very difficult.

“It feels very difficult to take the result, but a lot of circumstances that you can reflect on and say: ‘If, and if, and if.’ We need to be honest about that – we need to take chances in this league. It’s not a nice feeling.”

The scoreline certainly lent weight to Fabian Hürzeler’s insistence that Brighton have no attacking concerns despite Danny Welbeck’s summer departure. Brighton have scored more goals and created more big chances than any other club in the Premier League this season – indeed, they have never started a top‑flight campaign with more goals.

“It’s not about having one good goalscorer,” Hürzeler said. “It’s about the flexibility of having many goalscorers and a lot of players who have this desire to score. We were very efficient today and quite ruthless at the right moments in front of goal.”

That was certainly true, beginning with a moment of mastery from ­Kostoulas to break the deadlock, when the Greek teenager showed great poise to control an aerial ball with his foot, nod it between two defenders and then fire into the bottom corner.

That Brighton were not already behind by then was thanks to ­Verbruggen, who produced two excellent saves to deny Jack Rudoni, when palming a volley and a header to safety.

Lampard publicly urged his ­players to “have belief” during the half‑time interval, but then followed two ­minutes that instantly extinguished Coventry’s hopes.

View image in fullscreen Frank Lampard endures another glum day in the Premier League with Coventry. Photograph: Mike Egerton/PA

First came Brighton’s second goal, when Yalcouyé was played in behind the Coventry defence, and the Ivorian’s pace kept all at bay before calmly slotting past Carl Rushworth.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Moments later, the hosts were reduced to 10 men. At first glance, contact appeared accidental between Awoniyi and De Cuyper. But, to the refe­ree Tony Harrington’s credit, he spotted the Nigerian had led with his elbow, prompting a straight red card. To compound matters, the stadium announcer chose that period to tell fans that train cancellations meant there would be no departures from the stadium for 90 minutes after the final whistle.

Thomas’s challenge to bring down Kostoulas inside his own box was as clear a penalty as will be awarded all season and Gross duly stuck the spotkick into the bottom corner.

By the time Dunk sealed the rout with the finest strike of his career – smashed into the top corner from 35 yards – the mass exodus had already begun. It was an outrageous hit, with Dunk saying: “I shocked myself, but it was lovely.”

That was followed in injury time by another excellent finish, this time from Ayari, curled from range into the ­bottom corner.

The only other team to lose their first four Premier League games without scoring were Crystal Palace in 2017‑18. Palace finished 11th that season, but need to pull the emergency Roy Hodgson cord. ­Coventry will hope he is not required here.

Sports.title: European football: Kane helps Bayern edge Elversberg, Sassuolo stun Juventus
Sports.content:
Harry Kane scored his first Bundesliga goal of the season to help Bayern Munich edge to a 2-1 win at promoted Elversberg on Sunday. Handed the captain’s armband with skipper Manuel Neuer rested, Kane scored with 18 minutes remaining to break a 1-1 deadlock and put the defending champions on track for victory.

Bayern had taken the lead through teenage Germany winger Lennart Karl, but Elversberg – who had won their opening two matches in their maiden top-flight campaign – levelled things up just after the hour mark thanks to a stunning curling effort from Maurice Krattenmacher.

Kane scored 36 league goals last campaign, but after drawing a blank in his first two matches he told Dazn: “That’s football – sometimes you have to wait more than you’d have expected. It was nice to get the goal and the three points. It’s a tough place so we’re happy with the win. We probably haven’t reached our top level yet, but it’s still early days.”

RB Leipzig bounced back from their midweek Champions League defeat at Como by thumping strugglers Hamburg 5-0 at home. The Norway winger Antonio Nusa was the best of the bunch for the hosts, scoring one goal and setting up two more, including one for Christopher Nkunku, his first since returning to Leipzig in August.

Tidiam Gomis, Willi Orban and Rômulo also got on the scoresheet for Leipzig, who climbed to fifth in the table with the victory. Hamburg’s third heavy defeat in a row leaves the six-times German champions bottom of the table with a -12 goal difference.

In Italy Juventus suffered a 3-2 defeat after a frantic finish at Sassuolo on Sunday. Sassuolo broke the deadlock in the 65th minute when Nemanja Matic slipped a precise ⁠pass into the area for Sebastiano Esposito, who finished coolly.

Juventus levelled in the 82nd ​minute after Sassuolo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric misjudged a cross, ‌allowing Edon Zhegrova to tap ‌into an empty net. The hosts retook the lead through Scottish striker Kieron Bowie, who curled a first-time effort into the corner in the 89th minute.

Zhegrova appeared to have rescued a point for Juventus when he fired home from the edge of the area in stoppage time, but Sassuolo had the final say. Four minutes into injury time, Vasilije Adzic curled a superb finish into the far corner to seal victory for Alberto Aquilani’s side with virtually the ‌last kick of the game.

View image in fullscreen Sassuolo celebrate after Vasilije Adzic’s dramatic stoppage-time winner against Juventus. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters

Napoli ended a three-match losing run with a ⁠1-0 home win over ⁠Bologna. Midfielder Stanislav Lobotka turned in a second-half winner after Arthur Theate’s early header for the visitors was ruled offside by VAR. Elsewhere, Lassana Coulibaly scored twice as Lecce earned a 3-2 home win over Monza. Inter host Udinese, Como entertain Parma and Roma travel to Torino on Monday evening.

In Spain, Barcelona continued their perfect start to the ⁠season with a hard-fought 4-2 La Liga victory over Levante in Valencia ⁠on Sunday. Barça struck twice within the first 19 minutes, their goals coming from Xavi Espart and Lamine Yamal.

Just 42 ‌seconds into the second half, Barcelona were awarded ‌a penalty, won and converted by Lamine Yamal. An errant pass from Espart allowed Levante forward Iván Romero ‌to round goalkeeper Joan García and pass the ball into the net ​with 12 minutes to go.

With two minutes remaining, Roger Brugue burst through multiple Barcelona challenges to score a second for Levante, but the hosts’ hopes of an unlikely comeback were definitively ​ended ​by a mazy run ​and finish from Karim Adeyemi ​in the ‌93rd minute.

View image in fullscreen Lamine Yamal (right) celebrates with Raphinha after scoring his first goal against Levante. Photograph: Biel Aliño/EPA

Atlético Madrid scored three late goals ​to beat Real Sociedad 3-0, as new ​signings Alejandro Grimaldo and Jonathan David scored their ​first goals since joining the club.

The visitors took charge of a dull encounter when Grimaldo netted an 84th-minute penalty, ​before David doubled their lead ‌on ​the break six minutes later. Giuliano ​Simeone added a third in the 95th minute to complete the scoring for Atlético, who were without Julián Alvarez and Pablo Barrios due to muscle injuries.

Adrian Nino’s late goal rescued a 1-1 draw for Málaga against Celta Vigo, who had dominated the game at Balaidos. Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang scored his fifth goal in as many games as Deportivo A Coruña fought back to draw 1-1 with Getafe.

Ferran Torres kept up his scoring form as Paris Saint-Germain won their first Ligue 1 match of the season at the fourth attempt, edging to a 1-0 victory against Brest.

Torres took five minutes to put the visitors ahead, picking up ⁠a loose ball in midfield and passing to João Neves. The ball was worked to Ousmane Dembélé, whose back heel into Torres’ path gave him time and space to bend a low shot into the corner.

Torres has now netted ⁠six goals in five outings since moving to the European champions, who move up to seventh after starting their league campaign with two draws and a defeat.

Lille moved top of the table on goal difference with a 2-0 triumph over Troyes, with Ethan Mbappé adding a late second after Tiago Santos’s opener. Lens fought back from two goals down ‌to draw 2-2 at another promoted side, Le Mans.

Sports.title: Lauren James revels in free role as Chelsea show ‘respect’ by scoring five past Manchester United
Sports.content:
A swaggering Chelsea cast off any suggestion that they had lost the ability to kill off games, putting five goals past a worryingly lacklustre and lackadaisical Manchester United.

Sonia Bompastor, the Chelsea manager, said: “When you have the opportunity to really hurt a team, the best way to respect them is to score as many goals as you can, to create as many opportunities as you can.

“Of course, it’s never easy to see the other team or the other manager concede five goals because if I was the other team, I would be really sad. For me, showing respect to the opponent is having that desire and mentality to score as many goals as possible. That’s the difference between the great teams and the good teams.”

United’s players and fans may have preferred disrespect if that is the case. Instead, it was another bruising result for the new manager, Eva Olid, and her side after an underwhelming performance in their 2-1 defeat against London City Lionesses in the opening game of the season.

Olid needed a result to give her some breathing room and her team some confidence, having had just three weeks to get used to one another before the start of the season, and this early into a project there has to be some grace.

For their opponents this game had been talked about as something of a must‑win after the Blues were held to a 1-1 draw by Aston Villa on the opening weekend despite dominating that match.

View image in fullscreen Keira Walsh scores Chelsea’s side's second goal from the edge of the box. Photograph: James Gill/Danehouse/Getty Images

To some extent the concern over Chelsea’s profligacy did not need to be too deep. They were at their creative best against Villa and were without the injured centre-forwards Melvine Malard and Mayra Ramírez while Aggie Beever-Jones, who led the line against the Midlands side, had not scored in the Women’s Super League since September 2025. The off-target Beever-Jones was relegated to the bench for the trip to United. Instead, Lauren James and Sjoeke Nüsken worked away interchangeably up front.

The visitors were similarly fluid in other areas too, and that flexibility was super effective. Chelsea were unpredictable and James’s free‑to‑roam role put their star talent at the centre of everything.

Lucy Bronze’s marauding forward yielded the opener when she sent a looping ball over the top and Dominique Janssen should have been first to it, but the United defender misread the fall of the ball and a stalking Wieke Kaptein nipped it away from her. The Dutch midfielder squared to Nüsken who fired in from close range.

The second goal, which eluded them against Villa, arrived just over 10 minutes later. A diving header from the new recruit Andrea Medina cleared a cross whipped in from the left but the hard-working Bronze was there to meet it, clipping it into the path of Keira Walsh, who took a step and powered in from the edge of the box.

The hosts’ heads dropped, which left their manager unhappy. “In football we know anything can happen,” Olid said. “You can be losing 2-0 and can end up winning. I don’t like the heads down. Heads up and we have to continue. Everything is about confidence.”

A very brief brighter spell for United after the break was snuffed out by the visiting team and James finally got on the scoresheet after the hour, latching on to Walsh’s defence‑splitting pass and shrugging off Janssen before sending a low drive into the net.

Chelsea’s fourth goal rubbed salt in for a very wounded United side. Janssen, under no pressure, failed to respond to an ambitious burst from Kaptein and the Chelsea midfielder pickpocketed the centre-back and slipped the ball wide to the onrushing Ellie Carpenter, whose first effort was kept out by Phallon Tullis‑Joyce but her follow-up found the net.

Bronze then added to United’s misery during the final minute of added time, hammering the ball in after Walsh knocked a corner back into the melee in the six-yard box.

It became a training exercise for Chelsea and the hosts failed in their attempts to limit the damage. Things look as if they will get worse for Olid’s side before they get better, with a trip to the Emirates Stadium to play Arsenal coming up next weekend, but Olid said she will not divert from the style of football she wants the team to commit to playing.

“If you start changing, then you are never going to build what you want to build,” she said. “It’s a process. I know it’s so hard, the process, because this beginning is hard. Nobody wants to lose games, but we have to be faithful to what we want to do, because I think that long term will give us the wins.”

Sports.title: WSL roundup: Arsenal rue misses in Palace draw, Manchester City crush Villa
Sports.content:
Arsenal were left to rue 30 missed chances after dropping points in a 0-0 draw against Crystal Palace at the Emirates Stadium.

The Gunners hit the target nine times and had almost 80% possession but could not convert their superiority into goals. Promoted Palace put on a resilient performance, with the goalkeeper Pauline Peyraud-Magnin batting away attempts from Alessia Russo, Chloe Kelly and Mariona Caldentey to earn another clean sheet.

The reigning champions, Manchester City, continued their winning start to the campaign with a dominant 4-1 victory against Aston Villa. Jade Rose broke the deadlock for City in the early stages, tapping home after Akane Okuma failed to claim a corner. Assisted by Khadija Shaw, Mary Fowler doubled the advantage with a low-driven strike into the bottom-right of the net.

Amalie Vangsgaard gave Andrée Jeglertz and his players a fright after converting Chasity Grant’s pass in the 42nd minute, but Shaw returned to the scoresheet after half-time to restore the two-goal cushion. City wrapped up the victory in added time when Lauren Hemp’s strike was deflected in by Mathilde Harviken.

View image in fullscreen Khadija Shaw scores Manchester City’s third goal in their 4-1 win at Villa Park. Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/Reuters

Brighton came from two goals down to snatch a last-minute equaliser at Birmingham City. The promoted hosts took an early lead through Oceane Hurtre, who capitalised on a lapse in concentration from Caitlin Hayes before running into the box and slotting past Chiamaka Nnadozie.

Lily Crosthwaite made it two in the second half with a low driven shot across the goalkeeper, but Brighton gathered momentum when Olivia García came off the bench to close the gap in the 77th minute. As Birmingham attempted to hold on for the win, Kiko Seike raced into the box with just a few seconds remaining and made the most of a small gap between Sophie Baggaley and the near post to score.

At Goodison Park, Charlton fell to a 1-0 defeat by Everton following an own goal and two red cards. After a goalless first half, things quickly went downhill for the promoted side when Ashleigh Neville saw red for a high boot which caught Ruby Mace. With 13 minutes of normal time to play, the visitors found themselves behind when Holly McNamara’s cross deflected off the leg of Leighanne Robe and into the net. In the latter stages, Charlton went down to nine players after the substitute Hawa Cissoko received two yellow cards in quick succession.

Liverpool came from behind to earn a 1-1 draw against Tottenham thanks to a 60th-minute header from Aurelie Csillag. Spurs took the lead just before half-time when Signe Gaupset’s effort was deflected in off the foot of Liverpool’s Sam Kerr. The hosts levelled things up at the hour-mark after Csillag got in front of Lize Kop to head home Fuka Nagano’s cross.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo calls for lifetime bans in Saudi Pro League after Diogo Jota chants
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo said that fans who appeared to ⁠make chants referencing his former teammate Diogo Jota at Rúben Neves during a Saudi ⁠Pro League ⁠match ​should be banned for life from football stadiums.

The chants occurred on Saturday during ⁠a fixture between Al-Taawoun and Neves’s side, Al-Hilal, in Buraydah, Saudi Arabia.

Jota died last year in a car crash in Zamora, ​north-western Spain, along with ‌his brother André ‌Silva. A close friend of Jota, Neves was a ‌pallbearer at his funeral.

Footage filmed from the stands during the match and circulated on social media appeared to show supporters chanting “Jota”. The shouts attracted the attention of Neves, who pointed to his eye and ‌then up to the sky in response. Passing through the mixed zone after the game, ​Neves said: “I hope they don’t go to pray afterwards.”

In response to an Instagram post showing the footage, Ronaldo commented from his personal account. “The league must take ⁠action and punish this kind of fan behaviour,” he wrote. “This ​is no longer football, ​and there have to be limits. People ​who behave ‌like this should ​never ​be allowed to enter a stadium again.“

The game finished 6-0 to Al-Hilal, with Neves playing 75 minutes before being substituted.

Reuters has contacted Al-Taawoun and Al-Hilal for comment.

Sports.title: Rangers lay down Old Firm marker to send Celtic packing from Scottish League Cup
Sports.content:
Derek McInnes has endured a much‑scrutinised start to life at Ibrox but the Rangers manager got the old ground bouncing here as his side dominated Celtic in front of an all-blue crowd to decide the first Old Firm encounter of the season.

Against a backdrop of bouncing techno from the tannoy, Rangers fans celebrated three memorable goals in a thumping League Cup win. A brace for the captain, Dan Neil, bookended Kevin Kelsy’s second‑half finish to put Martin O’Neill’s side down with relative ease. It also showcased a nascent identity for McInnes’s side, one defined by unbending physical commitment and lots and lots of sprinting. The quality of the football may have been patchy, but the commitment was enough to get the 51,212 home fans at the top of their voices.

With away fans banned from Old Firm fixtures this season after the pitch invasion that followed a Scottish Cup tie in March, the atmosphere was always likely to be partisan, if perhaps less heated than is customary. Before the match there was a brisk trade on both Graeme Souness flags and boiled sweets. Inside the ground the Union Bears ultras unveiled a tifo showcasing the apparently resonant moment when Rangers’ Ian Ferguson grabbed Celtic’s Mike Galloway by the lapels during a clash in 1993. A deep cut of a banner, it did a good job of setting the tone for what was to follow.

McInnes said: “I’m delighted. The performance we gave today was the one required to overcome a team like Celtic. I thought the game demanded the players’ full attention and I’m delighted they’ve managed to deliver that. We’ve seen the strength of the club today and it does the players no harm to understand what this match means to so many people.”

Rangers went about the match with an intensity that Celtic struggled to equal from the off, some of their players looking distinctly overawed by the occasion. The former England goalkeeper Sam Johnstone was among them, flapping at two early openings, but he could do nothing about the opening goal when it arrived in the 22nd minute. After a Celtic counter broke down Rangers immediately turned play around with a long ball to the Celtic area where Cameron Carter‑Vickers failed to properly clear. Kelsy picked up the loose ball, slipped it to Neil and the captain, signed on a free transfer from Sunderland in the summer, placed an excellent shot just inside Johnstone’s left‑hand post.

After seizing the advantage, Rangers went on to dominate the second half and a second goal appeared inevitable. It duly arrived when a free-kick from the impressive James Penrice was flicked on by Ryan Naderi to the back post where Kelsy clipped his effort around the keeper and inside the left-hand post.

View image in fullscreen Kevin Kelsy lashes in Rangers’ second goal around the hour. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Neil then took matters into his own hands with a quarter of an hour remaining as he controlled a loose ball on the edge of the Celtic area and wrapped a shot into the top corner to unleash delirium in the Copland Stand. “I haven’t scored many goals in my career, so to come away with a brace is immense,” Neil said.

It was perhaps just as well for O’Neill that his supporters had been denied access to this match. Celtic began with a calmness that suggested confidence. Ultimately it was more likely to have reflected timidity. The Bhoys were unable to get a foot on the ball at all in the second half, and the big-money signing Kasper Høgh looked lost at the tip of the Celtic attack before he was substituted on 65 minutes.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“We were well beaten in the end, on the day we were second best,” O’Neill said. “There has to be a realisation how big this game is, it’s still one of the great fixtures in European football if not the world. We’ve got to know that. We have to learn from it. Hopefully it’s a wake‑up call.”

Rangers will play Aberdeen in the semi-finals, but McInnes was still being asked about Rangers’ stuttering start to the season after this match, generating the timeless response: “Why are you pissing on my chips?”

After this result the Rangers manager can at least look forward with optimism and he could be set to unleash the spirit of Ian Ferguson again as early as next weekend when a second Old Firm derby awaits, this time at Celtic Park.

Sports.title: Allowing Erling Haaland's match-winning Manchester derby goal was a MISTAKE, admits referees' body, after Michael Carrick's side fumed over baffling decision
Sports.content:
Referees’ bosses last night admitted it was a mistake not to rule out Erling Haaland’s controversial winning goal in the Old Trafford derby. Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick was furious after Haaland’s strike gave City’s 10 men a 1-0 win, and defender Lisandro Martinez branded the decision an ‘injustice’. VAR official Matt Donohue incorrectly allowed the goal to stand even though Enzo Fernandez was offside when he challenged Martinez for the ball in front of goal, on the basis that City’s new £125million signing did not touch it. However, the rules state that a player in an offside position will be penalised if they impact an opponent by attempting to play the ball. A statement from Pro Ref confirmed: 'Following the incident in the 60th minute of Sunday's Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Manchester City at Old Trafford, we can provide clarification regarding Erling Haaland's awarded goal. 'The on-field decision was offside against Erling Haaland – that was checked by VAR and he was found to be in an onside position. Erling Haaland has put Manchester City ahead in the derby after a VAR check ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/V0DCwryhFy — Sky Sports Premier League (@SkySportsPL) September 13, 2026 Pro Ref have apologised to Manchester United after Erling Haaland's controversial goal in the Manchester derby was allowed to stand Haaland's goal was given after a VAR review, with it having originally been ruled offside However, Enzo Fernandez was in an offside position and attempted to go for the ball 'In the same attack, it was established that Enzo Fernandez did not play the ball and therefore that makes any offside offence subjective, however, on this occasion, the VAR did not recognise the likely impact of his position and should have recommended an on-field review. 'Contact has been made with Manchester United this evening to acknowledge what we deem is an error of judgement. A review of the incident will take place.' While Haaland celebrated a record ninth Premier League goal in the Manchester derby, Martinez was fuming. 'It's the best league in the world, you have the best teams in the world, the best players in the world, and now we have to go home with this injustice,' he said. 'I think it was offside. What I can't understand is the rules. He (Fernandez) was there, in front of me, and I went to him. So that's why Haaland was free at the back. 'It's so hard because you lose a derby and you lose three points at home. Every season they're coming to our club and explaining the rules for an hour-and-a-half. They look so confident, and then after that five or six people are making these kind of mistakes. It's unacceptable.' United head coach Michael Carrick was just as upset as Martinez, saying: 'I really don't get it. 'I can't understand how they're trying to help referees by putting so many layers behind them – with so many people, so many bodies, so many screens – and you're not interfering with play because you've thrown yourself at the ball six yards from goal and nearly touched it. 'It's worrying if that's really how the game's seen by those who are officiating it.' When it was mentioned to Carrick that Pro Ref have issued apologies in the past, he replied sarcastically: 'That would be great, I can't wait for that one! It's best left, I think. I don't really know how you go and get another explanation on that one.' Join the discussion Should controversial VAR decisions be overturned after the match to restore fairness? A furious Lisandro Martinez claimed that United were the victims of an 'injustice' At the time of the incident, Gary Neville had been left confused on Sky Sports' commentary and criticised the decision, insisting the officials had got things wrong. He said: 'I will need the offside explained to me. The officials will be nervous about this goal. 'When they look back on this, they will recognise they got this wrong. The question is does Fernandez, who is offside, stop Martinez getting the ball? He does.' When reminded that the rules state a player can still be offside even if they don't touch the ball, Neville replied: 'They're the words that I think – emphatically – mean we will see an apology from Pro Ref. 'There is no doubt that Enzo is attempting to play the ball and putting Lisandro Martinez off. 'It's a really strange one. They'll recognise they got that wrong.' Before Pro Ref's apology, the Premier League Match Centre had attempted to explain the reasoning for the goal being awarded. On their X account, they wrote: 'VAR checked the referee’s call of no goal for offside – and determined that Haaland was in an onside position and recommended that the goal was awarded. 'The VAR also deemed that while in an offside position, Fernandez didn’t play the ball.' Meanwhile, Foden was shown a straight red card by referee Michael Oliver when he retaliated to Fernandes kicking him in the back while he was on the ground by lashing out at the United captain. City boss Enzo Maresca said: 'Phil Foden's red card is red card, but I also think it's a red card for Bruno. To win a game with 10 players is special, but it is even more special when it is Manchester derby.'

Sports.title: Goading, running himself into the ground and feeding off Man United distain - Enzo Fernandez showed what £125m buys you and his innate desire to win at all costs is gold dust for City
Sports.content:
A goal up and a man light, there is a specific type of person required when the heat of a derby tumble dryer is dialled up that little bit higher. Certainly not a shrinker. Probably the sort of person who might goad opposition supporters by cupping his ears and pulling a frankly ridiculously stupid face in a World Cup semi-final. That guy. The sort who craves and feeds off rival disdain. The sort of guy who, after a 22-minute masterclass following Erling Haaland's disputed winner, might grin his way off the Old Trafford pitch when substituted. The sort of guy who will enjoy playing the villain at Premier League stadiums all year. He may have joined on deadline day for a British record fee but Sunday was when Enzo Fernandez arrived as a Manchester City player, the exact personality Enzo Maresca needed to engineer an away victory that can serve as a springboard for a new project given the circumstances. It wasn't necessarily the buying of two free kicks in quick succession just inside Manchester United territory but those symbolised the management of the lead. It wasn't intercepting Diogo Dalot's errant pass and driving City forward 25 yards, ending in a foul, but that symbolised a determination. It wasn't riling up Harry Maguire during a mild flashpoint, nor was it almost bending in a second goal from outside the box. It was all of these things and more that made Fernandez such an integral aspect of a win that saw Maresca dancing down the touchline like a certain Portuguese all those years ago. There is a specific type of person required when the heat of a derby tumble dryer is dialled up - and that person is Enzo Fernandez At the time that the fourth official's board beamed Fernandez's number – 17, formerly Kevin De Bruyne's – nobody had covered more ground than his 10.2kilometres. This was a shift alongside the commanding Elliot Anderson, that was non-negotiable if City were to emerge with a positive result. Nobody broke up play more than Fernandez and, given United's penchant for fast breaks through central areas, City's back four are under significantly more stress without that. They are the little things that add up to £125million and that fee buys you somebody who can do everything, with the Argentine's role before Phil Foden's sending off more attacking and more lateral. As evidenced by the assist for Haaland in Porto on Tuesday, he fancies that side of the box-to-box role. 'Look at our midfield, if there is something they like to do, it is to fight,' Haaland said with a twinkle down the Old Trafford tunnel. He meant the collective, although his body language suggested a clear focus on one of them specifically. We all know who that is. And for Fernandez, this has been a rewarding first fortnight in sky blue, while the animosity among those in royal blue shows no real sign of abating. There has been amusement in City circles over the past few days at noises emanating from Chelsea about two written transfer requests handed in by Fernandez to force a move and the accusation that he told the hierarchy that his relationships with team-mates had deteriorated, seemingly beyond repair. A gentle bemusement as to why, some time after the transfer window closed, the 25-year-old continues to be such a hot topic of discussion. Especially after Xabi Alonso had praised his attitude and application after the mid-August deadline to complete a £120m deal passed without incident. It has been a summer – nay, a year – of blue on blue in this respect. Acrimony between Chelsea and City over Maresca, for starters. Then the saga attached to the failed attempt to lure Bunny Shaw away from City amid a reported £1m contract on the table. And to cap it, losing their best player to City as well. This after asking Hugo Viana to walk away from a deal to sign Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille during negotiations for Fernandez and suggesting a swap of Nico O'Reilly for Malo Gusto – suggestions that are denied by Chelsea, who lost last season's FA Cup final to Antoine Semenyo's clever flick. Chelsea – who in April announced the highest pre-tax losses (£262.4m) in Premier League history – have made it known that they could have pulled the plug on Fernandez's move north after their own pursuit of Monaco's Lamine Camara collapsed. Fernandez, who clashed with Harry Maguire, was described as 'unbelievable' by his manager, Enzo Maresca They didn't and that is to Maresca's benefit. 'Enzo was unbelievable,' he said at Old Trafford, Fernandez right in the middle of the winner after standing in an offside position, a contentious moment. City could have avoided the broader contention with Chelsea, having watched Fernandez extensively while at River Plate before he joined Benfica in 2022. So it is not only Maresca's whim that has demanded he join. What they have in him is this innate desire to win at all costs. There has been an argument that since the Treble campaign, City have lacked that bit of extra competitive spirit, the darker arts. The sort of player who burrows under the skin of those who love to hate him.

Sports.title: 'I wasn't welcome here but it's great to be back': Sheffield Wednesday legend DAVID HIRST is where he belongs - enjoying pints and pies with fans in his brand new bar at Hillsborough
Sports.content:
First there was an invitation to dinner, a handshake and a discussion about the protocol of nicknames when David Hirst met David Storch.

'Is it David or Dave or is it Hirsty?' the American millionaire plotting to buy Sheffield Wednesday wanted to know. 'Hirsty's good enough for me and then we'll know who you're talking to,' replied the local hero, scorer 149 goals across 11 years at Hillsborough from 1986.

'Well, that's great, because my name's Storchy.'

This was March, soon after Storch's Arise consortium became the preferred bidder to buy the Owls out of administration after a ruinous decade under the ownership of Dejphon Chansiri.

When they met again, it was at the West Bromwich Albion game in May.

'A fantastic carnival atmosphere exactly how it should be every game at Hillsborough,' says Hirst. 'He came into the guest lounge, and everybody is Mr Chairman this and that, and I'm like, 'Hey, Storchy, over here, mate'.

Sheffield Wednesday legend David Hirst is back at the club and in a bar bearing his name

Hirst was invited back from exile under the new ownership of American David Storch

Storch is helping to rebuild Wednesday in League One after a ruinous decade under the ownership of Dejphon Chansiri, pictured

'Even to me it felt a bit wrong, but he did give me permission to use it.'

Wednesday are reborn under Storch. Not only on the pitch, where Henrik Pedersen's team sit top of League One after six games but more importantly off it where the new owners have embraced the club's history and the city's heritage to re-energise one of the great clubs of northern football.

'We met just before the takeover in a little restaurant in Sheffield,' recalls Hirst. 'We had a great chat about plans they had if the takeover came to fruition. I was sold from the start.

'It was all about reconnecting and finding out who and what they needed to know to get our club back where it belongs.

'They've come with such a positive attitude into what was to be honest an absolute s***storm.'

Besides installing a serious executive team and recruiting 18 new players, including the return of Barry Bannan, the new owners restored to 70s owl as the club crest and struck a kit deal with Umbro to produce a classic home kit with blue-and-white stripes and black shorts.

Another popular move involved luring Hirst out of exile and back to Hillsborough as club ambassador.

A what better way to tempt a Yorkshireman who likes a pint than to give him his own bar in the heart of the South Stand.

Sheffield Wednesday are top of League One after recruiting 18 new players, including bringing back Barry Bannan to the club

A bar has been named in honour of Hirst, scorer 149 goals across 11 years at Hillsborough from 1986

Hirst had walked away from the club after a row surrounding his son George, now at Stoke, in 2018 after an unseemly contract dispute with Chansiri

'I don't know how the other lads felt but I wasn't welcome after my previous adventures with Mr Chansiri,' says Hirst, alluding to the row surrounding his son George, now at Stoke, in 2018 after an unseemly contract dispute.

'Things were well documented from one side and that was Mr Chansiri's side. He embellished and elaborated on things that weren't true and it wasn't something I was prepared to slug out in public, so I walked away.

'We weren't the bitter ones. We understood George had to leave through situations beyond our control. I was still a Wednesday fan. I still watched from afar. I'm a blue, George is a blue.

'Thankfully it worked out well for both of us and now it's great to be back.

'It was a no-brainer for me. I'd been away for 10 years and to come back and the welcome I received… the only thing missing was the fatted calf.'

Hirst in his natural habitat. Hirsty's Social opened at the start of this season. It is a casual corporate vibe with the focus on pies and ale rather than prawn sandwiches, and with fans mingling, chatting, keeping an eye on the live sport rather than wedding reception table service, all of which goes down well with the man with his name above the door.

'Come on, get the tellies on,' shouts Hirst as he strolls into his bar three hours before kick-off on Saturday against Wigan with news from Edgbaston that Joe Root has played only to be reprieved by a no-ball call in the Test against Pakistan and keen to catch up on the Solheim Cup latest.

He is engulfed by requests for selfies and autographs, resisting offers to buy him another pint. Well, some of them. He greets those he knows with a bear hug. 'Anyone who was here against Bromley, yes I am wearing the same clothes,' admits Hirst as he addresses his audience. 'Yes, I have washed them before you ask, but we all liked the 7-2 win, so I thought I'd give it another go.'

Hirst, 40 years on from joining the Owls, believes the club is more Sheffield centric than it has been in years under its American owners

Last month marked 40 years since he joined the Owls from Barnsley for £250,000. 'Thanks for the reminder,' the 58-year-old rolls his eyes. 'I've been here so long I know virtually everybody in the stadium.

'It's nice to come and have a drink with some of them and chat about yesteryear or what's happening going forward.

'We've had a good start. If we'd got beat every game and it might be different but everybody coming in here has a smile on their face.'

The room is dominated by an enormous 'WEDNESDAY' sign which once adorned the back of the West Stand. It was found unused and unloved beneath the stand and has been repurposed to hang over the bar.

There are plans to decorate the walls with Hirst's old shirts and photographs and other memorabilia, including his original contract, also unearthed among the piles of old documents.

Brecht Vierstraete, an artist and a Wednesday fan from Belgium, appears with a gift, a framed portrait of Hirst who promises it will go on display.

Among his guests are former players Mel Sterland and Rodger Wylde. Somehow Wylde topples from a small stage during a brief Q&A session on the microphone and returns smiling and thankfully unhurt and tells the American owners they're going to be need a bigger stage, only to be admonished by Hirst for bringing the x-rated language of the dressing room into his bar.

The soundtrack is peppered with Sheffield music. There's beer from the nearby Thornbridge brewery and fine pies by local bakers Jackson's. The logos and emblems stitched into the carpets have all been designed by creative agency Peter & Paul in Kelham Island, a mile or so from Hillsborough.

Sheffield pop artist Pete McKee presented Storch with an original painting at the first home game of the season against Bradford. 'This place has had three licks of paint since 1966, and now we're getting murals and paintings on the wall,' says Hirst.

The McKee painting, which now hangs in the boardroom, is of Storch in his Wednesday stripes, meta shades and a garland around his neck, an image taken from the West Brom game when the new owner walked out to tell a full house he had completed the takeover and convinced the EFL to waive the 15-point penalty they expected this season.

As far as first impressions go, it was emphatic. Hillsborough erupted and the aviation tycoon had lift off although Wednesday's identity under its new American owners is more Sheffield centric than it has been for years.

It is one of the vital differences. When Chansiri bought the club in 2015, he spent heavily on players and reached the play-off final, one win from returning to the Premier League, but they lost the game, broke the EFL's financial rules, suffered points deductions and descended into crisis.

By the time the administrators moved in, it was an empty shell of a club.

'I've seen Storchy and other members of his staff in and around the city,' says Hirst. 'They've been at Sunday League football, non-league football, in the city shaking hands and speaking to people. That never happened before.

'With Mr Chansiri, it was his box and that was that. There was no input or output. He ran things the way he saw fit and the guy spent a hell of a lot of money, but you can't buy dreams like that.

Hirst is in his natural habitat in the new bar, which has a casual corporate vibe with the focus on pies and ale, as well as mingling and chatting with fans

'He thought you could come from nowhere and run a football club his way. It turned out spending a vast amount of money wasn't the right way. The right way is to get the knowledge around you and listen to the right people.'

Hirst's attire fails to inspire another win so the Owls settle for a goalless draw against Wigan, enough to keep them top and remind everyone about the dangers of getting carried away.

Wednesday are building from scratch under strict EFL spending restrictions.

'Let's not kid ourselves,' says Hirst. 'We were weeks if not days from going under. We've an old ground that needs some care. They're working on it.

'Things are not going to be perfect this season on or off the field. Hopefully, it's good but I come from the real world, and I've been around football for long enough to know there's no magic wand in this game.'

Sports.title: Furious Man United fans tell club 'the way you treat us is a disgrace': Supporters unveil protest banner ahead of Manchester derby amid huge protests in front of onlooking Sir Jim Ratcliffe at Old Trafford
Sports.content:
Manchester United fans have displayed a solitary banner in the Stretford End at Sunday's Old Trafford derby branding the club a 'disgrace'.

The Red Army opted not to have any other flags or banners at the game against Manchester City in protest over 'the recent behaviour of the club'.

Fans group The 1958 staged a demonstration before the game over United's clampdown on ticket touts, which they claim has targeted innocent supporters.

The TRA, who organise and pay for the flags and banners in the Stretford End, issued a statement on Saturday explaining their actions.

It read: 'On Sunday there will be no flag display on the Stretford End. In its place, a single banner will hang above the players' tunnel with a clear message to the owners, directors and decision-making staff at Manchester United: 'The Way You Treat Us is a Disgrace'.

'This isn't a TRA message, it's a message on behalf of every genuine fan group, match-going supporter, supporters' club and fan representative who has either contacted us directly or been negatively impacted by the recent behaviour of the club.

Manchester United fans have displayed a solitary banner in the Stretford End at Sunday's Old Trafford derby branding the club a 'disgrace'

Sir Jim Ratcliffe was watching on amid huge protests from home supporters

Fans group The 1958 staged a demonstration before the game over United's clampdown on ticket touts, which they claim has targeted innocent supporters

The Red Army opted not to have any other flags or banners at the game against Manchester City in protest over 'the recent behaviour of the club'

'It's an honest, heartfelt cry for recognition from the maligned, vilified, and misrepresented beating heart of our football club – the generational match-going supporters.

'Neither is this solely a Manchester United problem, this is a league-wide crisis that should be addressed at every club, regardless of rivalries and history. Without drastic changes, there will be no rivalries in the future vision for football shared by the decision makers.

'Whilst we still advocate for a change in ownership, we believe that there should be a realistic roadmap for any protest if it is to act as a catalyst for change.

'Unless our generational match-going support is given a real voice that is actually listened to, the little that remains of our fan culture will soon be gone forever.

'TRA aren't a protest group, we're an 'atmosphere' group but we've never shied away from making our position clear when we believe not doing so would be to the detriment of the interests of match-going supporters.

'We hope that you'll understand and support our decision and that those of you who are asking for meaningful change and are able to help will stand up and be counted when called upon in the near future.

'Until then, we'll continue to fully back and support the players and manager throughout, starting with the derby on Sunday.'

United revealed the outcome of their ticket tout investigation on Friday, saying that a total of 685 suspicious accounts have been hit with bans for breaching season-ticket rules.

The club claim to have broken up large-scale organised networks involved in touting and denied that innocent fans have been targeted, adding that some examples of unfair treatment of supporters shared on social media are untrue and don't tell the full story.

Sports.title: Tearful Trinity Rodman dashes to New York to see boyfriend Ben Shelton's US Open final heartbreak... just hours after soccer match
Sports.content:
Trinity Rodman made a late dash to be in New York for the end of Ben Shelton's US Open final - only to be left in tears after her boyfriend's loss to Alexander Zverev.

Shelton was chasing a first Grand Slam title but his hopes of ending America's 23-year wait for a man to win the US Open were dashed by the No 1 seed.

Rodman has been a regular in her boyfriend's box during this year's US Open but the soccer star had a match of her own on Sunday afternoon. She missed most of the action as Zverev beat Shelton 6-3 7-6 5-7 6-2. At the end, however, cameras caught Rodman crying inside Arthur Ashe Stadium in the wake of her boyfriend's loss.

She was wearing a Ben Shelton t-shirt and she caught the attention of Zverev following the match. 'Trinity, I thought you had a game today?' Zverev said in his on-court interview.

Rodman, who this year became the highest-paid player in women's soccer, plays for the NWSL's Washington Spirit and they lost to Boston Legacy on Sunday afternoon. That match kicked off at 1pm ET – an hour before the US Open final – with Rodman named in the Spirit starting XI.

Trinity Rodman made a late dash to be in New York for the end of Ben Shelton's US Open final

The Washington Spirit star was in NWSL action against Boston Legacy on Sunday

Shelton was beaten by No 1 seed Alexander Zverev in Sunday's final at Flushing Meadows

'It means everything [that she came],' Shelton said afterwards. 'I knew it was going to be pretty close to impossible to get here, but even just making the effort and trying is insane. She kind of showed up as I was losing, which for her probably sucked.

'But we've made a lot of sacrifices for each other. We've traveled the world to try to support each other when we can. It means a lot.'

He added: 'So many people have showed up for me, and that's what this is all about, being able to share these moments, share these two weeks with my best friends, my family, people I love. That's why I'm out here doing this. That's why I enjoy it so much. That's who I want to get over the line for.'

With Rodman's game finishing shortly after 3pm, there was always a slim chance she could rush to New York in time to catch the end of the final. Flushing Meadows sits only a short drive from LaGuardia Airport, with direct flights from Washington DC taking around an hour.

Earlier this week, the 24-year-old daughter of NBA legend Dennis Rodman was in Shelton's box for his quarterfinal win over Carlos Alcaraz, which finished at 3:33am.

Despite the latest finish in US Open history, the forward made it to Washington Spirit training later that day, driving five hours to arrive in time for the 11am session.

Rodman has been dating Shelton - the No 8 seed - for more than a year, with the couple going public in early 2025.

Sports.title: Kimi Antonelli profits from a Lando Norris mess to win a race he never should have done. The Italian looks unbeatable this season and the chances of a world championship fight look finished
Sports.content:
Change the 'stupid' rules, cried Lando Norris, after this mugging in Madrid. And this is why.

First, every time there is a glimmer of a world championship fight breaking out, a ray of light behind the curtain, Kimi Antonelli closes the shutters.

His latest example of this knack came here, when he won a race he never should have done.

And the clear victim of ill-fortune was Norris, who finished third, a place back from Max Verstappen. For the Briton was in command of the Spanish Grand Prix at its shiny new venue, on the outskirts of the capital as he transformed a fabulous pole position into a lead over the 20-year-old Antonelli of more than six seconds in 15 laps.

Norris's McLaren is now seriously fast. And Norris was, therefore, on the scent of his third win in four races, driving more assuredly than Antonelli, who at least twice ran off the track but was holding on in second place. And, then, a huge stroke of fortune fell Antonelli's way.

This occurred as Lance Stroll's Aston Martin went into the wall, his brakes apparently cooked. A virtual safety car (VSC) was deployed. By this stage Norris was beyond the pit-lane entrance. Antonelli was not, and was called in. He was afforded the cheap stop as the action was slowed and Stroll's machine was cleared.

Kimi Antonelli celebrates on the podium after winning a race he never should have done

A stroke of fortune fell the Italian's way as he strengthened his grip on the championship

Lando Norris had been leading the way before making a mess of a change of rubber

Norris had to wait a lap later, the decisive fact, for his change of rubber. Adding salt to the wound, the stop lasted a yawning 7.0sec. Not the best.

The world champion came out in fifth place and 13sec back from Antonelli. How fortunes change. Norris's chances were extinguished immediately, and it is the Italian who is edging towards the world title at the youngest age ever.

'We didn't do anything that made us lose it and I am not complaining,' said Norris, trying manfully to be as sanguine as he could in the circumstances. 'We were just insanely unlucky. I was the only one of the whole grid who didn't get a chance to do a pit stop.

'I felt like I deserved more.

Asked about the VSC variants, he said: 'It is a stupid rule and the issue has been brought up many times over the years by different drivers. Perhaps you shouldn't be able to pit for a lap or you block the pit entry. There are things that can be done or make it more simple and fairer, but it is part of a wider discussion.

'It is something all drivers would want. It is complicated, but I hope it doesn't happen to anyone again. It is not the way a race should be lost.'

Whatever happens to the rules, or doesn't, Antonelli is rewriting some of Formula One's accepted truths, as he is well on his way to eclipsing the then 23-year-old Sebastian Vettel, the most youthful of title-holders. And this is in only his second season.

The old verity that experience counts super highly and you must bide your time is being ripped up as never before.

Antonelli has won eight times this campaign, including at Monza a week ago in front of his home crowd. He was cheered and rhapsodised, though his success was in a way only compensation for the partisans after Ferrari performed disappointingly.

He has also gained from the affection and favours of his Mercedes team, from boss Toto Wolff down (my assertion, which they deny). Poor George Russell is hardly the chosen one there. But, it has to be admitted, that in all racing teams love is lavished on the faster of every given pair, and that character is the man-child called Kimi. Russell has won just twice in 2026.

Mercedes believe they have found their star, their future, and who can say they are wrong? Antonelli certainly looks unbeatable this season. The arithmetic supports the assertion. His lead over Russell, who finished fifth, is 81 points with nine rounds remaining.

As for Norris? He is 106 points adrift, which leaves him with an uphill task almost as steep as the North Ridge of Everest.

And Lewis Hamilton, who retired six laps in with brake problems, is barely better placed, 101 off the summit. Ferrari are too error-prone and Hamilton is not quite as good as he once was – though he is admittedly rejuvenated this season compared to last – and it will be tough for him to scale the eighth world title he wants to leave as his lifetime's mark.

He clashed with Verstappen on the opening lap. Verstappen passed Hamilton and clawed his way into second place. 'He has to give the place back,' implored the Briton.

Verstappen countered: 'He was out of control.'

Red Bull told Verstappen to yield. He has never rushed to pull out of an arm wrestle, and he gave his race engineer and pal Gianpiero Lambiase a blast of industrial language. 'Mate, what the f*** are you guys going on about?'

After the tough talk, he yielded. But, in a boring race, pretty much devoid of overtaking, Verstappen did hand the place back. But Hamilton was soon plummeting down the field with his technical problems.

'I hit the brake, the car started stopping and then the pedal took a step and, all of a sudden, the car didn't decelerate as fast as it would normally,' he explained.

Charles Leclerc got the other Ferrari home in fourth place, having led for a long period prior to his late stop. Antonelli resumed the lead, coming home 4.3sec ahead of runner-up Verstappen. Norris harried his pal to the line, just 0.7sec back, to clinch the final podium place.

The last words here centre on Antonelli. 'Beautiful work, an absolute masterclass,' eulogised Peter Bonnington, his race engineer.

'Bono', once the voice in Hamilton's ear during his glory days at Mercedes, is chivvying his new student all the way to what now seems to be an inevitable title a few months out of his teens.

Sports.title: Alexander Zverev WINS the US Open: Ben Shelton's American dream ends in brutal fashion... but new champion is slow to realise he'd won!
Sports.content:
Alexander Zverev crushed Ben Shelton’s American dream to become the new US Open champion, downing the home favourite 6-3, 7-6(2), 5-7, 6-2 to spoil the party in New York

The weight of history finally told for Shelton, vying to become the first US man in 23 years to win a Grand Slam. In his majors final debut experience beat narrative, with Shelton’s fightback against the French Open champion too late, and too brief.

Not that Zverev was quick to realise he had even won, moving over to receive what he thought was Shelton's next service game as the Arthur Ashe Stadium erupted around him.

'I thought it was 5-1. I knew I broke him twice, I thought "okay, I'm going to have a relaxed service game here, and then get tight," he joked after the match. 'Teachers always tell you, forget about the score - I forgot about the score, and it helped me.'

Their earlier match-ups, of which Zverev won all five, were a prophecy fulfilled. Zverev, particularly potent against left-handers like the 23-year-old, was the picture of confidence in his own game, so rock-steady he could almost sit back and wait for Shelton to make errors when it counted.

He did. Shelton had walked into Arthur Ashe Stadium, roared in by its partisan crowd, with his face in a determined snarl. That was the last time he looked like he had the measure of the occasion, as the winners that had come off against Carlos Alcaraz and Frances Tiafoe earlier this week sprayed long or dropped into the net.

Alexander Zverev claimed his maiden US Open title just months after winning the French Open

Ben Shelton carried the hopes of a nation with him but could not pull off another comeback

His girlfriend Trinity Rodman - who had flown from her Washington Spirit game to make the final stages - was left in floods of tears

Nor did it take much for cracks to appear, with the number-one seed able to seize his opening break on Shelton’s first service game. The German was able to play the way he wanted to, off his fine backhand, or hanging tough in grinding rallies, and control tempo too, with Shelton frustrated early by his never-ending ball bounce.

A feature at this US Open only, Zverev has averaged 10 seconds of bouncing before either first or second serves. That’s two hours and 30 minutes of interminable up-and-down, before the final. Even a time violation from chair umpire Marijana Veljovic in the fourth set could not end his rhythm-breaking, rule-bending, habit.

After that opening wobble, Shelton was able to get the set back on track with the help of his weapon of a serve, which frequently hits 140mph-plus. But it was a meat-and-potatoes game, with only flashes of the inventiveness he showed against Tiafoe or Alcaraz.

When the serve didn’t work, it was fatal. Double faults sealed the opening break of Shelton’s serve, and handed Zverev the set. It also did little to help him in the second-set tiebreak, with Zverev capable of absorbing all of its zip and dictate from return.

Shelton was full of fight, keeping pace deep in the third and heaping the pressure on a player with a long history of tightening up in the biggest moments. Another double fault, this time the German’s, and the end of his 67 consecutive holds against Shelton.

Shelton has been the comeback king of New York, but his blood was too hot going into the fourth and Zverev pounced with a second break of his opening serve. That doused the flames of patriotism fired-up inside Ashe pretty quickly.

The crowd never truly died down for their battling player, at times slipping into classless heckling. But Zverev tuned out the noise capably, just as the type-1 diabetic impressively managed multiple injections of insulin during the contest to keep his blood sugar levels steady. Long tennis’ nearly-man, he had already survived the five-set scramble against Flavio Cobolli in Paris. Avoiding a second should be counted as growth.

Zverev will never be a universally popular champion. His game is considered and clinical, but lacks a flash and flair to tempt the neutral. There's the smog of domestic abuse allegations from two ex-partners, the second of which went to trial, and was settled by Zverev in 2024 with legal proceedings discontinued.

Zverev has repeatedly denied these claims but incorrectly stated in June that his innocence has been proven. Beating an American in New York will not do much to bolster his appeal Stateside.

But there is much to admire about Zverev’s capacity to seize his moment this year, after his previous four Grand Slam finals - including 2020’s in New York - slipped through his fingers.

He has been criticised for winning his two majors with fortunate draws en route, but he cannot choose his opponents, only beat them. And with the absence of Jannik Sinner and Alcaraz in the later stages in Paris and New York, Zverev has not wasted his opportunity. Of course, when they have been there, at the Australian Open, and at Wimbledon, his run has ended. He continues to look up at their singular rivalry.

Sports.title: Paolo Maldini's son in hospital after being involved in car crash just hours after scoring Serie A winner
Sports.content:
Daniel Maldini, the son of AC Milan and Italy legend Paolo, was rushed to hospital following a car crash, just hours after he scored the winning goal in a Serie A match.

Maldini, 24, netted a decisive penalty on Saturday night as Cagliari beat Atalanta 2-1.

However, the attacking midfielder was then involved in a collision while driving his Porsche Carrera at around 5:15am on Sunday morning.

Six people were said to be involved in the car crash, which involved two vehicles.

Those six people are understood to have suffered minor injuries and three ambulances and a medical car were dispatched to the crash location.

Five of those affected were taken to hospital, including Maldini - who was reportedly evaluated at Milan's Fatebenefratelli facility - with the other individual treated on the scene.

Daniel Maldini, son of Italian legend Paolo, was rushed to hospital following a car crash

That came just hours after he scored the winning goal as Cagliari beat Atalanta on Saturday

The incident came soon after Maldini, who has previously represented multiple clubs including AC Milan, Monza and Lazio, enjoyed a memorable evening on Saturday.

Not only did he score the winner from the spot, but ironically the attacking midfielder is on loan from Atalanta after being deemed surplus to requirements by his parent club.

It was Maldini's second goal in just four league games this season, with Cagliari currently in fourth place in Serie A following an extremely positive start.

Maldini's father Paolo is widely regarded as one of Italy's greatest footballers of all-time during a career where he represented just AC Milan and Italy.

His late grandfather Cesare also earned legendary status at the San Siro before enjoying a managerial career that included stints with his former club and his country.

Meanwhile, the 24-year-old previously came through the ranks at AC Milan during a period when his dad served as the club's technical director.

Maldini left in 2024 in search of more regular first team football, spending a year with Monza before he moved to Atalanta.

He has also won six caps for Italy, and could be back in action next Saturday when Cagliari travel to Udinese.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
