World.title: Diesel hits $15.96 per gallon as concerns grow over cost to Belize businesses
World.content:
Diesel hits $15.96 per gallon as concerns grow over cost to Belize businesses

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Concerns are growing over the cost of doing business in Belize following another increase in the price of diesel.

A social media post circulating this weekend highlighted that diesel has risen to $15.96 per gallon, describing the increase as another blow to the country’s business sector.

The higher price of diesel has implications beyond motorists filling their tanks.

Businesses that depend heavily on transportation, generators, construction equipment and delivery vehicles can face higher operating expenses when fuel prices rise. Those costs can eventually affect the prices consumers pay for goods and services.

The transportation sector is particularly exposed since buses, trucks, taxis, tour operators and other commercial vehicles depend on fuel to operate.

Businesses involved in agriculture and construction can also face additional pressure because diesel powers much of the heavy equipment used in those industries.

The latest increase comes amid growing public discussion over fuel and energy costs in Belize.

Opposition Leader Tracy Taegar Panton also criticized the latest diesel increase this weekend, arguing that businesses and working families are being placed under increasing financial pressure.

The price of diesel has therefore become another focal point in the wider debate over Belize’s cost of living and the cost of doing business.

World.title: Woman says electricity bill soared from $340 to $1,040, sparking questions online
World.content:
Woman says electricity bill soared from $340 to $1,040, sparking questions online

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A social media post questioning a sharp increase in a household electricity bill is generating discussion among Belizeans.

The woman behind the post says she normally paid approximately $340 per month, but a recent amount due reached $1,040.55.

She publicly questioned the steep increase and expressed frustration over the financial burden.

A screenshot accompanying the post shows the amount due, but does not include enough information to determine why the balance increased so significantly.

Factors such as higher consumption, unpaid balances, adjustments or other billing issues could potentially affect the total, but the exact reason is not known.

There has been no independent confirmation that the bill was incorrectly calculated.

The complaint comes at a time when the cost of electricity and household expenses remain major concerns for many Belizean families.

Customers who notice unusual increases on their electricity bills are encouraged to review their consumption history and seek an explanation directly from BEL.

World.title: House engulfed in fire in Otoxha Village, Toledo District
World.content:
House engulfed in fire in Otoxha Village, Toledo District

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A house was reportedly engulfed in flames in Otoxha Village in the Toledo District on Sunday morning.

Initial information reaching Breaking Belize News indicates that the fire broke out at a residence in the southern community.

Images from the scene show flames and smoke coming from the structure as the fire burned.

At this time, it is not known whether anyone was inside the house when the fire started or whether any injuries have been reported.

The cause of the blaze and the extent of the damage are also not yet known.

Further details are expected as information becomes available.

BBN will provide an update once additional information is confirmed.

World.title: Should Belize ever have taken independence, the forbidden question, argued both ways
World.content:
Should Belize ever have taken independence, the forbidden question, argued both ways

By Horace Palacio:

There is a sentence some Belizeans only say after the third drink, or the third blackout, and lately they have begun saying it in daylight, on timelines, under news posts.

Belize should never have taken independence.

It usually arrives with company. That the whole affair was a scheme by politicians to inherit a territory as their private milking cow. That a nation this small can never staff a real army, a real police force, a real fire service, or tax itself into greatness. That anyone comparing us to El Salvador understands neither history nor demographics.

The usual response is outrage, a lecture about the flag, and the conversation dies. Today this column will do something different, because a country that cannot examine its own founding is fragile, and readers know my rule. I have argued that Belizeans should examine what they inherit, whether creeds or constitutions. The founding itself cannot be exempt. So, as with the Speednet deal and the minimum wage, here is the full ledger, both cases argued at their strongest, and the verdict left where it belongs, with you.

First, the case against independence, and let me argue it properly, because it is not stupid.

Begin with the arithmetic. In September 1981 this territory held roughly 145,000 souls, fewer people than a single district of the nations around us. The skeptic asks a fair question. Can a tax base that size, even grown to today’s 430,000, genuinely fund a modern army, a proper police service, fire coverage, hospitals, pensions, and roads? And he does not need to invent his evidence. This column supplied it all year. A government budget where seventy cents of every dollar is spoken for before a single wire is bought. A Prime Minister flying to ask a neighbor not to cut our electricity. Ten dollars imported for every one exported. Our brightest boarding planes. The skeptic simply gathers my own receipts and asks, is this what nationhood was for?

Then his counterfactual. Look, he says, at the territories that declined the flag. Cayman, Bermuda, the British Virgin Islands, still under the Crown, today rank among the wealthiest places in this hemisphere, with British passports, British courts, and a superpower’s treasury behind them when hurricanes or volcanoes strike, ask Montserrat. We chose the anthem, he says, they chose the safety net, and compare the results.

And then his sharpest blade, the milking cow. Independence, on this argument, did not end extraction. It localized it. The flag changed, and a domestic political class inherited the machinery, the ministerial contracts, the politicized public service created in 2000 and lovingly preserved by both parties, the procurement darkness that finally exploded into scandal this year. From London’s milking, the skeptic says, to Belmopan’s. That is his case, and stated honestly, parts of it draw blood.

Now the case for independence, argued with equal strength, and it begins by demolishing a myth hiding inside the skeptic’s counterfactual.

The comfortable-colony option was never truly on the menu. By the 1970s Britain was closing its empire with both hands, and the United Nations voted repeatedly for Belize’s independence. The micro-territories that remained are special cases, offshore finance islands of a few tens of thousands, a model no farming mainland territory of 150,000 could copy. And staying under London carried a danger the nostalgic forget. Colonies do not control their own fate, and in 1968 mediated proposals would have handed Guatemala sweeping influence over this territory. It was Belizeans in the streets who killed that bargain. The lesson is brutal and clear. A colony can be negotiated away over its own head. A nation cannot. Independence, with its UN seat and its access to the world court, is precisely the armor that kept every inch of Belize Belizean, Guatemala’s recognition in 1991, the claim now before the ICJ, not one acre lost in 45 years. Sovereignty’s hardest test, passed without a single tank division, which brings us to the army question. Costa Rica abolished its military entirely in 1948 and became the most stable country in Central America. Iceland, our size, keeps no standing army at all. Small nations are defended by law, legitimacy and alliances, not by battalions they cannot afford, and Belize’s borders are the proof.

As for the milking cow, the ledger must record a documented fact. George Price died in the same modest family home he had always lived in, famously austere, daily mass, no mansion, no fortune, nothing offshore. If independence was his scheme for personal enrichment, he forgot, across sixty years of opportunity, to collect. The extraction critique is real, this column has spent a year documenting it, but it indicts the political culture that followed, not the founder’s bank account. Judging independence by its worst administrators is judging marriage by its worst husbands.

And weigh what the young nation did buy. While El Salvador, Guatemala and Nicaragua drowned those very decades in civil wars and coups, this improbable little country held peaceful elections and handed power back and forth without a shot, again and again, a regional rarity worth more than its size. It used its small voice on principle at the United Nations. It clawed its debt down from the cliff. And above all it bought the right to make its own mistakes, and therefore the right to fix them. A colony’s errors are made for it, forever.

There is the ledger, both columns full. And now notice something remarkable before you vote.

Strip the anger from the skeptic’s post and what remains is a demand, for services that work, taxes that build, a state that serves rather than milks. Strip the romance from the patriot’s reply and what remains is the identical demand. Both sides of this forbidden question want exactly one thing, a Belize worthy of its flag. The quarrel was never really about 1981, which no verdict can reverse. It is about whether we have used what 1981 gave us, and that question, unlike the first, still has a living answer, being written by this generation, in scorecards and megawatts and classrooms, right now.

So decide for yourselves, Belizeans, what you believe about that September morning. This column, for once, casts no vote.

But it does offer one closing observation, free of charge.

You are reading a Belizean newspaper, freely questioning the founding of Belize, under the byline of a Belizean, judged by Belizean readers, with no governor’s censor in sight.

Colonies do not get to hold this debate.

Only free people audit their own birth.

Whatever your verdict, you just exercised the inheritance.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: BEL says Westlake emergency generation helped prevent load shedding
World.content:
BEL says Westlake emergency generation helped prevent load shedding

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize Electricity Limited says its temporary generation facility at Westlake is already helping to support the national electricity system as testing and commissioning of new emergency generation units continue.

According to BEL, the Westlake facility is currently operating at approximately 40 percent of its planned capacity.

The company says the additional local generation has provided greater flexibility in meeting Belize’s electricity demand, particularly when imported electricity from Mexico is unavailable.

BEL reported that during periods over the past two days when electricity supply from Mexico’s Comisión Federal de Electricidad was unavailable, generation from Westlake helped sustain the system and avoid load shedding during those periods.

Testing and commissioning will continue as additional generating units are brought online.

Once the facility is fully commissioned, Westlake is expected to provide 20 megawatts of emergency generation capacity.

BEL says the additional capacity will provide support when other sources of electricity supply are interrupted.

The company thanked customers for their patience as work continues to strengthen the reliability of Belize’s electricity supply.

World.title: Belize should consider Warren Buffett’s radical rule for controlling government deficits
World.content:
Belize should consider Warren Buffett’s radical rule for controlling government deficits

By Horace Palacio:

Belize should consider adopting its own version of a fiscal accountability idea famously proposed by billionaire investor Warren Buffett: if politicians allow the national budget deficit to become too large, they should risk losing the ability to seek reelection.

Buffett made the proposal during a 2011 CNBC interview, saying he could end the United States deficit in “five minutes.” His suggested rule was straightforward: if the federal deficit exceeded 3 percent of GDP, sitting members of Congress would become ineligible for reelection.

The principle behind the idea deserves serious consideration in Belize.

Governments routinely make decisions about borrowing, spending and taxation whose consequences can extend years beyond an election cycle. Yet the politicians approving those decisions may face little personal political consequence if public finances deteriorate.

A Belizean version of Buffett’s proposal could change those incentives.

Instead of treating fiscal discipline simply as a campaign promise, Belize could establish a clear deficit threshold tied to GDP. If a government exceeds that threshold without a legitimate national emergency, elected officials responsible for approving the budget could face serious electoral consequences.

There would have to be safeguards. Hurricanes, pandemics, recessions and other emergencies can require governments to borrow heavily. Buffett himself has acknowledged that deficit spending can be appropriate during extraordinary economic crises, including the 2008 financial collapse.

Belize therefore should not blindly copy a 3 percent rule. It should examine a framework suited to the country’s economy, accompanied by independent fiscal reporting and clearly defined emergency exceptions.

The larger lesson from Buffett is powerful: politicians respond to incentives too.

If Belize wants governments to take deficits, borrowing and public debt more seriously, fiscal responsibility should carry consequences that elected leaders cannot easily ignore.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Make San Ignacio your Independence Day getaway this September
World.content:
Make San Ignacio your Independence Day getaway this September

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize Independence Day is one of the most exciting times of the year to experience the country, and San Ignacio is one of the best places to celebrate it.

Every September, Belize comes alive with flags, music, parades, cultural events and a strong sense of national pride. In San Ignacio, that energy blends with the charm of the Cayo District, giving visitors a celebration that feels festive, authentic and close to the heart of Belize.

The town offers a lively atmosphere without losing its laid back character. Visitors can enjoy Independence Day activities, explore local restaurants and bars, visit the market, and experience the warmth of the community during one of the country’s most important national holidays.

San Ignacio also makes it easy to turn the celebration into a full Belize vacation.

Between Independence Day events, travelers can explore ancient Maya sites such as Xunantunich, go cave tubing, visit waterfalls, take a jungle tour or simply spend time discovering the natural beauty of western Belize.

For accommodations, Cahal Pech Village Resort is an excellent place to stay.

Perched above San Ignacio, the resort offers sweeping views, a peaceful setting and convenient access to the town below. Guests can enjoy comfortable accommodations, swimming pools, onsite dining and a relaxing atmosphere after a busy day of Independence Day celebrations and sightseeing.

Its location also makes it a great base for exploring the Cayo District, with many of Belize’s top inland attractions within easy reach.

Celebrating Independence Day in San Ignacio gives visitors the chance to experience more than a holiday. It is an opportunity to see Belizean culture, pride and hospitality at their strongest while also enjoying some of the country’s best adventure experiences.

If you are planning a September getaway, make San Ignacio part of your Independence Day plans and stay at Cahal Pech Village Resort for the perfect combination of celebration, culture and relaxation.

World.title: Newcomers Tru Juice ambush Mt Pleasant for historic JPL win
World.content:
In this file photo, Tru Juice FC's Daniel Roberts attempts a shot as he is being closed down by Reno FC's Raheem Kerr in the semi-finals of last season's Jamaica Football Championship at Llandilo Sports Complex in Westmoreland. Tru Juice won the game on penalties after playing out a 0-0 regulation and extra time score. (Photo: Paul Reid)

ST CATHERINE, Jamaica – Daniel Roberts and Rodave Murray both scored braces as newly promoted Tru Juice FC stunned Mt Pleasant FA 4-0 in their first-ever Jamaica Premier League game, which was held at the Bramwell Clarke Complex in Linstead on Sunday.

Roberts created Tru Juice history when he gave them the lead in the 10th minute, their first goal at this level. He then added a second in the 42nd minute. Murray then scored in the 50th and 57th minutes to complete a brilliant start to the season for the newcomers.

Tru Juice had earned promotion to the JPL after qualifying for the final of the Jamaica Football Championships last season, after losing in the previous three semi-finals.

Fellow promoted club Humble Lion, who had been relegated from the JPL after the 2024-25 season, were not so lucky on Sunday, as they were beaten 3-0 by Tivoli Gardens.

Last season’s losing finalist, Cavalier FC came from a goal down to beat Dunbeholden FC 2-1 while semi-finalists Montego Bay United blanked Chapelton Maroons 2-0 at Jarrett Park.

At Jarrett Park, Deonjay Brown scored in the first half and then assisted Dwight Merrick in the second half as Montego Bay won their opening game for the second straight season.

Devontae Campbell created the opening goal after he dribbled circles around two Chapelton defenders on the left of the 18-yard box before proving a delicate cross for Brown to head past goalkeeper Roje Williams in the 22nd minute.

Brown then provided the assist for the second goal when he found Merrick, who came on at the start of the second half, putting a left foot volley just out of the reach of Williams’ outstretched left glove in the 85th minute.

Sunday’s games

Dunbeholden-1, Cavalier FC-2

Tru Juice FC-4, Mt Pleasant FA-0

Montego Bay United-2, Chapelton Maroons- 0

Tivoli Gardens-3, Humble Lion-0

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Alleged ‘high risk’ serial robber among three killed in reported confrontation with police
World.content:
file photo

KINGSTON, Jamaica — An alleged member of the Speculation Gang who the police have linked to two murders and a series of major robberies and break-ins across Jamaica was among three persons fatally shot during an operation in St Andrew early Sunday.

Dead is Dewar Archibald, otherwise called “Max”, described by police as a high-risk criminal target.

Reports are that a team from Specialised Operations was on patrol in the Red Hills area around 1:45 am when they received information that a group of armed men travelling in a red Honda HR-V and a white Toyota Probox were allegedly preparing to carry out criminal activities in the St Andrew North Police Division.

According to the preliminary police account, officers attempted to intercept the vehicles, but the drivers failed to stop. The driver of the Probox managed to elude the police.

The police report that they intercepted the Honda HR-V in the vicinity of Knightsdale Drive where occupants of the vehicle reportedly opened fire at members of the police team, who then discharged their service weapons.

Three persons were subsequently found suffering from gunshot wounds. The identities of the other two persons have not yet been released.

The Independent Commission of Investigations has been notified.

Archibald had been identified by investigators as one of the main organisers of robberies and break-ins targeting automated teller machines (ATMs), remittance agencies and other cash-intensive businesses. He was also implicated in two murders committed within the past nine months.

Archibald was linked to the murder of Chevardo Messam at Galleon Beach in Crawford district, St Elizabeth, on December 21, 2025.

He was also implicated in the January 9 murder of Kemar Brown, otherwise called “Mars”, in Bristol, Alexandria, St Ann. A woman was shot and injured during that incident.

READ: Man killed, woman injured at shop in St Ann

Archibald had also been linked to a shooting during an attempted theft of an ATM in Drax Hall, St Ann, in April. Investigators had further implicated him in a series of robberies and break-ins in Linstead, St Catherine, in February and June; Kingston in April; and Crofts Hill, Clarendon, in May.

Investigators believe Archibald was part of an organised criminal network operating across several parishes.

Investigations are continuing.

World.title: Surge in road deaths; at least 40 killed in crashes in last 28 days
World.content:
This file photo shows the motorcycle that collided with a Honda motorcar.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — At least 40 people were killed in motor vehicle crashes in the 28 days between August 14 and September 11, according to an analysis of the daily crash reports of the Island Traffic Authority (ITA).

According to the daily crash reports, 202 people were killed as a result of 174 fatal crashes as at August 14. Those figures included 49 motorcyclists. They also represented a 15 per cent decline or 36 fewer deaths when compared to the similar period in 2025. Fatal crashes were also down 16 per cent at that time.

Fast forward to Friday, September 11 and some of those gains have been eroded as is seen in the 242 deaths from 209 fatal crashes now being reported by the ITA. According to the ITA, fatalities have decreased by 10 per cent when compared to prior year while fatal crashes are down 10 per cent when compared with similar period in 2025. Overall, there are 26 fewer deaths when compared to the similar period in 2025.

As of September 11, motorcyclists account for 63 or 26 per cent of fatalities since the start of the year. Private motor vehicle drivers account for 55 or 23 per cent, while pedestrians account for 53 deaths or 22 per cent of all fatalities this year.

The ITA is also reporting that private motor vehicle passengers, account for 33 deaths or 14 per cent of fatalities, commercial motor vehicle passengers account for deaths 14 deaths or six per cent, and pillion passengers account for eight deaths or three per cent of fatalities since January 1.

Meanwhile, the group of road users determined to be the most vulnerable – pedestrians, pedalcyclists, motorcyclists and pillion passengers combined – account for 53 per cent of fatalities. Overall, passengers account for 24 per cent of all road deaths this year, while males and females account for 86 per cent and 15 per cent respectively of fatalities since the start of the year.

In the meantime, Westmoreland parish has recorded the highest number of fatalities, accounting for 13 per cent of fatalities since the start of 2026.

— Lynford Simpson

World.title: ‘Really, really sad’
World.content:
An undated picture of seven-year-old Keriecia Hutchinson and her four-year-old brother Samson Cameron, who died in a house fire in Smith Lane, Central Kingston, on Saturday.

GRIEF and anger were palpable in the Central Kingston community of Smith Lane on Saturday as it was confirmed that seven-year-old Keriecia Hutchinson and her four-year-old brother Samson Cameron had perished in a mid-morning house fire.

Residents remembered the two children who they said were promising and full of life while anger surged as people assigned blame for their deaths.

Keriecia was a grade one student at Calabar All-Age School, while Samson was a student of Calabar Basic School.

“The mother locked them up in the house and gone to a wholesale. She could have just left them out and asked any of wi to look on them,” charged one neighbour who, like her colleagues, refused to give their names.

“The mother do nothing wrong, the [son’s] father was here and him run go up there [to the room] before the fire get wicked and him run down back and say him can’t reach the children,” charged another neighbour.

Police on the scene refused to speak with the media to confirm or deny either claim, but the contention morphed into a physical battle between one woman — who was defending the children’s grandmother — and another female resident who was chastising the parents.

Police on the scene fired a number of shots in the air to separate the combatants and at least three people were later taken into custody.

But for most residents in Smith Lane the death of the two children was their main concern.

“Right yah now me feel really, really sad that the two kids lose them lives,” said one of the few residents willing to speak to the media on condition that she not be named.

“What I get to understand, the mother wasn’t here, she gone to the wholesale, but why did she lock the children inside? And when people call out and the father run inside, the door lock, and is like him forget the key so him panic. So when the door finally open and people a throw water — even me a throw out water — it did not save the children. It really, really sad,” said the woman.

She told the Jamaica Observer that Keriecia moved to live with her mother in Smith Lane when she was about two years old, while the son, “him a must be about four or five years old now, and him born right here so inna mi hand”, added the neighbour.

She said many residents tried to put the blaze out before the Jamaica Fire Brigade team arrived but they were unsuccessful.

Residents also had praise for a neighbour who they said soaked himself in water before entering the burning house after being told that the children were inside, but he was unable to rescue them.

“He is a hero, man. Him really try, but the children were not in the front room, they were in the back, and the little girl died hugging her brother trying to save him. You could see she was trying to help him,” said one man, who, like others, refused to give his name.

At press time Saturday the fire brigade had not determined the cause of the blaze, while there was no word on whether the people involved in the physical altercation had been charged.

An unofficial count by the Sunday Observer has shown four children have died in fires across the island since the start of this year.

World.title: ‘Why did my parents forsake me?’
World.content:
A 17-year-old boy is searching for answers, guidance, and assistance to turn his life around after a series of unfortunate events saw him moving in and out of five children’s homes without a solid plan for his future.

The recent high school graduate said he does not have a relationship with his parents, with both reportedly choosing not to play an active role in his life when he was just a few months old. He is being raised by his paternal grandmother who, he said, struggles to make ends meet and wants help to get him on the right track.

The young man shared that while in primary school he was bullied daily because he seemingly did not have any parents. He said he grew frustrated with the bullies and decided to fight back. During an altercation he said he accidentally damaged the car of a staff member of the institution.

He said attempts were made to contact his parents and grandmother, but they were unsuccessful. He ended up in State care.

“I went to five boys’ homes. I went to one in Clarendon, St Mary, Kingston, Spanish Town and Old Harbour [both in St Catherine]. The first three homes were nice, because I had friends there and people didn’t do anything to me, but the last home I didn’t like it because they started to molest me,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“I was sleeping in my dorm and this boy molested me. They held me down in my sleep. It was five boys who did that to me…I was very scared,” he recounted, his voice filled with sadness.

He said the incident was reported to a staff member, who contacted his case worker. The young man said he was taken from that home and provided counselling. Another attempt was made to contact his grandmother, who eventually agreed to take him back in her care.

He said financial struggles were heightened when the house they were living in was destroyed by fire, leaving them with little to nothing to recover.

“I lost most of my clothes and things that I had. It was a rental house, so we had to find somewhere else to live,” recalled the 17-year-old.

He said they eventually found a new place to stay but lost a lot of things that they still need to replace, such as clothes and other household items.

Now out of high school, the 17-year-old said he is seeking assistance to turn his life around. However, his greatest wish is to have a relationship with his parents, especially his mother.

“Every day I get up I just feel sad, and I don’t know why. I don’t know why I didn’t get to meet my mother…When I get up and I see a parent with a son or daughter, I always say to myself, ‘Why did my parents forsake me?’ because I never do them anything. Whenever I see children with their mother, I just start to cry and just feel sadness. I cry every single day,” he told the Sunday Observer.

The 17-year-old said he is still in contact with a counsellor who encourages him that better days are ahead, but he is still left with more questions than answers about why his life had to be this way.

“I would be happy if I had a relationship with them. I just want a relationship with my mom. People always trouble me that I don’t have any mother,” he said.

Now a high school graduate, he is uncertain about where life will take him, and needs some guidance and assistance.

“I would love to get some help to get my driver’s licence and maybe some clothes, because I want to get a job and go to work. I also want to go to school. I was thinking of applying to HEART [Human Employment and Resource Training/National Service Training Agency Trust] and learn a skill, but I need some help.

“I need support, because I’m going to be 18 soon and I want to learn how to drive and stuff so that I can take care of myself. I just want support,” he said.

His grandmother said that, over the years, she has tried her best, but with ageing and a lack of resources there is only so much she can do.

“I get help from my sisters, but that is it. Otherwise, it’s just him and me alone,” she said.

She added that the situation is made worse by the fact that she is often left with questions she cannot answer.

“Almost every day him get up and ask me what happened with his parents, and if somebody did something to run them away. I don’t know the answer. His mother just left him with me, and his father is not around,” she said.

She, too, pleaded for assistance for her grandson, wanting him to have a better future than his past.

“I would love it if him can get some assistance to go to HEART and learn a skill. He needs clothes and other things, too,” she pleaded.

World.title: Greatness Weekend marked as economic booster for Kgn
World.content:
Patron Shavo’neil Edwards poses at the last staging of Greatness Pink & White Brunch.

EXECUTIVE director of the Tourism Enhancement Fund (TEF), Dr Carey Wallace has underscored the importance of collaboration as Jamaica’s entertainment sector in driving economic growth and advancing the country’s development.

Wallace made the call on Tuesday during the official launch of Greatness Weekend at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston, where tourism officials, event promoters, and other stakeholders gathered ahead of the four-day entertainment series slated for October 16-19.

“For Jamaica to get to where we want — to a First World, developed country — we need to have more collaborations like what we’re seeing here tonight,” Wallace told the gathering.

He said Jamaica already possesses many of the ingredients necessary to become a developed nation, pointing particularly to the strength of its people, culture, and international brand.

“Jamaica has all the ingredients to be an amazing, developed country. In fact, when the British had it, it was their most-prized colony. We are a people that are revered anywhere in the world we go. When you say you are Jamaican you see people’s pupils dilate; people get excited. So, let us deliver,” Wallace said.

He added that tourism has an important role to play in ensuring Jamaica’s resources and global appeal translate into tangible benefits for its people.

“We, in tourism, recognise that we must play our part in developing the country, and so our mantra is ‘Building tourism for all Jamaicans’, and that includes entertainment,” he said.

Greatness Weekend, now in its second staging, will be held under the theme ‘I Choose Kingston’ and will bring together four events across the Corporate Area.

The festivities begin on October 16 with Pool Cooler Fete (PCF), followed by RECALL: Throwback Festival on October 17. Both events will celebrate their 10th anniversaries this year.

CUPS: Château Blanc follows on October 18 before the weekend culminates with the Greatness Pink & White Brunch on October 19.

Promoters representing the events were on hand for Tuesday’s launch which also welcomed mayor of Kingston, Councillor Andrew Swaby.

Mikisha Silvera, destination manager for Kingston and St Andrew at the Tourism Product Development Company Limited (TPDCo), lauded the promoters for their contribution to Kingston’s entertainment landscape, and said Greatness Weekend could further strengthen the capital’s appeal as a destination.

“When you look at what they have done so far, it’s amazing. Kingston is the cultural mecca of Jamaica. We’re talking about nightlife, daylife, gastronomy. The culture that exists here is a rich cultural heritage,” Silvera said.

She noted that the weekend provides an opportunity for Jamaicans and international visitors alike to experience the capital’s cultural offerings.

“We’re able to participate as citizens, as well as the visitors who will be coming here for Greatness Weekend. The brand being here is something special, and you’re going to be a part of Jamaica’s history,” she said.

Silvera said initiatives such as Greatness Weekend can help position Kingston as a premier destination by combining entertainment, culture, food, and tourism into a single experience.

The packed launch offered guests a taste of the festivities to come, with specially prepared rum mixes sponsored by Rich Rum adding to the evening’s celebratory atmosphere.

World.title: ‘It a mash wi up’
World.content:
Nicole Watson returns a cellphone that was left with her by a customer, shortly after she exited the embassy. Photos: Naphtali Junior

AT least two Kingston entrepreneurs whose livelihoods depend on charging US Embassy visitors a fee to store their mobile devices or provide them with phone calls are requesting a meeting with embassy officials, seeking ways to adapt after a new policy permitting applicants to bring cellphones inside the facility.

The applicants themselves have expressed mixed views about the policy change, with some welcoming the move, rejoicing that they no longer have to pay people outside the embassy to keep their devices while inside, and others expressing scepticism.

Cellphones are just one of the many items now permitted within the walls of the US Embassy. In an advisory on September 1 the embassy said small quantities of baby formula, baby food, milk, diapers, and baby carriers that can pass through an X-ray machine are now permitted. Other items include money, belts, watches, keys, earbuds, medical devices, and non-liquid medication, which must be declared before security screening.

Prohibited items include computers, intelligent eyewear, and other electronic devices, inclusive of media devices, such as compact discs (CDs), thumb drives, memory cards, flash drives, headphones, and speakers. Additionally, cameras or video equipment, flashlights, lighters and matches, weapons, knives, and other sharp objects are not allowed. Alcoholic beverages, purses larger than 18 inches, liquids, lotions, oils, and gels are also not allowed inside.

But for Nicole Watson, a vendor who, for more than 15 years, has made a living holding on to cellphones for visa applicants, the move to allow previously banned cellphones is most troubling.

“It’s something that we all live off [of]. I don’t know what transpired; it’s odd. We are out here to help each and every one. You have good, and you have bad, but we would just like the embassy to look over things or draw us in a meeting because this is our daily bread. If there are bad apples out here that they need to talk to, they can talk to them to keep the things flowing because we have kids to go to school,” she told the Jamaica Observer, lamenting the cost of living.

Watson said the change has destroyed her business.

“It a mash we up; it crush up, it gone,” she bemoaned.

“I normally have around four buses that come to me in the morning time from May Pen, Mandeville, Savanna-la-Mar, and Montego Bay. I reach here like five in the morning time, or if them call me four o’clock, I will reach down. If possible, I would get 30 people for the day, because I’m known down here, so people just come… On a good day, about 500 or 600 persons come to them [at the embassy], so I can get at least 35 people. Now, everybody passes,” she said.

Watson shared that she typically charges $1,000 to store cellphones, $300 for phone calls, and $500 for WhatsApp phone calls, money she said added up to support her and her children, but now she is barely making ends meet.

“It’s hard because the sun is hot and business is slow,” she said.

A look around the area outside the embassy proved her words to be true, as many other runners sat in the sun along the side of the road across from the embassy, eagerly awaiting business that never came.

Watson had just two phones in her bag; she said she got them from loyal customers who still support her business.

“Because I am out here long time, I will have my clients who come and I will say, ‘Alright, just give me a lunch money and gwaan,’ but from people hear what is going on now they just move along. We nuh bother press anybody; we just make them move along,” she told the Sunday Observer.

Despite slow business, Watson said she will not leave the area. Instead, she will continue to sell phone cards and beverages.

“Food have to eat, and gas have to buy. Me nah go do no nine-to-five work because me nah work for $17,000 a week. I cyaan bother with that because that can’t buy gas put in car,” she reasoned.

Another vendor, who chose to remain anonymous, expressed concern that she would not be able to take care of her children.

“My son inna 10 grade and my daughter inna eight grade, and it’s this send them go [to] school… I start it from them in basic school, then primary school, and now high school… I don’t know how me a go manage,” she said.

“A me alone a take care of them, no father, no nothing. Me nuh have no help,” she bemoaned.

“It mash up. If we can talk to them and bring it back, that would be good, but I don’t think talking a go bring it back either. We just have to have in our mind what else we are going to do after,” she said.

Outside the embassy, applicants and family members sat patiently, awaiting their appointment. For some, the move to allow cellphones was welcomed, but one man was sceptical.

“When I came here last week and I heard about it, I told the person, ‘Don’t take your phone inside there’, ” he said, adding that he planned to leave his phone in his car.

However, for a woman who gave her name as Jennifer, she loved the idea of not having to stress about where she would store her cellphone.

“The first time I came here I had to pay somebody to keep my phone outside, so it’s a good idea. At the time, I did not know that I could not bring in lotion and stuff in my bag, so when I got here I had to throw away things, so it’s good. At least we don’t have to pay money out here now because sometimes they charge $1,500 to hold the phone, and that can buy credit. It’s a good move,” she told the Sunday Observer.

World.title: ULTIMATE PUSH
World.content:
Jamaica’s Rushell Clayton will be in action in the women’s 400m hurldes final at the World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest, Hungary, today.AFP

JAMAICA came up short on the second day of the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships at the National Athletics Center in Budapest, Hungary, with Oblique Seville’s second-place finish in the men’s 100m the best result on Saturday.

Jamaicans contested four finals, including the men’s 100m, women’s 100m, women’s 400m and men’s long jump, and will be looking for better results on Sunday, the third and final day.

Commonwealth Games champion Sanique Walker and two-time World Athletics Championships bronze medallist Rushell Clayton have qualified for the final of the women’s 400m hurdles.

They will join Romaine Beckford, who is in the men’s high jump; Ackelia Smith, who is in the women’s triple jump; and the mixed 4x400m relay team.

Additionally, Jamaica will hope to get into the 200m finals, with Bryan Levell and Christopher Taylor in the men’s semi-finals and Ashanti Moore and Lavanya Williams in the women’s semi-finals.

Seville, the World champion and Diamond League winner, was upstaged by American Kenny Bednarek who won the final in a season’s best 9.85 seconds (-0.6m/s). Seville repeated the 9.90 seconds he ran to lead the semi-finals but was edged on the finishing line.

Another American, Ronnie Baker, was third in 9.93 seconds.

Seville had easily won his semi-final while Ackeem Blake failed to get past the semi-finals after running 10.21 seconds.

Jonielle Smith was the best-placed Jamaican in a quality women’s 100m final, placing fourth in 10.94 seconds (-0.2m/s), the same time recorded by her compatriot Tina Clayton, while Lavanya Williams was seventh in 11.07 seconds.

American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden ran a world-leading 10.62 seconds to win the title, just beating Julien Alfred of St Lucia, 10.74 seconds, with Sha’Carri Richardson of the USA third in 10.76 seconds.

Jodean Williams had run 11.16 seconds for fifth in her semi-final while Brianna Lyston had run 11.18 seconds in her first race.

National record holder Nickisha Pryce was third in the women’s 400m final, running 49.56 seconds as favourite Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic won in 49.07 seconds, coming from fourth place over the last 120 metres to take the title.

Norway’s Henriette Jaeger was second in 49.28 seconds.

In the other final that included a Jamaican, Diamond League winner Tajay Gayle was fifth in the men’s long jump with a best of 7.90m (-0.1m/s), after failing to make the top four for the fourth and final round.

Gayle improved with each jump, starting with 7.52m (1.0m/s) and then had a 7.72m (-0.2m/s) jump in the second round.

Walker lowered the 54.00 seconds she ran to win the Commonwealth Games, improving her personal best to 53.77 seconds as she placed third in her semi-final from lane nine behind Americans Jasmine Jones, who ran a season’s best 52.77 seconds, and Anna Cockrell, who ran 53.31 seconds.

Clayton was fourth in her semi-final in 53.84 seconds, after she came off the seventh hurdle in seventh place.

Emma Zapletalova of Slovakia won her semi-final in 52.93 seconds, followed by Panama’s Gianna Woodruff, 53.73 seconds, and Belgium’s national record holder Paulien Couckuyt, 53.81 seconds.

Commonwealth Games champion Navasky Anderson just missed out on a place in the men’s 800m final, finishing fifth in the first semi-final in 1:44.83 behind Kenya’s Emmanuel Wanyonyi who was fourth in 1:44.43 to secure a place in the final.

World.title: Merz zwischen Arktis und CDU-Abgrund
World.content:
Mitten im schwersten Sturm seiner bisherigen Kanzlerschaft sucht Friedrich Merz Abstand am Polarkreis. Während der Kanzler beim Arktis-Gipfel in Finnland über die EU-Strategie in der dortigen Region spricht, wackelt zu Hause die Koalition. Ein Blick hinter die Kulissen zeigt einen sichtlich angeschlagenen Regierungschef, dessen Rückhalt dramatisch schwindet. Rixa Fürsen und Hans von der Burchard sprechen über einen Kanzler, der europäisch Solidarität und Stärke zeigen will, den dabei aber die Ereignisse in Berlin bis nach Lappland verfolgen.
