World.title: Les lois physiques du réseau électrique ignorent la politique
World.content:
Il y a cinquante ans, à ma première Session du CIGRE à Paris, notre métier d’ingénieur était extrêmement simple. Nous avions de grosses centrales électriques, une demande prévisible, du fer et du cuivre. L’ « intelligence numérique » se résumait à un ingénieur avec un crayon bien taillé et un classeur. La « communication sans fil » ? Un collègue qui criait dans le poste.

Aujourd’hui, nous menons la transformation technologique la plus complexe de l’histoire de l’humanité : la transition énergétique. Et notre rôle est très clair : nous ne pouvons pas nous satisfaire de jouer les spectateurs, nous devons la piloter activement. Car si nous ne la gérons pas avec un savoir-faire technique solide, ce sont les lois physiques du réseau qui nous contrôleront — et ces lois physiques se moquent bien des mandats politiques ou des tendances sur les réseaux sociaux !

Chaque jour, nous équilibrons un système sous tension. La demande d’électricité explose à mesure que nous électrifions. Et nous devons électrifier les transports, le chauffage et l’industrie lourde, tandis que d’énormes data centers dédiés à l’IA engloutissent des mégawatts.

Dans le même temps, l’inertie des systèmes traditionnels disparaît. Nous remplaçons les lourdes turbines rotatives en acier par des énergies renouvelables à onduleurs fonctionnant à la vitesse de la microseconde, ce qui ne nous laisse aucune marge d’erreur. Les frontières physiques se sont complètement effacées : ce qui se passe au niveau d’une simple borne domestique de recharge pour véhicule électrique ou d’un panneau solaire installé sur un toit a désormais des répercussions sur les réseaux de transport à haute tension situés à des centaines de kilomètres de là.

Pour mener à bien cette transition complexe, la communauté énergétique mondiale doit s’aligner autour de trois piliers incontournables.

Premier pilier : transmission et distribution ne peuvent plus vivre dans des mondes séparés.

Historiquement, le transport et la distribution se comportaient un peu comme un couple marié depuis longtemps qui aurait cessé de se parler. Les gestionnaires de réseau de transport pensaient que les gestionnaires de réseau de distribution ne s’occupaient que d’ampoules et de lampadaires. Les distributeurs voyaient les transporteurs comme des opérateurs d’un gigantesque train électrique secret, quelque part dans les nuages.

Cette époque est révolue. Aujourd’hui, la distribution est un écosystème actif et dynamique, riche en énergie solaire, en stockage et en demande flexible. Ce qui se passe à la périphérie du réseau détermine directement la stabilité au cœur du système.

Transmission et distribution ne peuvent plus vivre dans des mondes séparés.

Un quartier qui injecte massivement du photovoltaïque à midi, un parc de batteries qui bascule en mode charge, une flotte de véhicules électriques qui se recharge en soirée : chaque décision locale a des répercussions globales. Ignorer cette réalité, c’est prendre le risque d’instabilités, de congestions, voire de blackouts.

Les régulateurs, les États et les investisseurs doivent traiter le réseau comme un tout, de la centrale au compteur, et non comme une collection de silos réglementaires et opérationnels.

© CIGRE

Deuxième pilier : nous ne pouvons pas ignorer l’importance capitale de l’accessibilité financière

C’est, à mon sens, la question que chaque bureau d’études devrait se poser : « Dans notre course pour construire le réseau de demain, n’oublions-nous pas ceux qui devront payer la facture ? »

Une transition énergétique qui creuse les inégalités ou alourdit la précarité énergétique n’est pas une transition réussie.

Alors que les dépenses d’investissement explosent à tous les niveaux, nous ne pouvons pas compter uniquement sur les subventions publiques pour nous sortir d’affaire. Nous devons intégrer directement l’accessibilité financière dans nos équations d’ingénierie. Cela implique d’éliminer les pertes de conversion superflues au niveau des interfaces complexes des onduleurs et d’optimiser nos solutions dans une optique d’économie circulaire, plutôt que de courir après du matériel flambant neuf.

Car si nos solutions ne sont pas abordables pour tous, nous aurons échoué dans notre mission. Une transition énergétique qui creuse les inégalités ou alourdit la précarité énergétique n’est pas une transition réussie.

Troisième pilier : des ingénieurs qualifiés, partout et à tous les niveaux, pour une vraie équité mondiale

Cela passe par la formation massive d’une nouvelle génération d’ingénieurs capables de penser simultanément physique du réseau, données, marchés de l’électricité et enjeux sociétaux. Cela passe aussi par un transfert de connaissances accéléré entre les systèmes électriques matures et ceux en développement, pour éviter que certains pays ne reproduisent des architectures obsolètes ou ne restent dépendants de technologies importées sans maîtrise locale.

Il n’y a pas de plan B, car il n’y a pas de planète B.

Le CIGRE, organisation indépendante à but non lucratif réunissant 25 000 membres dans 140 pays, contribue relever ce défi. Grâce à ses groupes de travail intégrant chercheurs, ingénieurs, industriels, fournisseurs, régulateurs et décideurs, il transforme l’expertise collective en recommandations, formations et solutions concrètes.

En responsabilisant les jeunes ingénieurs, nous garantissons que l’énergie durable et abordable soit accessible à toute l’humanité.

Il n’y a pas de plan B, car il n’y a pas de planète B

La transition énergétique n’est pas une option ; c’est une nécessité absolue. Et nous ne pouvons pas laisser cette tâche aux générations futures. Comme l’a si bien dit Barack Obama : « Nous sommes la première génération à ressentir les effets du changement climatique, et la dernière à pouvoir y remédier. »

Nous ne pouvons pas non plus laisser cette transformation aux seuls décideurs politiques. Nous devons assumer cette responsabilité ensemble : pour nos familles, pour nos communautés et pour le monde qui dépend de nous.

Car lorsque nous regardons vers l’avenir, une vérité prime sur tout le reste : il n’y a pas de plan B, car il n’y a pas de planète B.

World.title: Sweden’s election too close to call after late right-wing surge
World.content:
Speaking after midnight on Monday, she said the results so far pointed to an “even” outcome. “But right now we are leading and if this holds up, Sweden will get a new government,” she said, to cheers from thousands of supporters gathered at her party’s glitzy election night reception.

The vote is a watershed moment for Sweden and will be watched closely elsewhere in Europe, where other nationalist parties are gaining ground.

If he continues in office, Kristersson has promised to give ministerial posts to members of the populist nationalist Sweden Democrats, a strongly anti-immigration party founded in the 1980s by neo-Nazis. That would be a first in a country that had until recently shunned the far right.

Kristersson has been governing for the past four years with support from the Sweden Democrats in parliament, but without giving them a formal role in the coalition.

He said the closeness of the result would make forming a government “complicated,” but insisted the left had failed to win a majority for its “socialist” economic program.

Kristersson added he would talk to other party leaders. “Where it ends remains to be seen,” he told his supporters at the Moderates’ election night party in central Stockholm. “But we are not in a hurry.”

World.title: Sweden exit poll: Left on course for election win in blow to far right
World.content:
Two separate exit polls for Sweden’s SVT public broadcaster and TV4 showed Andersson’s left bloc on track to take 51% of the vote. (Sweden’s electoral system is based on proportional representation.) Kristersson’s alliance on the right was projected to win 47%.

Exit polls have not always been accurate in the past, but the picture should become clearer later on Sunday night when broadcasters are expected to announce updated forecasts after a critical mass of districts declare results. Whoever ends up winning, party leaders will take weeks to finalize a new coalition agreement.

“Swedish elections are always close,” Andersson told POLITICO earlier on Sunday as she toured the suburbs of Stockholm in her dark red campaign bus. “When I’ve been around Sweden, a lot of people I’ve spoken to said they see things that the government has done that they like but there are also lots of things that they don’t like. And many people say to me that it’s enough now.”

With the prospect of the far right entering government for the first time, the vote marks a watershed moment for Sweden that will be watched closely elsewhere in Europe, where other populist nationalist parties are gaining ground.

Even Andersson accepts that a victory for her left bloc would not consign the Sweden Democrats to history, especially if the final result is a narrow one.

“The hate that they have spread through this election, and if they would become ministers and use their platforms as ministers to spread hate? Well, we’ll see if the Swedish people are very tempted on that,” she said.

World.title: Suspected Russian spy behind drone attack in Leipzig
World.content:
Some 1.8 kilograms of the explosive Semtex was to be used across all three drones — about 600 grams per drone — according to the high-ranking German security official. The Antonov aircraft, which was the target of the attack, was fueled with approximately 25,000 liters of jet fuel.

Two of the senior security officials, both directly involved in the investigation, said that if the charge had detonated, it would have triggered a massive explosion and destroyed parts of the airport. Previously unseen surveillance camera footage obtained by Welt shows the drone lying right next to the Antonov aircraft. According to authorities, the explosive was concealed inside a food can. The explosion did not occur because a detonator broke off.

One day after the attempted attack, police officers found an antenna structure secured with tape in a tree near the airport. It is believed to have been used to control the drones, according to the confidential documents. On the structure, forensic technicians found remnants of a glove with traces of DNA previously recorded in Finland and Lithuania. The Belarusian suspect has a criminal record in those countries, according to one of the senior security officials (in Finland, for example, he was charged with theft, among other offenses).

The Polish authorities also believe the suspect was involved in a fire at a home improvement store in the city of Łódź in the summer of 2024, according to a senior security official. (The Łódź public prosecutor’s office has likewise classified the incident as sabotage.) German investigators view the fact that he was also involved in the Leipzig attack as further evidence of Russian involvement.

According to the high-ranking German security official, the explosives used in Leipzig were transported to Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia. Investigators believe they were transported in hidden compartments in trucks and subsequently cached underground. Police found several possible hiding places near Leipzig airport after analyzing data from a rental car used by the suspects.

The confidential police documents also refer to a concrete slab with two handles that was discovered near a pedestrian bridge south of the airport, in the city of Schkeuditz. Authorities believe it had provided access to a hidden storage site. Shortly thereafter, police found another suspected hideout north of the bridge; both storage sites were empty. Investigators also located a hideout in the city of Merseburg, part of the Halle-Leipzig area. According to the police documents, the Russian suspect may have temporarily stored the explosives there.

World.title: The ideas shaping von der Leyen’s pitch to Carney
World.content:
The most ambitious proposals would bring Canada closer to the EU’s single market, expanding its existing trade ties with the bloc and moving it toward the level of integration enjoyed by nations such as Switzerland and Norway.

Spanish Socialist lawmaker Javier Moreno, who chairs the Parliament’s delegation to Canada, called for the EU to integrate the country “even further” than Switzerland into its market. That could include giving Canadian citizens the freedom to live and work across the 27-country bloc and Canadian businesses smoother access to its 450 million consumers. Such an arrangement would be unprecedented for a country so geographically distant.

“Canadians are the most European people outside of Europe,” he said.

The push for closer ties comes after the U.S. banned imports of key Canadian manufacturing and agricultural goods, as the North American neighbors spiraled into a trade war with reciprocal tariffs after the collapse of negotiations last month.

Mark Carney, left, António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen meet in Brussels on June 23, 2025. | Olivier Matthys/AFP via Getty Images

“You don’t want to cause disappointment before the summit,” said an EU diplomat, referring to the October meeting, adding that von der Leyen should offer something tangible to Carney on Wednesday. They were granted anonymity to speak about the proposals under discussion, like others in this article.

That Carney will be seated in the chamber to hear von der Leyen’s address carries symbolic weight and “is already an important signal of the closeness of the relationship,” Geneviève Tuts, the EU’s ambassador to Canada, told POLITICO.

World.title: Le Pen vows to put French citizens first, tackle housing and cost-of-living crisis at first campaign speech
World.content:
Marine Le Pen put housing and the cost-of-living crisis at the heart of her presidential campaign on Sunday, using her first major speech in the former northern mining town of Hénin-Beaumont to promise French citizens that they would come “first in their own country” — regardless of skin colour, religion or origin.

 

"We will guarantee all French citizens a natural and fair right, as is done in every country in the world," said the far-right National Rally party's figurehead.

The presidential hopeful railed against the cost-of-living crisis, pledging to fix issues in the social housing sector but also in the private realm — pointing a finger at environmental and administrative restrictions governing planning laws.

Le Pen announced that the policy of "national priority" would apply to housing, adding that French citizens should receive preferential access to social housing.

She also told her supporters that she promised to cut VAT from 20% to 5.5% for gas, electricity and heating oil, while also chastising taxes: "Where is the money going when taxes and levies are getting heavier while the services delivered to French citizens are crumbling?"

Hénin-Beaumont: The National Rally's stronghold

Over the years, Hénin-Beaumont — which has an estimated population of 26,000 people — has become a National Rally stronghold. The mayor, Steeve Briois, has been in power for 14 years, while Le Pen has represented the Pas-de-Calais department — where the town is located — since 2017 in France's National Assembly.

Almost 20 years prior, she won her first political mandate as a regional councillor for the Nord-Pas-de-Calais region (which has now become Hauts-de-France) in 1998.

"How can I express my gratitude at seeing so many of you this year again, here, on this beautiful patriotic former mining land," Le Pen told the crowd on Sunday.

National Rally deputy and party spokesperson Laurent Jacobelli told Euronews that it’s clear why the party has won over locals.

“The Pas-de-Calais region was formerly a mining hub, where people worked hard, paid their taxes, and gave everything to France to support their families and build homes. But they were violently let down by globalisation, by the failure of public services. Here we understood that sovereignty means something, that homeland and the nation are important values,” he told Euronews.

“This is why Marine Le Pen has won over voters: because she is proving that sovereignty and re-industrialisation are achievable."

Although Jordan Bardella — who is running to become France’s next prime minister — did not address the crowd on Sunday, Le Pen got supporters to sing “Happy Birthday” to him. A show of unity, as rumours about possible tensions between the two National Rally figureheads have swirled in recent weeks.

Le Pen had a busy weekend: before heading to Hénin-Beaumont on Sunday, she met with MPs from her party for a closed-door political meeting in the coastal town of Le Touquet on Saturday.

What do locals think of the National Rally?

But for locals, Le Pen's visit was not the only item on the agenda: Sunday also marked the town’s annual flea market. Although Le Pen cancelled her parade through the market due to "meteorological conditions", locals and residents from neighbouring towns still turned out in force to sell their second-hand goods, undeterred by the rain.

Local resident Cathy told Euronews that there was a time when the National Rally party's positions were "harder to defend", but that this is no longer her view today, describing Marine Le Pen as "very brave".

Jean-Marie Le Pen, the founder of the National Rally, openly promoted racism and antisemitism, while his daughter, Marine Le Pen, has spent over a decade working to normalise the image of the party, formerly known as the National Front, both at home and abroad, as part of an effort to distance it from her father’s legacy.

Last week, the National Rally party found itself in the crossfire when the French regional newspaper Midi Libre released a video filmed in November 2025, which showed several municipal police officers in Carcassonne making racist, sexist and conspiracy-related comments during a night-time patrol.

Although the emergence of the video made headlines across France, local supporters said they either hadn’t heard of it or didn’t attribute much importance to it.

“I don’t think that just because we vote for Marine Le Pen that we are racists," responded Antoine, a 19-year-old National Rally activist, who did not comment on the specificities of the video.

A young boy holds an French flag during the rally of French far-right leader Marine Le Pen Sunday, Sept.13, 2026 in Henin-Beaumont, northern France. (AP Photo/Jean-Francois Ba AP Photo

Meanwhile, many locals, such as policeman Laurent, said they firmly backed Le Pen. For him, she fits his ideal presidential brief: “someone who prioritises national interests and fights for the people.”

For Catherine, a local who works in Lille, local authorities do a good job keeping the city safe, clean and with plenty of activities for young and old alike.

Multiple residents also praised local tax rates — the local council has repeatedly lowered the municipal property tax rate on buildings.

When questioned about Marine Le Pen's 2027 presidential bid, lots of locals said they supported her but either refrained from commenting on her specific policy proposals or said they weren't aware of the finer details.

One recent retiree, who has lived in Hénin-Beaumont for the past 25 years and spoke to Euronews on condition of anonymity, said that the National Rally was doing all in its power to "dazzle" locals."

"Many businesses here are run by Algerians, Moroccans, and Tunisians. Some people think that if the National Rally is voted in, then all the Arabs will leave, but we are French, we have French passports, and many of us are dual nationals."

"I know that many of my neighbours vote for the National Rally, but I turn a blind eye. We do know how to live together here, as a community," she said.

For Sana, a Spanish-Moroccan local business owner, Marine Le Pen's proposal to hold a referendum to ban the hijab in all public spaces is not an acceptable measure.

"I don't wear a headscarf, but for the rights of other women, I am against this kind of measure," she told Euronews.

Meanwhile, activists from the anti-fascist collective of the mining area (Collectif Anti-Fasciste du Bassin Minier) set up a protest banner outside the Hénin-Beaumont train station on Sunday.

Activist Ludivine told Euronews that there are plenty of residents in Marine Le Pen's constituency who "firmly stand against the far-right."

"We are in post-industrial abandoned areas, where unemployment is rising, so the narrative that this is all the fault of scapegoats is rising very quickly," she said.

Meanwhile, fellow activist Laurence stressed that "the fact the National Rally is in power does not remove the fact that plenty of people are unhappy; they may just stay quiet, be scared, or not know how to express their opposition and resistance to the horrible and dangerous ideas espoused by this party.

When asked about his opinion about the National Rally, one local businessman said that he did not even want to speak on the condition of anonymity, out of fear he would have "issues" with local authorities and face possible intimidation.

World.title: Could nuclear fusion power save planet Earth – or is it just a money sink?
World.content:
It is a special moment when the doors of one of the world’s largest laser-fusion fuel laboratories swing open: scientists slip on blue full-body protective suits, mechanics tinker with precision milling machines, and laboratory technicians peer through high-powered microscopes at fuel pellets just four millimetres in size.

 

We are in Darmstadt, an industrial city in the western German state of Hesse. Here, at the headquarters of the start-up Focused Energy, an international team of highly motivated specialists aims to develop laser fusion to the point where it is ready for industrial application. The company’s goal is to have its first commercial laser-fusion power plant operating in 15 years at the earliest.

The fuel pellets are just four millimetres in size. Hans von der Brelie

Is nuclear fusion really the answer to energy security?

“As humanity, we need carbon-free energy. Renewable energies alone will not be enough. Humanity’s energy demand is far too great,” argues Ulrich Sigel, Vice President of Focused Energy. “If we want to decarbonise, we need fusion energy for all sectors: transport, aviation, shipping, industry, heating – this is where a huge market for CO₂-neutral energy generation is emerging.”

Renewable energies alone will not be enough. Humanity’s energy demand is far too great. Ulrich Sigel VP Focused Energy

Professor Sven Linow of the Scientific Climate Advisory Board of the Hessian state government, however, is sceptical. “My personal view is that we should not go for it,” he replies when asked by Euronews Earth whether large sums of money should continue to be poured into the development of fusion energy.

Meeting Sven Linow at the futuristic high-rise building at Darmstadt University of Applied Sciences: “No one has yet demonstrated that it works.” Hans von der Brelie

It is a sweltering hot day when we meet Linow for an interview in the shade of the futuristic high-rise building at Darmstadt University of Applied Sciences. “No one has yet demonstrated that it really works,” says Linow.

No one has yet demonstrated that it really works. Sven Linow Scientific Climate Advisory Board of the Hessian state government

In the US, experiments have shown that, in the crossfire of numerous high-power lasers, light atomic nuclei can actually fuse, releasing energy in the process. However, in order to generate a stable supply of electricity for consumers, these extremely complex experiments would have to be ‘scaled up’.

For a commercial power plant, such laser-induced fusion would have to take place 10 times per second – around the clock. Even the most optimistic staff at Focused Energy admit they are still a long way from achieving this.

For a commercial power plant, laser-induced fusion would have to take place 10 times per second – around the clock. Hans von der Brelie

Problems with fuel supply aren’t deterring investors

Linow’s main argument against fusion energy, however, is a different one: the fuel supply. “The problem is tritium,” says the professor. “There are [an estimated] 50 kilograms of it worldwide. In 12.3 years, only half of that will remain; it decays with a half-life of 12.3 years. To start up a fusion power station, you need a few kilograms of it, and then you use it up. You’d have to regenerate the tritium within the power station. Nobody has ever tried that before. There is no demonstrator; there is no laboratory experiment in which this has been successfully tested. There are only ideas,” he says.

Speaking to Euronews Earth at Focused Energy’s head office, Sigel admits there are still “unresolved issues” with tritium recovery, but says this is more of an engineering challenge than a fundamental problem of physics. For research labs trying to tackle fuel cycle problems, “this is an exciting engineering task, and that’s something we’re good at in Germany,” says Sigel. “I’m optimistic that we’ll solve it.”

“I’m optimistic that we’ll solve all remaining challenges”, Focused Energy VP Ulrich Sigel (at the right) tells Euronews Earth (left). Hans von der Brelie

Sigel’s optimism is shared by some politicians. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) has thrown his weight behind the project, announcing Germany’s goal to put “the world’s first fusion power plant online”, as has the Hessian state government. As the Minister-President of Hesse, Boris Rhein (CDU), said: “Nuclear fusion could be the game-changer in energy supply.”

Nuclear fusion could be the game-changer in energy supply. Boris Rhein Minister-President of Hesse

International investors also seem enthusiastic: in an initial funding round in the spring, $240 million (€207m) was raised – the largest series A financing in the global fusion industry. The German energy company RWE increased its investment by €60 million.

In an initial funding round in the spring, $240 million (€207m) was raised – the largest series A financing in the global fusion industry. Hans von der Brelie

So why are Professor Linow and the Hessian state government’s Scientific Climate Advisory Council speaking up against fusion energy?

Is nuclear fusion diverting funding away from more realistic solutions?

In part, they question whether the money and political attention devoted to fusion would be better spent on technologies that can cut emissions today.

“The region’s energy supply is set to be climate-neutral by 2045. Will the first large-scale fusion power stations be connected to the grid by then? And the answer is: no, that’s not going to happen,” says Linow. His message is clear: first and foremost, renewable energy sources should be rapidly expanded, the electricity grids modernised and sufficient electricity storage capacity created.

Ulrich Sigel of Focused Energy emphasises that they do not wish to compete with renewable energy sources. In his concept, fusion energy would complement renewables by providing low-carbon electricity even when the sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing.

The company is pressing ahead. “We want to have the demonstrator up and running in five years,” Sigel tells Euronews Earth. “The first pilot power station should be operational in 10 years, and the first commercial power station in 15 years.”

"The first pilot power station should be operational in 10 years, and the first commercial power station in 15 years", says Focused Energy VP Ulrich Sigel. Focused Energy

Nuclear power vs nuclear fusion: What’s the difference?

Fusion power stations are intended to replace their climate-damaging coal- and oil-fired counterparts and serve as an alternative to nuclear fission power stations.

Nuclear fission splits heavy atoms to release energy and is used today, while nuclear fusion joins light atoms to release even more energy but remains experimental.

Nuclear fission splits heavy atoms to release energy and is used today, while nuclear fusion joins light atoms to release even more energy but remains experimental. Focused Energy

Compared with nuclear power stations, “fusion power stations really only have advantages,” says Sigel. “We don’t need enriched uranium, which might have to come from Russia or elsewhere. We don’t produce long-lived radioactive waste that then has to be managed for an eternity in some final repository."

Ulrich Sigel: Our operations are much safer. There are no chain reactions, no uncontrollable reactions. We can press a button to switch off the laser, and the power station shuts down,” he claims.

Compared to nuclear fission plants, "our laser fusion operations are much safer. There are no chain reactions", Focused Energy VP Sigel says.. Hans von der Brelie

Professor Sven Linow counters that, in fusion power plants, the inner reactor compartment must be replaced “roughly every two years”. After all, even nuclear fusion is not entirely free of radioactivity. “The reactor vessels must be removed regularly and allowed to decay,” he explains.

In some cases, “you can’t handle them again until several hundred years have passed – perhaps even 1,000 years. Consequently, at some point there will be 200, 400 or 500 of these reactor vessels – which are relatively large – stored on the site. And you’ll have to secure them first.”

After all, even nuclear fusion is not entirely free of radioactivity. “The reactor vessels must be removed regularly and allowed to decay,” Sven Linow explains. Hans von der Brelie

Focused Energy’s Sigel acknowledges that radioactive “activation of, for example, the reactor wall” does take place. However, he claims, “We can reduce this activation to 60-to-80 years by using special low-activation steels... The steel will simply be stored on the power station site for that long and can then, once the decay period is over, be returned to the cycle and recycled as normal,” he claims. “We’re talking here about manageable doses and very manageable timeframes.”

Is nuclear fusion a sound investment?

Renewable energies are now relatively inexpensive in terms of investment. Fusion energy, on the other hand, requires very high investment. Is it even worth the effort? Yes, says Sigel; no, says Linow.

“When it comes to renewable energies, you mustn’t just calculate the production costs, but also the system costs,” says Sigel. “In other words: what does it cost to get the energy from A to B? We need transmission grids. Then, of course, we don’t always have wind and sunshine, so we have to provide back-up power stations and battery storage. That’s why fusion energy will be absolutely competitive [compared to] renewable energy,” he claims, though fusion plants would have their own system costs to consider too.

Professor Linow takes the opposite view: “It is foreseeable that fusion power will be by far the most expensive form of energy, significantly more expensive even than nuclear fission power. At least 20 cents per kilowatt-hour, perhaps even two or three times that.”

"Fusion power will be by far the most expensive form of energy, significantly more expensive even than nuclear fission power", says professor Sven Linow. Hans von der Brelie

Sigel counters: “We use water as fuel and breed the tritium in the reactor itself. The main cost factor for us is the capital expenditure. However, the power station will be able to operate for a very long time, and that will result in low electricity generation costs within the power station itself.”

Linow arrives at a very different conclusion when looking at the big picture: “I don’t have a good feeling about this. An estimated €35 to 40 billion will be invested in ITER (a magnetic fusion demonstrator). Then DEMO is to be built, which will cost at least as much. On top of that, we have around 50 fusion start-ups, all working simultaneously to prepare fusion power stations.

“Many billions are currently being poured into this, and that is money that is lacking elsewhere. We should set priorities and say: first of all, let’s build what’s necessary to prevent the climate from spiralling completely out of control. We must ensure that we have a reasonably stable society on this planet. Once we’ve achieved that and still have the funds to spare, then we can move forward with fusion.

World.title: US push to cut drug prices could mean longer waits for European patients
World.content:
Last May, US President Donald Trump pushed to align drug pricing with the lowest levels among other developed nations — so-called most-favoured-nation (MFN) pricing. However, the pricing policy might have negative consequences.

 

European patients might have to wait longer for some novel medicines as the US forces drugmakers to offer prices that match other high‑income countries, such as Germany or France, according to a new modelling study published in The Lancet.

Researchers looked at 195 patented medicines that together account for $87.9 billion of US’ annual spending. They found that for three in four medicines studied, the money companies would lose by lowering prices in the US would be greater than their total yearly sales in the countries used to set US prices.

To minimise losses in the US — the world’s largest pharmaceutical market, companies “could be incentivised to delay market launch in the lowest-priced countries in the reference market," researchers said, as by delaying launches drugmakers could avoid having to match those lower prices in the US.

“Policies in the US may impact access to medicines globally,” study author Kerstin Vokinger of ETH Zurich and the University of Zurich said in a press release.

The ones who would feel the impact ultimately are patients.

“The risk is very concrete: if pharmaceutical companies delay launching medicines in Europe because European prices may be used to determine prices in the United States, patients here could wait longer for treatments that are already available elsewhere,” European Patients Forum told Euronews Health in a written comment. “For someone living with a serious or progressive condition, an additional wait can have a real impact on their health and quality of life.”

The US policy already has an impact in Europe.

Reference countries in Europe that were included in the modelling study. MapChart

Implications in Europe

Europe has seen a fall in drug launches in recent months. 10 months after Trump's executive order, drug launches in EU markets fell by some 35% compared with the previous ​10 months, Reuters reported in March.

While it is not clear whether the fall is directly linked to the policies in the US, it was announced in February that a drug for treating particularly severe cases of high cholesterol withdrawal from the market could be due to the US President Donald Trump's drug pricing policy.

“It's true that even in bigger countries like Germany, we see companies reconsidering whether they launch or when they launch,” Alexander Natz, chief of biotech entrepreneurs' lobby Eucope, told Euronews, explaining that the current situation forces drugmakers to think twice before a launch.

”We shouldn't expect that we're not getting access to any medicine, but we should expect that decisions are made in a much more careful way by companies,” he added.

Natz believes that to ensure Europe has new medicines without a delay, governments need to be willing to spend more.

“We must have a debate, an internal political debate in Germany and in other countries, how much are we willing to spend for healthcare?” he said.

The countries are already feeling that pressure on their tight budgets.

“Referenced countries, from Germany to Japan to Australia, are facing substantial pressure from the US administration and industry to raise prices and spending on medicines,” said Thomas Hwang of Brigham and Women’s Hospital and lead author of the study.

“But this is colliding with the reality that other countries have limited budget room to give.”

To minimise the negative outcomes, authors of the study note that manufacturers and countries might turn to list prices — that is, the manufacturer’s sticker price before discounts — rather than net prices, which reflect confidential rebates.

In the meantime, under recently updated European Union pharmaceutical rules, a company has to launch a new medicine if requested by a country within three years — or lose two years of monopoly rights.

This conditionality serves as a “counterweight” to the aftermath of Trump’s drug pricing policy; however, it is “unlikely to meaningfully alter the magnitude of savings by themselves,” authors wrote. Natz was also sceptical whether this could be enough for erasing posible negative consequences of US pricing policy.

How much is the US saving?

While the US drug pricing policy is risking delays in Europe, it could allow the US to cut expenditure by $5.2 billion for medicines used in hospitals and $6.4 billion for medicines bought in pharmacies, according to the Lancet study. Those savings could rise to $21 billion and $25.5 billion, respectively, under a broader application of the policy.

But as 17 companies have struck confidential deals with the administration, excluding them from these rules, the potential savings would be cut by 71%.

While the most-favoured-nation pricing has the potential “to deliver real savings to the US federal government and taxpayers … if manufacturers can evade participation in these models by striking side deals, most of those savings might not be realised,” said Hwang.

European Patients Forum said that if US drug pricing policy’s “implementation leads to delayed launches in other countries without delivering the expected savings for Medicare [US health insurance program], this risks becoming a lose-lose situation for both health systems and patients.”

The European Commission is looking at the issue too, as health ministers in mid-June tasked the European Health Commissioner to assess the impact of the US’ most-favoured-nation policy on the bloc: whether MFN is resulting in delayed launches, significantly higher prices — and, ultimately, reduced access to innovative medicines.

In the study, which is yet to be published but seen by Euronews Health, the Commission says that it is currently nearly impossible to indicate whether the delays or price pressures can be linked directly to US pricing policies or are rather a result of current uncertainties around it, pointing to the following years for greater clarity.

“I understand the commission study that it basically says it's too early to really benchmark individual prices. So far, so good. Maybe that's true. But the implications are much wider,” Natz said, adding that “it's not only about that price; it's [also] about is that product will ever be launched in Europe? Will that reach patients in Germany? That is a real question here.”

World.title: Leaf-peeping by rail: Europe’s best autumn train journeys
World.content:
Gazing out the window at the ever-changing landscapes whipping past is one of the great pleasures of train travel.

 

All seasons have their appeal, but watching autumn's foliage colour transformation is particularly mesmerising.

Overtourism, scorching temperatures and hefty tourist taxes have also made travelling in the shoulder season even more attractive.

So, if you’re looking to take advantage of the calm that comes with the colder months, why not consider some leaf-peeping aboard a train?

Europe’s best train journeys for autumn

Japanese rail operator JR Pass analysed popular routes from across Europe using online ratings, Instagram hashtags, search insights, and seasonal weather data, to compile five of the best rail journeys in Europe with the “crispiest fall settings”.

The travel experts found a “growing appetite for immersive experiences” during autumn, arguing that travelling by train is the perfect way to witness the seasons change.

GoldenPass Line, Switzerland

Ranking first is Switzerland’s acclaimed GoldenPass Line, which runs on historic railways that date back to the 1890s.

Starting off in Montreux and ending up in Interlaken, this 191km journey showcases iconic Alpine landscapes from Lake Geneva to panoramic views of Mont Blanc, Matterhorn, and Eiger.

A train running along the Golden Pass Railway. Shutterstock. Supplied by JR Pass.

Highlights include the historic Châteaux de Chillon, a medieval fortress perched on the shores of Lake Geneva, as well as Tsanfleuron Glacier, which is located around 3,000 metres above sea level.

“With the route boasting clear skies for over half the autumn season (52.55%) and around one in four days seeing rain, the climate provides promising autumn viewing conditions,” JR Pass tells Euronews Travel.

A second-class ticket can be bought for around €60, without a seat reservation.

Tren de Sóller, Mallorca

If you’re searching for something a little warmer, Spain’s Tren de Sóller could be the perfect alternative.

Built in 1912, with original wooden carriages still in use, this electric railway stretches from Sóller to Palma, winding through the island’s underrated mountains and citrus groves.

A train track on the Sóller Railway journey. Shutterstock. Supplied by JR Pass.

Ranking second thanks to Mallorca**’**s lack of rainfall and clear skies, this train journey is perfect for art lovers. At Sóller train station, you’ll find two permanent exhibitions with original works by Miró and Picasso.

Other highlights include the Cathedral Basilica of Santa Maria, the World Heritage Site of Serra de Tramuntana, and endless scenic views.

Return tickets are priced at €40.

Rhodope Narrow Gauge Railway, Bulgaria

Bulgaria’s Narrow Gauge Railway is a great way to explore one of Europe’s “most unspoiled landscapes”.

The 125 km route links the Gornotrakiyska Valley with the Rhodope and Pirin mountains, and is considered one of the country’s best engineering feats to date.

“The line is undoubtedly a cherished national treasure, celebrated for its rich history, remarkable technical specifications, and breathtaking landscapes,” the railway’s official website says.

A train running on the Rhodope Narrow Gauge Railway. Shutterstock. Supplied by JR Pass.

Each station and stop offers tourists a wide choice of hiking trails and scenic views of the mountain ranges, as well as golden beech forests and quaint villages that appear “frozen in time”.

With an average of just five rainy days in autumn, passengers can expect “crisp, pristine conditions”.

Day tour package tickets start from €79, but may be lower depending on your travel date.

Semmering Railway, Austria

Famed for being the world’s first standard gauge line across a high mountain pass, the Semmering Railway is one of the greatest feats of civil engineering still running today.

Departing from Gloggnitz and ending in Mürzzuschlag, travellers will be able to marvel at stone viaducts, carved tunnels, and spectacular mountain landscapes.

Scenic views of mountains and a viaduct on the Semmering Railway. Shutterstock. Supplied by JR Pass.

JR Pass hails the journey for showing off Austria’s “vibrant tapestry of colours”. This, combined with clear skies for almost half of the autumn season, makes it an ideal journey to embark on during the colder months.

Standard class tickets for the 36-minute journey start from around €10.

Schneeberg Railway, Austria

One of Europe’s last remaining cog railways, this mountain line whisks passengers up to Hochschneeberg station at an elevation of 1,800 metres.

“Baumgartner station is a great place to stop off on the way,” says Schneeberg Railway’s official website.

Scenic views on the Schneeberg Railway. Shutterstock. Supplied by JR Pass.

“This is because you can sample delicious Schneeberg buchteln – sweet rolls filled with jam that are a treat for the taste buds.”

At the top of the trail, tourists can soak up panoramic views of the surrounding mountain peaks.

Low season rates for adults begin at €33.50 one way.

Further afield: A leaf-peeping rail journey in Japan

Earlier this year, insurance experts InsureandGo turned to eye-tracking technology to analyse the attractiveness of the scenery on some of the world’s most popular rail routes.

Participants were shown multiple images of iconic views from train journeys. The analysts then tracked how long they spent looking at the scenery and how quickly their eyes were drawn to it.

A leaf-peeping rail journey in Japan note thanun

The top spot went to Japan’s Sagano Romantic Train, which passes by the Arashiyama bamboo forest in Kyoto.

This is a short 25-minute ride along the Hozu River between Saga-Arashiyama and Kameoka, but it packs some of the most eye-catching scenery in Asia, easily admired from the train’s open-sided carriage.

It is particularly mesmerising in autumn when the maples turn fiery shades of red and gold.

World.title: EU to further tighten migration policy after Ceuta crisis
World.content:
The European Commission is expected to further harden its migration policy in the wake of the Ceuta crisis, with major changes set to be adopted in the coming months and potentially announced by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in her State of the Union speech this week.

 

The events of 30 July represented the largest influx of irregular migrants in recent years, with around 80,000 people entering the Spanish exclave in a single day, adding pressure to an already clear political initiative to tighten migration rules in EU-wide legislation.

Despite a steady decline in both irregular crossings and asylum applications in the EU since 2023, three new options are now on the table to strengthen the bloc’s external borders and increase the return of irregular migrants, according to several EU officials, diplomats and MEPs who spoke to Euronews.

“The images we have seen this summer are too disturbing for Europeans,” one EU official said. "Something major on migration has to be announced for sure."

The options are not mutually exclusive, and von der Leyen could ultimately decide to pursue more than one.

Temporary suspension of the right to asylum

The most disruptive proposal currently being discussed concerns a temporary suspension of asylum rules in cases of sudden, large-scale arrivals.

This would mean EU countries would no longer be obliged to process asylum claims from people who have entered irregularly in circumstances such as those seen in Ceuta.

“This idea is floating, and it would be a significant change,” another EU official told Euronews.

Under current rules, any foreign national present in an EU country has the right to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered Europe, with their claim assessed on an individual basis.

The change is being pushed by some member states that have already adopted similar measures in recent years.

Greece suspended the processing of asylum claims for three months for migrants arriving by sea from Libya in July 2025, while Poland has had a similar ban in place for migrants crossing the border from Belarus since March 2025.

It would mark a further step in the tightening of asylum rights, after new rules that entered into force last June accelerated the asylum process through a “border procedure” for people arriving from countries considered safe.

More powers for Frontex

The European Commission’s desire to increase both the powers and the size of border agency Frontex is not new, but it has been given fresh impetus by what happened in Ceuta, according to an EU official.

Von der Leyen promised to triple the EU border agency’s staff in her re-election speech to the European Parliament in July 2024, bringing its personnel up to 30,000 officers. Frontex is also set to receive €12 billion under the EU’s next seven-year budget, doubling its previous allocation.

A wide-ranging reform of its mandate is expected by the end of the year, although the details remain unclear.

“Changes could include involvement in migrants’ returns, wider cooperation with third countries and a more active role in surveillance,” a Frontex official told Euronews, adding that a concrete proposal is likely to be put forward in October.

At this stage, even the agency’s board is not fully aware of the Commission’s plans, and Director Hans Leijtens has not been informed by von der Leyen's office about the content of the speech.

“The main question is whether Frontex will be able to take over from national authorities in crisis situations such as the one in Ceuta,” a senior MEP with knowledge of the matter told Euronews, expressing doubts that this could happen.

The agency could instead be given a role in deporting irregular migrants to third countries other than their country of origin, as provided for under the new Return Regulation, which is due to be formally adopted in the autumn.

Related European Parliament to debate Ceuta crisis amid fierce political backlash

EU money for return hubs

The deportation centres enabled by the regulation are another area in which the Commission could take a bold step.

The legislation gives member states broad autonomy in defining agreements with third countries that are set to host the so-called “return hubs”. Five EU member states are already in advanced talks with some partner countries, whose names have not been disclosed, with the aim of starting deportations by 2026.

The current rules do not foresee any financial involvement by the EU in these agreements. National governments are expected to fully finance the hubs and may also provide additional funding, commercial partnerships or other incentives to partner countries.

The major new development could be a promise to finance the hubs through the EU budget, with the Commission’s proposal allocating €74 billion to migration management for 2028-2034.

“The majority of member states have expressed interest in this kind of project. A common way of financing them in the future cannot be excluded,” an EU official told Euronews, referring to a joint letter dated in June in which 19 EU countries praised “innovative solutions” aimed at reducing irregular migration flows.

Beyond the support of most member states, all three proposals have the backing of the European People’s Party (EPP), which could facilitate their approval in the European Parliament.

As has happened with all migration-related files under the current legislation, the EPP could secure support for the changes with a majority drawing on support from right-wing conservative and far-right MEPs.

NGOs, civil society organisations and left-wing political groups, meanwhile, are expected to challenge whatever is announced in the State of the Union, having already strongly criticised the Commission’s recent migration policy guidelines.

“Pursuing in the same direction is a terrible mistake,” Greens MEP Mélissa Camara told Euronews.

World.title: Germany's Alexander Zverev beats Ben Shelton to win US Open title
World.content:
Germany's Alexander Zverev on Sunday conquered the US Open, defeating American Ben Shelton in four sets at the Arthur Ashe Stadium to claim his first US Open title and the second Grand Slam trophy of his career.

 

Six years after letting a two-set lead slip against Dominic Thiem in the 2020 final, the German top seed returned to New York and this time finished the job beating Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2 on Sunday.

Zverev knew what he was up against, playing a US Open final in a stadium full of people desperate to at last see another American champion.

He tuned out the screams for Ben Shelton for so long that he didn’t even realise when he won, not hearing the chair umpire’s announcement that the match was over.

“In that moment I was in the zone, a lot,” Zverev said. “I didn’t hear noise at all. I was in this kind of tunnel where I just didn’t hear anything.”

The German's win in New York redeems the painful 2020 loss, where he let things slip away.

Being a no. 1 seed in a Grand Slam for the first time, Zverev capitalised on Shelton’s shaky start in his first major final, played a nearly flawless tiebreaker on serve and then turned back a comeback attempt in front of a crowd that feverishly cheered Shelton on — including girlfriend Trinity Rodman, who made it from her own soccer match in Washington before the finish.

“I know today 99.9% of the people wanted Ben to win, so I’m very sorry first of all,” Zverev said during the trophy presentation. “But second, it was an incredible atmosphere to play in. Even though I know that the crowd was against me, the crowd was always incredibly fair.”

Shelton was trying to win the first title by an American man since Andy Roddick won in Flushing Meadows in 2003, as well as become the first Black player to win the men’s crown since Arthur Ashe in 1968.

“It’s such a cool moment. Walking out on that court today, there’s nothing like it. I’ve never felt anything like that before,” Shelton said.

But Zverev was too good in majors this year and apparently didn’t even know how good he was. After hitting a serve winner, he dropped back behind the baseline as if set to return. Zverev, who later explained he thought the score was 5-1, eventually did figure out he had won, raising his arms in celebration.

Zverev's US Open triumph extends his majors streak

Zverev improved to 25-2 in major matches this year and won $5.5 million, matching the prize earned by women’s champion Elena Rybakina on Saturday as the largest in Grand Slam history.

“You’re one of the very best players in the world, maybe the best player in the world this year,” Shelton told Zverev.

He thought this title would come in 2020 and still acknowledges it should have. He won the first two sets against Dominic Thiem and got within two points of victory before becoming the first man to blow a two-set lead and lose in the final since 1949.

Alexander Zverev, of Germany, left, poses with the trophy after he won the men's singles final of the U.S. Open tennis championships against Ben Shelton, of the United States AP Photo

Whatever ghosts were left from then are long gone now.

Zverev also reached the final at Wimbledon, falling to Jannik Sinner, and became the No. 1 seed in New York when the top-ranked Sinner had to withdraw with a knee injury. He made the most of opportunities that came when Carlos Alcaraz had to sit out two majors and Sinner missed another after they played in three straight Grand Slam finals in 2025.

“I think God has seen how hard we worked, how much we suffered, and how much pain we went through, and I think 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before,” Zverev said, addressing his team.

Shelton had already eliminated the defending champion when he beat No. 2 seed Alcaraz in a five-set quarterfinal that ended at 3:33 a.m., the latest finish in US Open history.

But he fell short on Sunday in his attempt to become the first man to beat the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds en route to the US Open title since 1975.

The No. 8 seed fell to 0-6 against Zverev, winning a set Sunday for only the second time.

World.title: Film director Isabel Coixet bequeaths a defence of the analogue world to future Cervantes
World.content:
A cassette with 18 songs in which Camarón, Lucho Gatica and, very significantly, the Catalan rumba of "La lista de la compra" by La Cabra Mecánica and María Jiménez all rub shoulders. A personal collage, with a distinctly Lynchian feel, intentionally devoid of any explicit meaning. And a letter written with a Bic biro, with which Isabel Coixet underlines the handmade nature of her gesture and, in passing, pays tribute to torrijas, clay water jugs and open-air summer cinemas.

 

The filmmaker (Sant Adrià del Besós, 1960) nostalgically champions, in short, a present that is on the verge of extinction, which may have vanished altogether by 2076. That is the year when box 1586 at the Instituto Cervantes will be opened, where the honouree has deposited these objects as part of her legacy to the public institution devoted to promoting the Spanish language.

The collage, pen, cassette and letter by Isabel Coixet that the Caja de las Letras will safeguard for the next 50 years Instituto Cervantes

"Understanding makes the mind lazy," says Florence Green in "The Bookshop". Coixet (historian, publicist, screenwriter and standard-bearer of the third wave of Spanish women directors) quoted her in her speech to explain why she chose not to assign any meaning to the collage in her Cervantes legacy, created on the cover of an abandoned 1913 book.

"I am writing this with a Bic biro, my favourite. I wonder if they still exist. You, whoever you are, do not be taken in by treatises on the wonders of the world. The Bic biro is one of humanity's great inventions," she writes in her letter, which was read out during the ceremony at the Institute. Not everything is a rallying cry: Coixet also takes the opportunity to rail against speciality coffee chains. "I hope," she wishes her anonymous reader, "that you never have the misfortune of coming across them."

Perhaps for that reason, among the selection of songs Coixet is sending into the future, she has chosen to highlight "La lista de la compra". "It seems to me that in 50 years' time all the things that song talks about - the kitchen table covered in crumbs, those unbearable mixed plates, sweat, scrubbing, scouring - may well be a thing of the past."

The Catalan director, who is to receive the Antonio de Sancha Award 2026 from the Madrid Publishers' Association ("for her outstanding work in bringing literature closer to the general public and for her defence of bookshops as spaces of cultural resistance"), has immersed herself in the world of film adaptations in her penultimate creative phase. In the already mentioned "The Bookshop", in a kind of metafiction, the protagonist defends her new business in rural England as both an exercise and a weapon of liberation.

The event continued with a conversation between Coixet and the former president of the Association of Women Filmmakers and Audiovisual Media, Cristina Andreu, in which the two looked back over their prolific careers. Earlier, the director of the Cervantes, Luis García Montero, had also dedicated a brief speech to her: "Her films have travelled far and wide, but it would be a mistake to confuse that international trajectory with simple geography, because she has turned freedom and travel into a way of working her way towards the heart of things."

Actress Juliette Binoche (right) receives the Donostia Award from Coixet (left) for her contribution to cinema at the 70th San Sebastián Film Festival Álvaro Barrientos / AP

The filmmaker has been nominated four times for the Golden Bear at the Berlin Film Festival, and once (for "Map of the Sounds of Tokyo") for the Palme d'Or in Cannes. Over the course of her career she has also won eight Goya Awards, as a director, screenwriter and documentarian. Since 2015 she has been a Chevalier of the Order of Arts and Letters in France, and she has received Spain's National Film Award as well as the Gold Medal of Fine Arts in 2009.

The Caja de las Letras at the Institute stores almost 1,800 tributes in the vault at its Madrid headquarters, a tradition that began in 2007 for all kinds of figures - individuals and institutions, living or dead - from the Spanish-speaking cultural world.

World.title: Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is signalling a move to expand nuclear power cooperation with Russia, just as his country’s first Russian-built nuclear station prepares to go live later this year. The deepening partnership is likely to unsettle Turkey’s western allies.

Advertising

On the sidelines of a recent gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan told his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that Russia and Turkey “will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant”.

The Akkuyu nuclear power plant, built by Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due to go online later this year.

Erdogan’s announcement comes amid strained ties with Russia, as the Turkish leader has deepened relations with United States President Donald Trump.

Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, head of the Ankara office of US think tank the German Marshall Fund, describes Erdogan’s move as a “gesture” to Putin.

“Although Turkey is competing with Russia geopolitically, and although Turkey is firmly anchored in NATO and is improving its relationship with the United States, it does not intend to sever all ties with Russia,” Unluhisarcikli explained.

“Indeed, Turkey sees the Turkey-Russia relationship as a long-term strategic one. And this is, by the way, consistent with Turkey's balancing act.”

Trump tests Turkey's energy dependence on Russia with lure of US power

Nuclear lifeline

For Ankara, nuclear energy promises to help it break free from its heavy reliance on imported power. Once operational, the Akkuyu plant in southern Turkey will supply as much as 10 percent of the country’s electricity.

Rosatom owns the Akkuyu power plant and will recoup the estimated €21.5 billion construction costs by selling electricity to Turkey, generating annual income of around €2-3 billion.

Such income could be a vital tool for Moscow to mitigate tightening sanctions by both the European Union and the United States.

“The Akkuyu nuclear power plant allows Russia to build itself various state-to-state payment channels to store liquidity in Turkish banks without necessarily interfering with any sanctions regulations,” according to George Voloshin of Acams, a global organisation dedicated to anti-financial crime, training and education.

Voloshin believes that, given the project's 60- to 80-year lifespan, Turkey’s commitment to Russian nuclear power will shape bilateral ties for the long term, with consequences.

“It will be a source of scrutiny from western partners of Turkey. At the same time, nuclear energy has been so far shielded from any sanctions, so for Russia it is clearly a kind of lifeline,” he said.

The Akkuyu plant, currently under construction, will be Turkey's first nuclear power station. © AFP/Dogan News Agency/Ibrahim Mese

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ankara has maintained that it is not bound by EU or US sanctions on Moscow. Yet behind the scenes, it has quietly followed many restrictions and secured crucial waivers, especially for Russian gas.

By leveraging its pivotal location near Syria and Iran, Ankara has walked a diplomatic tightrope between its western partners and Moscow.

However, deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia threatens to complicate the already difficult balancing act.

“It would reinforce the already existing distrust between Turkey and Europe and Turkey and the United States,” warned Unluhisarcikli.

“But at the same time, Turkey is in talks with other countries, the United States and South Korea. These are the main two competitors for Russia.”

Mutual dependency

Turkey’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels has stirred unease at home, and the idea of doubling down with Russian nuclear energy only heightens the sense of anxiety. “It is a dilemma,” Unluhisarcikli conceded.

Yet with Russia willing to shoulder the hefty construction costs, cash-strapped Ankara has a strong incentive to continue the partnership.

Russia expert Zaur Gasimov of Istanbul’s Turkish-German University points out that more than a decade of joint investment makes it tough for Turkey to turn to alternative suppliers.

"It's quite a profound project,” said Gasimov, “Russia conducts the training of Turkish specialists in the field of nuclear energy, which started 15 years ago. We now have three or four waves of Turkish engineers who stayed for longer periods in Russia; they learn the Russian language for two years, and you have an infrastructure of specialists.”

However, Gasimov stresses that, given the scale of investment by both sides, it has created an important mutual dependency. “Its importance makes the two sides, somehow, at the end, interested in preserving a certain level of the relationship,” he said.

This shared reliance might help keep Turkish-Russian rivalries in check, from North Africa to the Middle East, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

Yet any step toward deeper nuclear cooperation is bound to invite sharper scrutiny and rising suspicion from Ankara’s western allies.

World.title: Cuban dance teacher ordered EU sabotage attacks from Russia
World.content:
In 2024, a Cuban man coordinated a series of arson attacks in four EU countries while operating on behalf of Russian intelligence services. DW Investigations tracked him back to a Latin dance studio in Russia.

On social media platforms, the man called himself "Adrian" or "Dios," meaning "God” in Spanish. In 2024, accounts linked to the man posted job ads on Telegram. "Work as a photographer," one offered in Russian in a chat about opportunities in Poland. "To those interested in applying, send resume, phone number and passport," another advertised in a group for Cuban expatriates in Russia. "Looking for people with military experience in monitoring, intelligence, logistics and tactical maneuvers," one said in Spanish in a group for Latinos, promising $1,500 plus a bonus for each operation completed.

Dios lured multiple people into carrying out sabotage for Russia in at least four EU countries, an investigation by DW and three other European broadcasters has found. Most of the recruits came from Spanish-speaking countries.

For months, DW and its partners conducted dozens of interviews with security officials and people close to the suspects. We pieced together classified court documents, official statements, social media posts and leaked data to find out who Dios is and reconstruct how he built a network of saboteurs to commit arson attacks across Europe.

Not all of them completed their tasks.

Recruiting vulnerable people

One of the people Dios recruited was Luis Alfonso Murillo Diosa, who was 34 years old at the time.

Originally from Caicedo, a rural town in western Colombia known for its mountainous landscapes and its crops, Murillo was raised in a family of coffee farmers. But several years of poor harvests pushed the business into debt, according to someone close to the family.

Murillo spent six years in the Colombian army. According to court documents, he left in 2015. He then hopped between jobs like many ex-soldiers, juggling barista courses, stints as a bodyguard and his family's coffee business.

In early 2024, Murillo decided to enlist in the Ukrainian army, where foreign fighters can earn a few thousand euros a month when deployed to the front line, court documents show.

Looking for information about the process, he joined a Facebook group for Latin Americans seeking to fight in Ukraine. That's when he was contacted by Dios.

"It's often vulnerable people who are being targeted,” said Daniela Richterova, an associate professor in Intelligence Studies at King's College London. "Vulnerable people who need money and are willing to travel for money and are willing to not ask many questions about the purpose of what they're carrying out."

Murillo said he sought to join the Ukrainian army, not work for Russia Image: Facebook

Arrested for attempted sabotage

In a private Facebook message, Dios introduced himself as a member of a "special group," and asked Murillo to work with him on "special missions" in Europe instead of going to Ukraine, according to classified court documents reviewed by DW.

Murillo took the offer, and Dios organized everything remotely: flight tickets, accommodation, ground transport. They never met in person.

Once Murillo reached Bucharest in July 2024, Dios sent him a satellite image with a recycling facility and an oil well marked. Murillo was supposed to take photos and videos of the locations — and later start a fire. However, he was detained while walking near the recycling facility one night after taking photos. According to court records, Murillo told investigators that he never intended to commit arson. He said he was trying to get to Europe to reach Ukraine, and didn't know for whom he was working.

In 2025, Murillo was sentenced to six years in prison for attempted sabotage.

Russia's 'disposable agents'

DW and its partners have confirmed that Murillo was one of at least a dozen people recruited by Dios for acts of sabotage across Europe. Such recruits are frequently referred to as "disposable agents": people often hired online who at times don't even know the identities of their employers or the real aim of their assignments.

The Kremlin has increasingly used disposable agents after EU governments expelled scores of Russian diplomats suspected of espionage and disinformation following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the conflict researcher Keir Giles told DW.

"That left a gap in Russia's capability, and it took time for them to find this new means of recruiting random people to carry out sometimes apparently random attacks," said Giles, who has written several books about Russia's military.

In 2024 alone, disposable agents burned down a shopping center in Poland, set fire to an Ikea store in Lithuania and delivered incendiary packages that ignited at logistics hubs in several countries. German authorities said throwaway agents, as they are also called, steered a drone with explosives toward a Ukrainian freight plane in Leipzig in August.

The 2024 attack on a Warsaw shopping center has been attributed to disposable agents Image: Attila Husejnow/SOPA/IMAGO

The suspected perpetrators of such attacks are often not Russian — nor do they have a known prior connection to Russian intelligence services. Many of the people prosecuted have been Ukrainian refugees, low-level criminals or local youths looking to make quick money.

"Russia doesn't have to be particularly careful about covering its tracks, because there is no downside to being detected," Giles said. "And, of course, it boosts the idea that Russia wants to project that it is omnipotent, that it can cause damage wherever."

Russian arson made in Cuba

DW confirmed that, over a span of four months in 2024, Dios instructed his recruits to set fire to two construction-supply businesses in Poland, a bus garage in the Czech Republic, a recycling facility in Romania and equipment destined for Ukraine produced by a company in Lithuania.

Lithuanian prosecutors were the only ones to publicly attribute the series of arson attacks to Russia's military intelligence service, known as GRU. They also put a Cuban man living in Russia on an international wanted list.

After reviewing classified court documents and dozens of leaked files, DW and its partners were able to confirm that Cuban national Oemis Romagoza Durruthy is the man behind the alias Dios.

Lithuanian prosecution has added Oemis Romagoza Durruthy to an international wanted list Image: LRT

Born in Camaguey, Cuba's third-largest city, Romagoza has lived in Russia for at least seven years.

A Latin dance teacher in the northern Russian city of Petrozavodsk, Romagoza is listed as a contact person on the social media channels of a local dance studio, Made in Cuba. In dozens of online videos of his dance classes, he shows off his salsa, bachata and kizomba steps.

Romagoza married a Russian woman in 2022 and later obtained Russian citizenship. A series of wedding to photos DW found on social media show the couple posing next to a grand piano. Other pictures show them with their two children.

DW was unable to determine when and how he came to work on behalf of Russia's secret services. Leaked data indicate that Romagoza might have run into financial trouble. In 2023, he borrowed money from several credit lenders. In one of the entries, he listed a supermarket chain as his employer.

A few months later, Romagoza joined several Facebook groups of Latin Americans looking for work in Poland or seeking to fight for Ukraine. Around the same time, Dios started posting job offers on Telegram.

Born in Cuba, Romagoza has lived in Russia for at least seven years Image: Instagram

Sabotage continues in EU

It is unclear whether Dios continued recruiting people or directed more attacks after September 2024. But Russia's relentless sabotage campaign across Europe hasn't stopped.

In August alone, Estonia arrested two suspects for an arson attack targeting a company that supplies unmanned military vehicles to Ukraine, and Poland reported fires at two other facilities where components for drones and helicopters are manufactured. Authorities in both countries suspect that Russia is behind the plots.

"It seems like there are still people out there who are either naive enough or are really hungry for money and motivated by monetary rewards for these kinds of activities," said Richterova, whose research focuses on Russian intelligence.

At least nine of the disposable agents Romagoza recruited have been caught. Two are serving sentences of six to eight years for attempted sabotage or terrorism. Others are currently awaiting trial.

Meanwhile, European authorities are still after Romagoza, who might still be in Russia. In April, the Made in Cuba studio posted a video of him teaching a salsa class. Romagoza is seen facing the mirror, leading a group of women who follow his steps and his commands. "Because that is what I am. In heaven, I am the chief," sings the Cuban salsa tune playing in the background.

Around the same time the Latin dance studio posted the video, Romagoza joined at least two more Facebook groups for Latin Americans looking for work in Poland.

Oemis Romagoza Durruthy did not reply to requests for comment.

Additional research by: Andrei Popoviciu and Katarzyna Tuszynska

In cooperation with Indre Makaraityte (LRT), Adéla Pacliková (CT) and Pilar Requena (RTVE)

World.title: Trump dismisses report China supplied intel to Iran
World.content:
The US president downplayed reports that Chinese entities had given Iran satellite imagery before a strike on a military base in Jordan that killed three American soldiers.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday dismissed reports that Chinese entities had supplied Iran with satellite images of a military base before an Iranian strike killed three American soldiers.

Iranian missiles struck the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, which houses US forces, in July.

"You know, when they say that China spies on us, I say you're right, and we spy on them too," Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One as he returned from a visit to Ireland.

"That's what we do. They basically do what we do," Trump said.

The Wall Street Journal's report said unnamed American officials declined to say which Chinese entities had provided the images to Iran, and did not suggest Beijing was directly involved.

The White House has tried to play down tensions with China during Trump's second term Image: Kylie Cooper/REUTERS

Trump keeps tensions low ahead of Xi meeting

Trump refused to answer questions about whether he would raise the incident with Chinese President Xi Jinping, who is expected to visit the White House on September 24.

China has not officially confirmed that the meeting will take place.

Trump on Sunday reiterated his belief that he has a good relationship with Xi.

"I ⁠think ​he's behaved reasonably well, and we ​behave reasonably well," the US president said.

Trump's remarks follow a pattern set by his administration, which has sought to downplay tensions with China, despite frustration in Washington over Beijing's support for Iran.

Trump has previously warned China not to provide Iran with weapons. The US sanctioned three Chinese satellite companies in May for working with Iranian military entities.

China is one of Iran's top economic and diplomatic partners and main buyers of its oil.

World.title: Sweden election 'very close' as left bloc claims tight lead
World.content:
The left-wing opposition is narrowly ahead of the incumbent's right-wing bloc and could be poised to return to government after four years. The far-right Sweden Democrats surprisingly lost ground.

The left-wing alliance led by former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson was on course to narrowly win Sweden's election.

With more than 90% of ballots counted on Sunday night, Andersson's Social Democrats were expected to win 176 seats in the 349-seat parliament, the Riksdag, Sweden's electoral authority said.

The Social Democrats lead a left-wing opposition coalition and are hoping to return to power after four years.

Acknowledging the narrow lead, Andersson said early on Monday morning that "it looks like it will be very close."

"We Social Democrats will always be ready to assume responsibility for the result... For now, we are in the lead. And if that is confirmed, Sweden will have a new government," she told supporters.

What do we know about the election results?

The center-left party was on course to win 28% of the vote, which would be its worst result in over a century.

The right-wing alliance led by incumbent Ulf Kristersson was projected to win 173 seats.

The outcome of the election will not be confirmed before Wednesday, after early ballots and votes from abroad are counted.

"The voters have had their say, but we still don't have a final result. Which government will lead Sweden in the coming years is still an open question, and we will do everything we can to ensure that this government will be the very best for our country," Kristersson said.

Kristersson ​​​​​said he would reach out to other party leaders for potential coalition talks.

His alliance includes the far-right Sweden Democrats, which lost support compared to the last election in 2020.

Kristersson said he would respect Andersson's bid to form a left-wing coalition government Image: Christine Olsson/TT News Agency/picture alliance

Far right loses support for first time

The night's biggest surprise was the underwhelming performance of the Sweden Democrats, which had gone into Sunday's election hoping to get into government for the first time since its foundation in 2010.

Unlike in Germany, where most parties have ruled out working with the far-right Alternative for Germany as part of the political "firewall", Kristersson had promised the Sweden Democrats key government posts if his alliance wins, with party leader Jimmie Akesson set to be given the role of migration minister.

But as the results came through early on Monday, the anti-immigrant party had lost support for the first time. It was winning 17.9% of the vote, a more than three-point drop from the 20.5% it won in 2022.

Akesson told supporters in Stockholm that while the results are not yet final, "it's obvious that we've lost a few percentage points compared with our result four years ago."

Some of the founders of Akesson's party had ties to Sweden's neo-Nazi movement Image: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP

What do we know about the main parties in Sweden's election?

The Social Democrats have governed in Sweden for most of the last century and remain the country's largest party.

The left-wing bloc has promised to boost the welfare state and address rising costs.

Kristersson's campaign, meanwhile, focused on his government's record of reducing violent and organized crime and clamping down on immigration.

Eight million people were eligible to vote in a country of 10.6 million people. Turnout exceeded 80%.

Around half of the votes were cast in advance.
