World.title: The world Sept. 11 set in motion remains broken
World.content:
At 8:46 a.m. on Sept. 11, 2001, I was on a plane somewhere over Connecticut. I was flying from Logan to LaGuardia, on my way from my home near Boston to teach my second week of class as a baby professor at New York University Law School, when the pilot told us we were going into a holding pattern because a plane had just hit the World Trade Center.

I did not know it then, but my career would be shaped by the events and aftermath of that day. Half of the books I’ve written are about the Middle East and the trajectories of war, terrorism and democracy there. The other half have focused on the U.S. constitutional system, especially its protections of speech and civil liberties, both of which have been deeply inflected by the war on terror. As for my teaching, my current students take for granted a broken world that, in many ways, began that day.

When I was applying for law-school teaching jobs the year before, no one had shown the slightest interest in the Islamic studies doctorate I had earned before law school. Suddenly things were different. The dean of NYU’s law school took me uptown to meet Bill Clinton at his foundation offices, introducing me as the faculty member who would organize an international conference with the former president. My mentor from Yale Law School told me I should write a book on Islam, democracy and what might happen next. He introduced me to an agent, who introduced me to an editor, who agreed to publish the book.

World.title: Supermarket competition intensifies in Chugoku with Lopia’s advances
World.content:
The supermarket sector in the Chugoku region is being reshaped with the entry of discount supermarket chain Lopia in Hiroshima and Yamaguchi prefectures this year.

Local supermarket operators are responding by strengthening their fresh-food offerings while seeking greater efficiency, including the introduction of new store formats designed to keep costs down.

Since opening in April, crowds are still a common sight at Lopia’s store in the Hiroshima Pacela shopping complex in Hiroshima’s Naka Ward, which is the Kawasaki-based chain’s first outlet in the Chugoku-Shikoku region.

World.title: Suppliers asked to install sensors in enclosed spaces with gas piping
World.content:
The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) said it has asked gas suppliers to install alarm units in enclosed spaces where gas piping is present, such as warehouses and other buildings, in response to an explosion at a shopping mall in Kumamoto Prefecture in July following a major earthquake.

Such buildings include schools and hospitals, which total tens of thousands nationwide.

Currently, gas sensor alarm systems must be installed near tanks and devices that use gas, such as kitchen stoves, but this requirement doesn’t extend to areas where gas pipes run through.

A member of an expert panel discussing measures to prevent a recurrence of incidents like the Kumamoto explosion suggested the new move when talks began on Sept. 8.

“If there are measures that are considered effective in mitigating damage, we will take the steps swiftly without waiting for determination of the causes,” industry minister Ryosei Akazawa said during a news conference on Friday.

The industry ministry carried out on-site inspections at the Kumamoto shopping mall jointly with police and fire authorities in the wake of the explosion. They agreed it was highly likely that the explosion was caused by liquefied petroleum gas supplied to the facility.

Gas that leaks from pipes damaged by earthquakes tends to accumulate in enclosed spaces such as in warehouses and rooms with few or no windows.

Translated by The Japan Times

World.title: Group lending cars for free to disaster victims struggles to meet demand
World.content:
A nonprofit organization is lending out cars for free one month after torrential rain killed 13 people in Chiba Prefecture and left more than 10,000 vehicles with water damage due to flooded roads.

Some 3,100 of the cars were stranded and temporarily abandoned on the streets in August.

To support those who lose their means of transportation in a natural disaster, the Japan Car Sharing Association, a nonprofit organization based in Ishinomaki, Miyagi Prefecture, has been lending cars for free since 2011 to those in disaster-hit areas.

World.title: Crown Prince Akishino and Prince Hisahito visit area hit by 2011 tsunami
World.content:
Crown Prince Akishino and his son, Prince Hisahito, on Sunday visited the city of Kesennuma, Miyagi Prefecture, which was hit hard by major tsunami after the March 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake.

They visited the Ruins of the Great East Japan Earthquake Kesennuma City Memorial Museum, which preserves the former building of Kesennuma Koyo High School, heavily damaged by the tsunami.

This was Prince Hisahito’s first visit to an area devastated by the 2011 disaster.

According to an aide, the visit was made at the wishes of both Crown Prince Akishino and Prince Hisahito to mark the 15th anniversary of the disaster.

The old school building remains much as it was at the time of the disaster, including a car that was swept from the ground up to a third-floor classroom, about 8 meters above ground, where it overturned.

Crown Prince Akishino and Prince Hisahito toured the building intently as Junnosuke Oikawa, 72, the museum director, and local high school students serving as disaster storytellers explained what happened.

Prince Hisahito asked Yamato Miura, 18, a third-year student at Kesennuma High School, whether even the window frames had been swept away.

As he looked at the gymnasium, whose roof had been swept away, the young prince asked Mio Fukuoka, 17, a third-year student at Kesennuma Koyo High School, “Where was the roof swept away?”

The former school building was flooded to a height of about 12 meters on the fourth floor, but all students, teachers and staff workers were evacuated safely. Crown Prince Akishino, the younger brother of Emperor Naruhito, said, “It’s good that everyone evacuated and was safe.”

On Monday morning, Crown Prince Akishino and Prince Hisahito visited Kesennuma’s fish market, which has been restored after suffering tsunami damage.

Wearing caps and rubber boots, they observed the landing of bonito and other operations at the market.

World.title: Okinawan businesses lament stricter rules for drone flights
World.content:
Following a revision to Japan’s drone law on July 14 that expanded no-fly zones to protect critical facilities from terrorist attacks, cases of purportedly illegal flights have emerged in Okinawa Prefecture.

Investigative sources said they have already confirmed more than 10 cases.

In Okinawa, where many defense-related facilities such as U.S. military bases are located, extensive areas are covered by the new regulations, which opens up the possibility of drone users unintentionally violating the law.

World.title: SoftBank gets upsized $11.9 billion loan in OpenAI funding push
World.content:
SoftBank Group secured an $11.87 billion loan to support its investment in U.S. artificial intelligence firm OpenAI, people familiar with the matter said, up from its earlier target of $10 billion.

The Japanese conglomerate sealed the two-year facility last week, attracting commitments from around 20 banks, said the people, asking not to be identified because they’re not authorized to speak publicly.

Softbank declined to comment.

The financing comes as some executives are now voicing the need to slow the pace of AI development due to escalating risks from the technology. OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman said in an interview with Fortune that his company wouldn’t proceed with a public offering this year as it addresses safety-related concerns.

SoftBank shares tumbled as much as 13% Monday, the most since July 17.

The latest borrowing would add to SoftBank’s wave of recent debt financing activities tied to its bet on OpenAI. That includes a $10 billion margin loan backed by its OpenAI stake and a potential bond sale of as much as $20 billion, despite concerns about growing credit risks in the artificial intelligence sector.

SoftBank said last week that it would repay the balance of a $40 billion loan it obtained earlier this year to finance its investment in OpenAI. The company plans to pay down the $25.9 billion it owes on Sept. 15, according to a statement. The non-collateralized borrowing was due to mature in March next year.

Meanwhile, SoftBank is set to hold meetings with investors in New York this week to sound out interest for the potential U.S. dollar junk-bond sale. It is considering raising $10 billion to $20 billion from the bond offering, people familiar with the matter said last month.

SoftBank, founded and led by billionaire Masayoshi Son, is slated to invest close to $65 billion in OpenAI by October. The company has already raised the equivalent of about $37 billion so far this year from offshore and domestic bond sales and loans, including the latest facility, according to Bloomberg-compiled data.

World.title: Grand Slam drought for U.S. men reaches 23rd year after Ben Shelton falls at U.S. Open
World.content:
An American men’s Grand Slam drought will stretch into a 24th year, after German Alexander Zverev beat Ben Shelton in the final of the U.S. Open on Sunday to the bitter disappointment of the home crowd in New York.

Shelton was not even a year old when the last American Grand Slam winner, Andy Roddick, hoisted the U.S. Open trophy in 2003. The golden era of Andre Agassi and Pete Sampras appeared an ever-more distant memory as eighth seed Shelton fell 6-3, 7-6 (7-2), 5-7, 6-2 at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

“I’m sorry it’s the wrong winner this year,” said Zverev. “But I did my job.”

Beating the American men is a job global tennis has performed quite well over the last quarter century.

As the likes of Venus and Serena Williams, Sloane Stephens, Coco Gauff and Madison Keys collected hardware on the women’s side, the U.S. men have rarely found their way into a championship final.

Roddick reached his last final at Wimbledon in 2009. It took another 15 years for another American man to reach a title match, when Taylor Fritz played Italian Jannik Sinner in New York.

Shelton said he was eager to get another taste of the spotlight on tennis’ biggest stage.

“It’s such a cool moment,” he told reporters. “Walking out on that court today, there’s nothing like it. I’ve never felt anything like that before. Yeah, it’s an addicting feeling being in positions like this.”

The U.S. Tennis Association previously pointed to Fritz’s 2024 campaign as a sign of progress, after announcing a massive overhaul to its player development program in 2008. Fritz was a product of USTA camps, along with Frances Tiafoe, who reached the semifinals for a third time this year.

The sport’s national governing body has also moved to diversify its talent in a partnership announced last year with American Tennis Association, focusing on building Black representation in an overwhelmingly white sport.

Shelton made history just by stepping onto the court on Sunday as the first Black American man to play in the New York final in 54 years — since Ashe, the man for whom the tournament’s showpiece court was named.

“I don’t think I’m anywhere near the player that I want to be,” Shelton said. “I think I’m a great competitor. I think I compete really well out there on the court.

“I’m able it stay focused and stay there on the court for many, many hours. I think that’s going to help me in the future moving forward.”

World.title: Huge gaps in sanitary pad absorption speeds, over half poorly labelled: survey
World.content:
Disposable sanitary pads sold in Hong Kong show wide discrepancies in absorption speed, with more than half of tested products also lacking adequate labelling, the consumer watchdog has found.

The Consumer Council on Monday revealed the results of a survey of 36 winged sanitary towels, in which one sample took 73 seconds to fully absorb simulated menstrual blood – exceeding the mainland China national standard recommendation of no more than 60 seconds.

“The council calls on suppliers to strengthen quality management and conduct regular testing to ensure product hygiene and safety, while improving product labelling so consumers can make informed choices,” it said.

The samples were purchased from personal care stores, supermarkets and online platforms, with prices ranging from HK$1 to HK$5.60 (12 US cents to 71 US cents) per piece.

The tests were conducted in accordance with the national standard for sanitary absorbent pads and examined deviations between the actual and stated values for length, weight, absorption speed, adhesive peel strength, moisture content, chemical balance and the presence of hidden preservatives.

After grouping the products into four categories by length, the watchdog added 5ml of synthetic fluid simulating menstrual blood to each sample, recorded the time required for complete absorption and calculated the average absorption speed based on five pieces per model.

World.title: Apple to review Hong Kong iPhone orders amid HK$14.7m of unauthorised transactions
World.content:
Apple is reviewing all current orders for suspicious transactions after more than 700 unauthorised credit card charges were reported in Hong Kong involving orders for its latest iPhone models.

“All current orders are being reviewed before they are processed, and we are working to quickly identify and cancel any fraudulent transactions that may have been placed,” an Apple spokesman said on Monday.

Over the weekend, many Hong Kong social media users reported unauthorised credit card transactions involving orders for Apple’s newly released iPhone 18 Pro series, which went on pre-order on Saturday. The cards had been issued by different banks.

Police said they had received more than 700 reports involving HK$14.7 million in unauthorised transactions.

Speaking on a radio programme on Monday, Election Committee sector legislator Johnny Ng Kit-chong said Apple should ultimately be held responsible, while estimating that the actual losses would not be significant.

He described the incident as “rare”, given the large number of victims and the involvement of a platform operated by a major company such as Apple.

Ng said he suspected that hackers might have stolen and stored the credit card details over time while waiting for an opportunity to use them.

World.title: Hong Kong 5-year plan to stick with capitalism, uphold ‘one country, two systems’: John Lee
World.content:
In an opinion piece published in the South China Morning Post on Monday, the city leader also stressed that the blueprint, in focusing on the economy, would ultimately “enable citizens to flourish” by creating employment opportunities and upward mobility.

Lee will unveil Hong Kong’s first-ever five-year plan on Wednesday, alongside his annual policy address , to map out the city’s priorities and align with the national blueprint covering the country’s development between 2026 and 2030.

In the article, he sought to address concerns that introducing the five-year plan, a practice in mainland China for over seven decades, meant the city was walking away from its long-hailed laissez-faire system.

“I have also been asked whether formulating a five-year plan would change Hong Kong’s original system. The answer is no,” Lee wrote.

“The five-year plan will uphold Hong Kong’s rule of law and capitalist system, implement the Basic Law and adhere to ‘one country, two systems’ without distorting Hong Kong.

World.title: How the 5-year plan can serve the nation and deliver for Hong Kong
World.content:
This year marks the opening year of the national 15th five-year plan . Faced with accelerating change globally and significant opportunities brought by national development, Hong Kong must better integrate into and serve the overall national development, enabling our economic progress to reach new heights while enhancing people’s livelihood and well-being.

This February, I announced that the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government would formulate the city’s first five-year plan . I led the compilation work, with the Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs taking primary responsibility for implementation, and all principal officials and heads of departments participating. Producing Hong Kong’s first five-year plan carried significant responsibilities, including meeting Hong Kong people’s earnest expectations for the city’s long-term development.

The five-year plan, with all its demanding tasks, was devised under an exceptionally tight schedule. It often takes mainland cities one to two years of preliminary research and discussion to construct their five-year plans. We had less than a year to complete Hong Kong’s first five-year plan from scratch. I am grateful to all policy bureaus and departments, and the individuals involved, for their outstanding efforts under pressure – a breakthrough in the Hong Kong government’s public governance capabilities.

My team and I began by reviewing the five-year plan experiences of Macau and mainland cities. Officials from the Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Bureau visited mainland cities to learn from their experience.

In April, I introduced a research and public-opinion gathering channel between the government and the Legislative Council . My thanks to all Legco members for organising multiple opinion-collection sessions based on professional and sectoral divisions, and for submitting research reports covering six major areas to the government.

Working together, the executive and the legislature allowed the government to race against time while ensuring that the plan was representative and its scientific foundations remained solid.

World.title: Beijing’s ‘trust issue’ with Hong Kong and what the city can promise in its 5-year plan
World.content:
In the final instalment of our series of previews on the five-year plan and policy address, to be announced on September 16, Natalie Wong and Matthew Cheng look at how national security spans areas such as finance and technology and what Hong Kong must do to earn Beijing’s trust. Read part one here , part two here , part three here and part four here

With the recent sentencing of former leaders of Hong Kong’s Tiananmen Square vigil concluding a key high-profile subversion case, it would be easy to assume the city’s national security agenda has been largely settled.

Now would be the time to focus entirely on economic growth and downplay national security, some experts have argued, warning the issue could deter potential investors.

But that would be an erroneous and narrow understanding of national security, overlooking how inextricably it is tied to economic development, other insiders familiar with the government’s thinking have said.

Indeed, in the coming inaugural five-year plan Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu will announce on Wednesday, a full chapter will be dedicated to national security, the South China Morning Post has learned.

The emphasis will be another clear rebuttal to detractors on why national security extends well beyond law enforcement or combating “soft resistance” efforts, and is the framework that ensures economic development can enhance value rather than expose vulnerabilities for the country.

Authorities are expected to lay institutional safeguards across key areas – most notably finance and technology among China’s 11 critical domains – to shield Hong Kong in its path to better support the country’s growth and its navigation of geopolitical risks.

World.title: Will Hong Kong’s educators learn from sliding Pisa results?
World.content:
The latest Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) results are out and unfortunately for the Education Bureau, Hong Kong’s performance looks bad . Is this the outcome of not learning from the last assessment?

In the 2022 Pisa assessment, a metric for creative thinking was introduced to measure the ability to generate, evaluate, improve and communicate ideas, as well as social and scientific problem-solving. Hong Kong scored below the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) average, prompting an education expert to warn that it was “a wake-up call” revealing “our students are really not good at … thinking outside the box”.

That is not to say that this was our students’ fault, because what needs changing is what happens inside classrooms. Have our education authorities been thinking outside the box to address this?

Let the 2025 Pisa scores released last week speak for themselves: our scores have dropped across the core subjects of mathematics, reading and science.

While the Education Bureau chose to highlight the “outstanding performance” in digital learning and that mathematical, scientific and mother-tongue reading literacy remained above average, we must be alarmed that scores for the three core subjects of mathematics, reading and science are “the lowest ever measured”, according to Pisa, and “reinforce a negative trend that began after 2012”.

As much as the authorities and experts would like to chalk this up to being Covid-19-related, pointing to a global decline in domain subject scores, the steepness of the decline since the last Pisa exercise warrants deeper consideration. For the first time, Hong Kong has fallen out of the top 10 in science, sliding to 17th from 7th place in just three years.

World.title: Top-level online schooling offers route to leading universities
World.content:
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]

For families who are regularly on the move or simply looking for a high-quality alternative to traditional modes of teaching, an easy-to-access option is now available offering flexibility, rigour and a proven track record.

Operating since 2019, the Crimson Global Academy (CGA) conducts small live group classes alongside one-to-one classes where a more personalised pace is helpful. Everything follows a well-structured weekly timetable, with a choice of curricula that lead to globally recognised qualifications including the IGCSE, international A-Levels, AP (advanced placement) programmes, and the US high school diploma.

Children sign in to learn from home or, in principle, from anywhere in the world. Individual progress and assignments are closely monitored by expert teachers who maintain close contact with students and parents via direct messaging and updates. And regular classes are supplemented by a diverse range of extracurricular activities, including special interest clubs and Model UN debates, to ensure a whole-person approach and a positive, unifying school culture.

The aim at all times is to provide an education which is effective, challenging and transformative. This is done by giving students access to cutting-edge technologies, a global learning environment, and even an AI chatbot on hand to offer extra support when needed.

Results show it is an approach which can accelerate academic performance and broaden perspectives, while also allowing sufficient flexibility to adjust personal timetables and pathways or opt for one-to-one classes in certain subjects if preferred.

“We have rolling admissions, but students will join one of three virtual campuses – centred in Hong Kong, London and the United States – where live classes, with an average of 8-10 students – are taught remotely in the morning or early afternoon in each time zone,” says Liya Sun, CGA’s admissions officer for Asia.

“Each campus follows its own academic year, but we make it easy to switch between them if families or students move, and there are the usual term breaks, internal exams, reports, parent-teacher exchanges and check-ins with group tutors.”

Already, children from more than 70 Hong Kong families are studying with CGA, usually choosing to do so for one of three reasons.

World.title: Supplier to end classroom lunch portioning at Sha Tin school after 39 fall ill
World.content:
A lunch supplier will stop portioning meals in classrooms at a Hong Kong primary school following a suspected food poisoning outbreak that hit 39 pupils and staff members last week.

Danny Catering Service said in a statement on Sunday to its school partners, parents and teachers that the incident was “isolated” and linked to the school’s portioning arrangement, and did not affect its services at other locations.

“To ensure student food safety and avoid potential cross-contamination or temperature fluctuation risks during classroom portioning, the company has decided to discontinue the ‘classroom on-site portion’ mode at the affected school from Monday,” it said.

Baptist (Sha Tin Wai) Lui Ming Choi Primary School. Photo: Handout

The Centre for Health Protection said on Saturday that it was investigating a suspected food poisoning cluster, in which 37 students and two staff members at a Sha Tin school developed stomach pain and diarrhoea about eight to 22 hours after eating the same type of lunchboxes last Wednesday.

Twenty-three boys and 14 girls, aged between five and 11, from Baptist (Sha Tin Wai) Lui Ming Choi Primary School, and two employees, aged 34 and 38, were affected.

Two pupils sought medical advice and were in a stable condition, while the others experienced mild symptoms and did not need to see a doctor.

According to the supplier, inspections at its factory carried out by authorities on Friday confirmed that the production and cooking processes “fully comply with food safety standards”.

The official investigation and test results had yet to be released, the supplier added.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019019/A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.title: A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019019/A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.content:
Thanks to years of ecological restoration, endangered Oriental storks have been expanding their range around Gaoyou Lake in the eastern Jiangsu province. In recent months, dozens have descended on crab farmer Hu Dingsong’s ponds, bringing him online fame — and huge economic losses.

Hu first spotted two or three storks in April. After learning they were a nationally first-class protected species, he was delighted. “I even joked online that my pond had crabs to spare,” he said.

But the numbers quickly grew: over 20 by mid-May, to more than 40 by early June, to their present numbers of around 80. Hu estimates that the birds collectively eat roughly 2,400 crabs a day, costing him 30,000 to 40,000 yuan ($4,200-$5,600) daily. His agricultural insurance does not cover wildlife damage.

Forestry officials have alo banned Hu from using firecrackers to drive the birds away, as they are a protected species. Netting such large ponds is also impractical, and offering the birds other food sources — such as fish — introduces disease risks, leaving him with little recourse.

Lu Changhu, a wildlife ecology professor at Nanjing Forestry University, said storks staying in the province during summer is not new. Once mainly winter visitors, more have begun staying around Gaoyou Lake and nearby wetlands as their population has grown. Some may skip migration when food is plentiful, he said.

Local officials have provided Hu with a drone to monitor the flock and are helping address his losses, but farmers currently lack official channels to pursue compensation for wildlife damage.

Hu is now urging authorities to work with farmers on solutions that protect both the birds and their livelihoods.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019013/Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.title: Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019013/Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.content:
A mobile game beloved by millions of Chinese users about a traveling frog is set to shut down after the game operator and the IP holder failed to reach a licensing agreement.

Announced Tuesday by its official account on microblogging platform Weibo, the game, Travel Frog: China Journey, will discontinue on Dec. 8.

“This time, the little frog is going on a long journey, with no set date of return,” the announcement read. “But that quiet companionship will always remain in our hearts.”

A video game insider told domestic media that the IP holder, Japanese gaming studio Hit-Point, sought harsher terms from domestic operator Lingxi Games, including stripping it of its right to collaborate with other companies and sell game-related merchandise. After multiple rounds of negotiations, the companies could not reach an agreement, though the insider disclosed that they are in a final round of talks.

Travel Frog, released in 2017, is an idle game, meaning gameplay progresses with little player input. Chinese users began downloading the Japanese version before tech giant Alibaba secured authorization to publish it exclusively in the Chinese mainland under its gaming division, Lingxi Games, a year later. By then, the original version was already popular, with iOS downloads in China alone exceeding 30 million.

At its peak, the game was more popular than the domestic, Tencent-produced game Honour of Kings, topping the domestic App Store free chart. Lingxi Games was acquired by the private equity firm Trustar Capital in August this year.

In Travel Frog: China Journey, the protagonist, a frog who lives alone in a cave, passes its days reading, writing in its diary, eating, and whittling wood. It also travels around China, such as to the Great Wall in Beijing and West Lake in the eastern city of Hangzhou. While on the road, it meets fellow animal travelers, brings back local specialties, and sends home postcards, which devoted users post on WeChat.

After learning that the game would be discontinued, a graduate student in Shanghai surnamed Fang spent a day trying to redownload it. She had played since her first year of university but hadn’t reinstalled the game after changing phones, not thinking it would shut down permanently.

“(I will have to) think of it as a child growing up and setting off on a new journey — a solo trip where the parents don’t need to worry anymore,” Fang said. “I really loved my frog … It felt like a real little baby.”

Another player, surnamed Wang, in the southern city of Guangzhou, first tried the game’s Japanese version in 2018. The frog’s ability to travel, rest, and meet friends whenever it wanted — moved her, as she said that adult life is all about KPIs, responsibilities, and pressure.

When she learned the game would be taken offline, Wang told Sixth Tone that she was devastated. “This isn’t just a game,” she said. “It’s a second life.”

Online, some called the move the “tears of an era,” a Chinese internet slang term referring to something that evokes a strong sense of nostalgia. Others lamented that their “youth is over,” or said they could not bear to delete the game, hoping it might one day be restored.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot from Travel Frog: China Journey. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.title: She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.content:
Chang Shana, one of China’s most treasured artists, is sitting on her living room sofa in Beijing, her eyes fixed on a TV documentary about Dunhuang, the northwestern oasis city where she spent much of her childhood. When a familiar face appears on screen, the 95-year-old breaks into a broad smile.

“That’s my father,” she says, pointing out Chang Shuhong, an accomplished painter best known for his research on the ancient Buddhist murals at the Mogao Grottoes.

Alzheimer’s disease, the most common cause of dementia, has robbed Chang Shana of most memories, yet her face still lights up the moment anyone mentions Dunhuang.

“Apart from Dunhuang, her family, and the caregivers who attend to her day and night, my mother has largely forgotten the people and things outside her immediate world,” says her son, Cui Donghui.

Gone are her memories of studying under world-renowned masters, of her mother walking out on the family, of helping design state gifts and landmark buildings like Beijing’s Great Hall of the People and the Cultural Palace of Nationalities, of losing her beloved husband, and of her tenure as the longest-serving president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, now Tsinghua University’s Academy of Arts and Design.

On a desk in her bedroom is “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” which compiles 328 color illustrations of cave murals and sculptures from various periods. “I drew this book. It’s all decorative motifs,” says Chang, standing up. After catching her breath, she points out another book: “This one, ‘Dunhuang! My Father’s Call,’ was written by my father, but I contributed many of the illustrations and written materials.”

Would she like to return to Dunhuang one day? “Yes,” she replies in a soft voice, without hesitation. Then, she slowly wanders back to the sofa to continue watching her documentary.

Life on the move

Chang Shana was born in Lyon, France, in 1931. Her father was among China’s first generation of French-trained artists, and both her parents went on to attend the prestigious Beaux-Arts de Paris school.

After being moved by a photobook about the Mogao Grottoes that he discovered in a secondhand book stall beside the Seine, Chang’s father returned to China alone in 1936 to head the fine arts department at the National Art School in Beiping, predecessor of Beijing’s Central Academy of Fine Arts.

However, as invading Japanese troops advanced toward Beijing, he was forced to flee, eventually moving with the academy to Nanjing in the eastern Jiangsu province — where he was joined by his wife, Chen Zhixiu, and daughter — and then to the southwestern city of Chongqing, which served as the nation’s wartime capital during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression. In 1943, the family relocated again to Dunhuang in the northwestern Gansu province, where Chang Shuhong was appointed director of the National Dunhuang Art Research Institute.

Chang Shana found it difficult adjusting to their austere life among the arid dunes. In her 2013 memoir, “Yellow Sands and Blue Sky,” the artist recalls that first winter night, eating cold noodles with only salt and vinegar, and her father promising, “Things will get better.”

Yet despite the lack of material comforts, she instantly found an abundance of inspiration at the Mogao Grottoes. On days without school, she would walk the dirt roads, past the shimmering poplars, and climb into the grottoes to copy the murals. “I loved going into the caves to draw. I was always eager to do it. My parents never had to tell me to go,” she wrote. She would also chat with the many visiting artists and scholars, laying a strong foundation for her artistic development.

Previously, students had typically copied the murals with tracing paper, which they secured to the walls with thumbtacks, leaving tiny holes. Chang Shuhong prohibited this practice to prevent further damage to the relics, meaning his daughter had to recreate the originals stroke by stroke through observation alone. Although laborious, it helped her develop extraordinary levels of precision.

But the desert took as much as it gave. Under the strain of his responsibilities, Chang Shuhong was often irritable, and his relationship with his wife became fractious. She eventually left him and moved back east in 1945.

Chang Shana was 14. She dropped out of school and stayed home to help with the housework and to knit sweaters for her 4-year-old brother.

That same year, the Nationalist government ordered the Dunhuang Art Research Institute to close. As funding dwindled and workers left, Chang Shuhong traveled extensively to enlist fresh support, eventually recruiting a group of teachers and students from art academies in Chongqing and Chengdu, capital of the neighboring Sichuan province.

With the institute’s future secured, he instructed his daughter to make copies of representative murals covering various Chinese dynasties. In her memoir, Chang recalls her work to recreate the figures of warriors from the Western Wei dynasty (535–556): “The lines followed my feelings; my brushwork was especially free and expressive.”

Finding faith

When Chang turned 17, a Canadian friend of the family sponsored her to study in the United States at what is today Tufts University’s School of the Museum of Fine Arts. There, she took classes in drawing, anatomy, art history, perspective, color, painting, and design.

Although confident in French, she initially struggled with some of the highly specialized English terminology. What baffled her most, though, was the painting course. With abstract expressionism on the rise, her professors required students to create work without recognizable forms or subjects. In a letter to her father, she wrote, “Perhaps I just don’t understand.”

According to her son, Chang’s diary entries from the early 1940s are filled with confusion and unease. She occupied her time with sketching and knitting, often questioning the meaning behind such pursuits. Yet her letters home in 1950 reveal “a completely different person,” he says.

In one, she wrote about “finally finding faith,” and expounded on her belief that art should be accessible and serve the people. In other letters, she displayed a weariness with life overseas. “Staying here, depending on others for everything, life feels so empty,” she wrote. “I have a perpetual sense that something is missing, like I owe a debt.”

Chang returned to China in December 1950 without completing her degree. She immediately began helping her father organize an exhibition of Dunhuang cultural relics in Beijing, featuring copies of murals she and several art researchers had made.

The following year, she was introduced to the influential architects Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin, who agreed to recommend her for a teaching assistant position at Tsinghua University’s School of Architecture. Under Lin’s guidance, she and two other students applied traditional cloisonné enamelwork techniques and motifs to everyday items such as table lamps, cigarette cases, and plates.

With a growing portfolio, Chang was commissioned to design themed gifts for the 1952 Asia and Pacific Rim Peace Conference, held in Beijing. She created a silk headscarf and large cloisonné plate with peace dove motifs, inspired by Dunhuang cave paintings from the Sui dynasty (581–618).

When China began reforming its university system in the early 1950s, she transferred to the Department of Applied Arts at the Central Academy of Fine Arts before ultimately joining the Central Academy of Arts and Design in 1956.

Gone too soon

Chang met her first husband while studying in the U.S. The couple married in China in 1953 but divorced after just a few years. The artist barely mentions this time in her memoir, not even naming him.

Her second husband, Cui Taishan, was a Japanese-language interpreter. They met while part of a Chinese cultural delegation to Japan in 1961 and were married two years later, spending 26 years together until Cui’s death in 1989.

The artist’s friend, Huang Xuanzi, recalls that Chang often talked to her late husband’s photo before she developed dementia. “She’d grumble at him for leaving her too soon, then turn to me and say, ‘Look at him, always smiling at me like that,’” she says, adding that Chang still sometimes recognizes him in photographs. “One day, she suddenly smiled and said to me, ‘Cui Taishan was very handsome.’”

Huang recalls a thick stack of flower studies Chang had painted when she was pregnant, each accompanied by a short poem handwritten by her husband. “They were never published, so almost no one outside the family knows about them,” she explains. “You can clearly feel the depth of their affection in those paintings and poems.”

In 1983, Chang was appointed president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, leaving her less time for family. Around the same time, Cui was diagnosed with diabetes and then liver cancer. Even during his final days, she was unable to stay with him full time, yet he would always reassure her, “You go ahead with your work. I’m fine.” He was just 62 when he died.

The artist struggled to cope with the combination of grief and work stress. “There were photos of her husband everywhere in the house,” says her sister-in-law, Wang Fulan. “She would always say, ‘He left us too soon. He was so young.’ She felt that she had devoted herself entirely to her work and left household matters to her husband, and that was what had worn him down.”

In later years, Chang told a friend: “I have done right by everyone and everything in my life. My father Chang Shuhong wanted me to carry on the cultural legacy of Dunhuang, and I spent my life doing so. Lin Huiyin mentored me to become a designer, and I devoted myself to that career. The only person I failed was my husband, Cui Taishan.”

Forever home

Shortly after losing her husband, Chang’s father was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. His condition remained largely stable until he took a serious fall at age 92. After that, his memory began deteriorating rapidly, and he passed away two years later in 1994.

Huang says Chang Shana was also healthy and mentally sharp until her early 90s. She might forget small things, but a little prompting was enough to bring her back.

During the pandemic, her son Cui Donghui couldn’t visit in person; he could see her only through the security camera installed at her home. When he checked late at night, he often saw her lying alone on the sofa watching television. When he was finally able to return, she opened the door, looked at him, and said, “Who are you?”

Leafing through his mother’s book, “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” he proudly remarks, “This is her life’s work. She systematically cataloged the motifs from different periods and defined their evolutionary progression. This foundational body of work is still essential today, whether for research or for the development of cultural products.”

All the detailed illustrations inside were completed during a special trip Chang took to the Mogao Grottoes in 1959 with two colleagues. For the artist, it was a joyous return to the place she once called home.

“We were young then,” she wrote in her memoir. “We rode horses and camels, climbed the Singing Sand Dunes barefoot, and had an absolutely wonderful time.”

At 95, the journey to Dunhuang is impossible. Yet smiling at that flickering TV screen, she is already back among the caves. The memories are gone, but the patterns remain.

This article, reported by Li Mei, edited by Peng Wei, originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.
