World.title: Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s strategy: why South Korea interested in Kazakhstan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. On September 14-16, Head of State Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, at the invitation of President Lee Jae Myung, will pay a state visit to the Republic of Korea.

On September 15, high-level talks will be held in Seoul, during which the sides will discuss prospects for strengthening the expanded strategic partnership between Kazakhstan and South Korea. In addition, Tokayev is scheduled to hold meetings with the heads of leading South Korean companies.

On September 16, the President of Kazakhstan will also participate in the first “Central Asia - Republic of Korea” summit, which is expected to bring together the leaders of South Korea and the countries of the region - Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

The upcoming visit continues Tokayev’s consistent work to expand cooperation with South Korea. In April 2026, Tokayev received Kang Hoon Sik, the special representative of the President of South Korea and chief of staff of the presidential administration. The sides discussed expanding cooperation in the trade and economic, investment, energy, and transport and logistics spheres. These areas may now receive further development during the high-level talks, Tokayev’s meetings with the heads of South Korean companies, and the first “Central Asia - Republic of Korea” summit.

The economic component occupies a central place in relations between the two countries. For Seoul, Kazakhstan is of interest due to its natural resources, transit position, and the largest economy in Central Asia. For Astana, the Korean partnership provides access to technologies, investment, and industrial expertise needed to develop raw material processing and higher value-added production.

Existing industrial cooperation shows that this is a practical interaction. South Korean companies such as Kia, Doosan Enerbility, Samsung, and SK Ecoplant are involved in projects in Kazakhstan’s automotive industry, energy sector, mechanical engineering, and other sectors. The expansion of such projects allows Kazakhstan to increase the volume of higher value-added production and strengthen its industrial base.

A separate area is critical minerals. South Korea is interested in diversifying raw material supply chains for high-tech industries, including battery and electronics production. Kazakhstan, which has a significant resource base, views this sector as one of the areas for attracting investment and developing processing.

It is at the intersection of these interests that the economic agenda of cooperation is taking shape: Kazakhstan offers a resource base, industrial and transit potential, while Korean companies offer technology, capital and production expertise. For Tokayev, the development of such cooperation creates opportunities to expand the circle of investment partners and promote projects with higher added value.

The transport component also strengthens Seoul’s interest in Kazakhstan. The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, connecting China, Central Asia, the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Europe, gives Kazakhstan an additional advantage as a transit hub between Asian and European markets. For South Korea, the development of alternative logistics routes is important amid the restructuring of global supply chains.

The Korean direction of cooperation allows Tokayev to address several economic objectives of Kazakhstan simultaneously - attracting investment and technology, developing industrial processing, and using the country’s transit potential. For South Korea, Kazakhstan, in turn, is becoming a platform for expanding its economic presence in Central Asia and developing new supply chains.

The first “Central Asia - Republic of Korea” summit adds a regional dimension to bilateral cooperation. Seoul gains a platform for direct interaction with all five Central Asian states, while Kazakhstan can use its accumulated experience of cooperation with Korean companies in promoting regional projects.

For Korean businesses, the possibility of locating production in Kazakhstan with access to the markets of Central Asia, China and Europe is of particular interest. At the same time, Kazakhstan’s resource base, industrial infrastructure and location along routes between China and European markets are important.

The effectiveness of this rapprochement will depend on the extent to which political agreements are transformed into concrete investment, technological and industrial projects. Their implementation will show whether the current expansion of contacts can lead to deeper economic cooperation.

For Tokayev, the visit to Seoul is another step in expanding Kazakhstan’s economic interaction with Asian partners. At the same time, its significance goes beyond bilateral relations: participation in the first “Central Asia - Republic of Korea” summit allows Kazakhstan to promote its own economic interests in a regional format.

World.title: TOYO eyes role in Turkmenistan's industrial development (Exclusive interview)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. TOYO reaffirmed its interest in contributing to Turkmenistan's industrial development, particularly in gas-chemical and fertilizer projects.

The Japanese company made this statement in an exclusive interview in response to a request from Trend about the prospects of its cooperation with Turkmenistan.

"TOYO remains interested in contributing to Turkmenistan's industrial development, particularly in the gas-chemical and fertilizer sectors, while evaluating each future opportunity on its technical and commercial merits," the company stated.

According to TOYO, the company is already using AI and digital technologies in its industrial projects, including for project execution and plant operations.

"TOYO is already applying AI and digital technologies to both project execution and plant operations. Our publicly disclosed initiatives include an AI-based system for identifying potential construction-schedule risks during the plant design stage, as well as DX-PLANT™, a cloud-based service that combines industrial IoT, AI-based data analysis and remote monitoring to support plant operation, anomaly detection and predictive maintenance," the company said.

The company said these technologies are used to support plant operations, anomaly detection and predictive maintenance.

"Under our Medium-Term Management Plan 2026–2030, we intend to expand the use of digital transformation and AI to strengthen EPC execution, risk management and plant lifecycle services," TOYO said.

The company believes these capabilities could be relevant to future projects in Turkmenistan, particularly in the modernization of existing facilities.

"These capabilities could be relevant to future projects in Turkmenistan, particularly for modernizing existing facilities, improving operational reliability and energy efficiency, and supporting operation and maintenance," the company noted.

At the same time, TOYO said that the specific application of such technologies would depend on the requirements of each project.

"Any specific application would be tailored to the client’s requirements and the conditions of the project," the company added.

The company stressed that it sees gas processing, gas chemicals, and fertilizer production as key areas for industrial cooperation with Turkmenistan.

"Areas most closely aligned with TOYO’s current expertise are natural-gas processing and gas chemicals, petrochemicals, and ammonia and urea fertilizer plants," the company said.

According to TOYO, plant modernization, major overhauls, and ongoing operation and maintenance support also represent strong areas for potential cooperation.

"TOYO has experience in Turkmenistan through the Kiyanly Polymer Plant, which includes gas-separation, ethylene, polypropylene and high-density polyethylene facilities," the company added.

In 2025, TOYO and its consortium partner were awarded the first phase of a major overhaul of the Kiyanly complex. The company said this experience, combined with its broader international track record in gas chemicals and fertilizers, provides a strong foundation for further cooperation with Turkmenistan.

"Power and GX-related infrastructure could also be considered where TOYO’s capabilities match the specific needs of the Turkmen side," TOYO added.

Furthermore, TOYO Engineering expects to participate in the upcoming Japan-Turkmenistan Economic Committee meeting in Tokyo.

"TOYO is a member of the Japan–Turkmenistan Economic Committee and will most probably participate in the forthcoming joint meeting in Tokyo as a member of the Committee," the company said.

According to TOYO, the meeting is expected to bring together government institutions, state-owned enterprises and Japanese companies to discuss industrial priorities and identify practical areas for cooperation.

"We understand that the meeting is intended to provide an opportunity for government organizations, state-owned enterprises and Japanese companies to exchange views on industrial priorities and identify concrete areas of cooperation," the company noted.

TOYO described the committee framework as an important mechanism for expanding bilateral industrial cooperation.

"We regard the bilateral committee framework as a valuable platform for promoting industrial cooperation," the company concluded.

For reference, TOYO Engineering Corporation is one of Japan's leading engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) companies, founded in 1961 and positioning itself globally under the concept of "Engineering for Sustainable Growth of the Global Community." The company specializes in gas processing, petrochemicals, fertilizers, power infrastructure, hydrogen, carbon management, and other industrial projects, while also expanding digital engineering and sustainability-oriented solutions across its international operations.

Turkmenistan has become one of TOYO's longest-standing markets in Central Asia. In 2018, the company completed the Kiyanly Polymer Plant for Turkmengaz, delivering a gas separation unit, a 400,000-ton-per-year ethylene plant and an 80,000-ton-per-year polypropylene plant using its proprietary COREFLUX technology. Since 2025, TOYO has been carrying out a major overhaul of the Kiyanly complex together with Türkiye's Rönesans Endüstri Tesisleri, while in February 2026 the partners signed a second-phase cooperation memorandum with Turkmenhimiya. Earlier this year, TOYO President and CEO Eiji Hosoi described Turkmenistan as one of the company's main partners during talks with President Serdar Berdimuhamedov.

World.title: Iran’s geological copper reserves rise 10.6%
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Iran’s geological copper reserves have increased by 10.6% compared with the beginning of the current Iranian year (March 21, 2026).

According to the National Iranian Copper Industries Company (NICICO), the company CEO Seyed Mostafa Feiz made the announcement.

"At the beginning of the current Iranian year, Iran’s geological copper reserves stood at 22.2 billion tons. They have now increased to 24.5 billion tons," he said.

The company official added that exploration activities had accelerated during the period from March 21 to Aug. 22, 2026. More than 198,000 meters of exploration work was carried out during the period, accounting for 40% of the 500,000-meter target set for the current Iranian year (March 21, 2026 to March 20, 2027).

Feiz said the company’s mineable copper reserves had risen to 18.2 billion tons by the end of the period, compared with 16.8 billion tons at the beginning of the year, representing an 8% increase.

He added that the Miduk copper mine accounted for a significant share of the increase. Its mineable reserves rose 123%, from 793 million tons to 1.77 billion tons. At the same time, its geological reserves increased 186% to 2.88 billion tons.

According to the company official, the mineable reserves of the Sarcheshmeh copper mine stand at 7.7 billion tons, and the mine’s operating life has been extended through 2050. Its proven reserves exceed 4.5 billion tons. "As exploration activities increased during the period, mineral extraction also accelerated. Production rose 4% compared with the same period last year, reaching 153 million tons," he said.

According to Trend’s analysis, the 10.6% increase in Iran’s geological copper reserves to 24.5 billion tons points to a significant expansion of the country’s raw-material base for the mining industry. Completing 40% of the annual exploration target during the period also creates potential for further growth in reserves. The sharp increases at the Miduk deposit — 123% in mineable reserves and 186% in geological reserves — are particularly notable. Meanwhile, the 4% increase in copper production to 153 million tons indicates that production capacity is expanding alongside exploration activity. This trend could strengthen Iran’s long-term copper production potential and create additional opportunities for processing and exports.

World.title: KazTransOil reveals scope of oil transport via Kazakhstan-China pipeline
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. KazTransOil transported 13.121 million tons of oil through the pipeline system of Kazakhstan-China Pipeline LLP in the first eight months of 2026, up 2% compared with the same period of 2025, the company said.

Oil freight turnover along the route amounted to 11.879 billion ton-kilometers, increasing 3% year-on-year.

Meanwhile, the volume of oil transported through the pipeline system of MunaiTas Northwest Pipeline Company LLP reached 4.302 million tons, up 10% compared with the same period of 2025.

"Oil freight turnover increased by 8% compared with the same period of 2025 and amounted to 1.784 billion ton-kilometers," the company said.

Additionally, the Batumi Oil Terminal group handled 1.251 million tons of oil, petroleum products and gas, up 3% year-on-year.

Overall, KazTransOil transported 30.639 million tons of oil through its main pipeline system in January-August 2026, up 4% year-on-year.

The figures come amid Kazakhstan’s efforts to expand and optimize its oil transportation and export routes. The country is also working with Azerbaijan to increase oil transit volumes via the Caspian route.

In an exclusive interview with Trend, Deputy General Director for Commercial Affairs at KMG Kashagan B.V. Kuanysh Keskinbayev said Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan are working to optimize oil supply chains.

"We have a general agreement under which we operate. Under this agreement, we are constantly working to increase transit volumes. However, frankly speaking, the most important issue is the economics of the route. Because it's a very long, multimodal route, we are currently actively working to resolve this issue," Keskinbayev noted.

He said nearly 250,000 tons of oil from the Kashagan field and approximately 1.5 million tons from Tengiz are shipped via Azerbaijan annually.

World.title: EDB notes resilient performance of Kyrgyzstan’s trade sector
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. The turnover of wholesale and retail trade in Kyrgyzstan increased in the period from January through July 2026.

This was announced in a report published by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB)

According to the EDB, the trade turnover increased by 21.1% year-on-year in January 2026, 11.6% in February and 11.9% in March.

According to the bank, growth remained positive in April and accelerated sharply in May, before slowing in June and declining in July.

Furthermore, the EDB added that wholesale and retail trade turnover increased by 31.5% year-on-year in January 2025, 8.2% in February and declined by 8.5% in March. Growth stood at 1.3% in April, 16.1% in May, 16.5% in June and 18.2% in July, before slowing to 3.2% in August and 0.7% in September.

Trade turnover declined by 5.1% in October and 8.1% in November, before increasing by 26.9% in December.

The bank noted that trade activity in 2026 remained generally positive, although the latest reporting month saw a decline in turnover.

Trend’s analysis indicates that trade activity in Kyrgyzstan remained generally resilient during 2026, despite fluctuations in the pace of expansion.

The EDB noted that wholesale and retail trade maintained positive momentum through most of the reporting period, with activity strengthening notably in spring before losing pace toward the summer.

Compared with 2025, the trade sector has shown a more stable growth pattern during most of 2026. However, the decline recorded in the latest reporting month indicates that momentum has weakened and may require closer monitoring in the coming months.

World.title: Tajikistan’s population income shows positive growth trend
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Tajikistan has seen a significant increase in average wages and pensions over the years of independence.

According to the press service of the President of Tajikistan, President Emomali Rahmon stated this during his speech on the occasion of the 35th anniversary of the State Independence of the Republic of Tajikistan.

"Over the years of independence, the average wage increased 178-fold, while pensions increased 126-fold, significantly expanding the economic opportunities of the population," he said.

The president emphasized that during this period, more than 4.3 million jobs were created to provide employment opportunities for the population.

Trend’s analysis indicates that the increase in wages and pensions cited by President Emomali Rahmon points to a significant expansion of household income and social payments in Tajikistan during the independence period. At the same time, the creation of more than 4.3 million jobs indicates the scale of employment generation over this period.

If the average wage were to continue increasing at an illustrative annual rate of 7.7%, matching the long-term economic growth rate cited by Rahmon, its current level could increase by approximately 45% over the next five years and by around 110% over the next ten years. Under the same scenario, pensions could also increase by approximately 45% over five years and 110% over ten years.

These calculations are illustrative rather than official forecasts and would depend on economic growth, productivity, inflation, fiscal policy and labor-market conditions.

World.title: Teenager dies after suspected overdose in Qld state care
World.content:
A 15-year-old girl has died of a suspected drug overdose in a residential care home in Brisbane.

The teenager was in the care of the Queensland government.

The girl's death comes roughly a year after the ABC revealed that a 15-year-old Indigenous boy died by suicide in an Ipswich residential care home.

A spokesperson for Acting Minister for Child Safety Ann Leahy said they were "heartbroken to hear about the death of a child in residential care".

"The loss of any child is an absolute tragedy," the spokesperson said.

"My thoughts are with all those who are grieving at this incredibly difficult time and I have asked the Department to conduct a full investigation into the circumstances."

Advocates call for action

Sisters Inside chief executive Debbie Kilroy said the news of the girl's death was "devastating" and there must be transparency and accountability.

"We need to stop treating the crises of children in care as isolated individual tragedies," she said.

"It should force us to ask much bigger questions about what we mean when we say our state is caring for our children," she said.

Debbie Kilroy says the death of kids in care should not be treated as isolated tragedies. (ABC News)

Ms Kilroy said children in residential care homes were the most vulnerable in the community.

"When the state takes responsibility for a child, that cannot simply mean providing a bed, supervision and compliance-based interventions," she said.

"It must mean creating environments where children are genuinely safe, heard, supported and connected."

Aboriginal boy dies by suicide in residential care home The death has prompted calls from advocates for Queensland's child protection inquiry to investigate.

A youth worker, who is not being named due to concerns over their employment, called for the death to be reviewed.

"The minimum job [of residential care] is to keep children physically safe," the worker said.

"All decisions leading up to that death need to be scrutinised, including why this child was in care to begin with."

A spokesperson for the Department of Child Safety said legislation prevents them from commenting on individual cases, "however, the death of any child or young person in care is a tragedy".

"When a child dies while in care, the department undertakes a comprehensive review process conducted by a specialist internal systems and practice review team," the spokesperson said.

"The findings are considered by the independent Queensland Child Death Review Board and provided to the Queensland Coroner in accordance with legislative requirements."

World.title: Why the NRLW finals are all about one question
World.content:
Ahead of the NRLW finals, there is only one question to be answered because it is the only one worth asking.

Can anyone in the league stop the Sydney Roosters, who enter the semifinals as undefeated minor premiers after a record-breaking regular season that has been a wonder and a terror to behold?

There have been perfect seasons in the NRLW before, but the last one came when the league had just four teams, and none of them were like this.

The Roosters have already broken the record for most points scored in an NRLW campaign and are equal second for fewest average points conceded.

They have won their past five matches by a combined 200 points to 34 and have three players — Jess Sergis, Jayme Fressard and Brydie Parker — who have scored more than 10 tries at a rate of one per game or better.

Sergis has 16 four-pointers, the second most of any player in a single NRLW season, and both their halves, Tarryn Aiken and Jocelyn Kelleher, have broken the old record for most try assists in a season, with Aiken recording 17 in just nine games.

Captain Isabelle Kelly swears there has been little talk of perfection around Bondi way in what could be a case of once bitten, twice shy.

The Roosters have already broken the record for most points in an NRLW season. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The Roosters also went through 2025's regular season undefeated, but were struck by several key injuries late in the year and ended up losing an epic grand final to Brisbane.

"It's so weird; it probably wasn't until we won the game the other day that it came up.

"But as a player, I don't reflect on that. I know the girls aren't reflecting on that.

"We didn't even talk about the minor premiership, let alone being undefeated.

"Finals footy is a different beast. You can go all the way through, build consistency and be undefeated, but we've bowed out twice in the semifinals [in recent years] and had that heartbreak of losing a grand final.

"Everyone steps up. The game goes to a new level."

Every other team that now finds itself at the new level is framed by its suitability to taking down John Strange's winning machine.

Sixth-placed Newcastle ran them closest. They went down 12–10 back in round two and are the only team to hold the Tricolours to fewer than 20 points this season.

The gritty Knights have been through an unusual season; they've made the finals with a losing record and have not beaten another top six team all year, but will face the Roosters should they upset third-placed Brisbane this Saturday.

Lock Kayla Romaniuk believes forging tight bonds is the only way to take down a top side, let alone a team like the Roosters.

"They have strike everywhere, so it's a lot. But staying connected is the best way," she said.

"Those top teams, we can get in an arm wrestle with them, which is good, but sometimes we've lacked a little consistency. But finals is a whole new competition. It's do or die."

Canberra gave the Roosters one of their sternest tests of the season. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Just a week after that tight finish, the Roosters snuck home 22–18 against Canberra in one of the best games of the season and their only other match decided by one score or less.

The fifth-placed Raiders, who open the finals against the Tigers on Friday night in Campbelltown, led 14–4 early in the second half and 18–16 with less than 10 to go courtesy of a controversial try to Fressard.

According to Canberra halfback Zahara Temara, it was the Roosters' poise that got them home more than raw skill or brilliance.

"A bit of their class showed. We were ahead for most of that game, but in those big moments they stood up and showed their experience," Temara said.

"That's something I've started to learn and see, because we do have some inexperience in our team, how much those pressurised moments matter."

The likeliest challenger is Gold Coast, which has put together a season with its own share of blinding light.

Gold Coast shape as the greatest challenger to the Roosters' dominance. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

After going down 34–10 to the Roosters in round one, the Titans have ripped off a 10-match winning streak of their own.

They scored the biggest win of the season in a 58–0 destruction of fourth-placed Wests Tigers just two weeks ago and enter the play-offs having downed four semifinal teams in a row.

Karyn Murphy's side is battle-hardened and unrecognisable from the side that was so off the pace in the season opener, a game skipper Georgia Hale said they might revisit during their week off just to see how far they have come.

"We were still finding our combinations. We knew what we wanted to eventually get to and the steps to take to get there," Hale said.

"I think any team can be beaten in this competition. Every team has their cracks. Every team has a little bit of weakness in them.

"When you go about your business, when you buy into it and back it and believe in it, your process can outdo anyone."

Hale's belief is powerful, and in Jaime Chapman, Teagan Levi and Evania Isa'ako, the Titans will like their chances in a firefight, but the great danger is the Roosters might still have gears to find.

Their regular-season finale against Canterbury was marred by a flat first half and they trailed the Bulldogs 12–10 at the break.

The second stanza was a procession as the Tricolours ran in 30 unanswered points, but Kelly believes it is the lows and not the highs that are driving her team to what could be the most dominant season in NRLW history.

"There's games we weren't at our best. Bulldogs stood out, Raiders stood out, there's a few games at the start of the season where we knew we weren't up to our standards," Kelly said.

"I think, going into the back end, we started to find little areas of our game that needed to be improved."

World.title: Sydney band attempts world record for most gigs in 12 hours
World.content:
A Sydney band has pulled off a herculean effort to play nine shows in 12 hours across NSW and into Canberra in an attempt to break a Guinness World Record.

Dream pop duo Fathom had to play at least nine 15-minute shows at venues at least 50 kilometres apart, in areas with populations of more than 15,000, with half of those areas having populations of at least 100,000.

Vocalist Cate Guirguis and keyboardist Jaxon Italiano travelled on Saturday from Singleton to Newcastle, Gosford, Sydney, Penrith, Lithgow, Bathurst and Goulburn before playing a final set in Canberra.

Jaxon Italiano wore a camera on his chest during the record attempt for evidence. (Supplied: Nicole Tabuena)

A tour bus took them between all the venues, except for a helicopter flight over the Blue Mountains between Penrith and Lithgow, a car ride between Lithgow and Bathurst, and a plane flight between Bathurst and Goulburn.

The attempt was almost derailed three times, but they were able to finish their last show in Canberra with 15 seconds to spare.

"It was right down to the wire," Mr Italiano said.

"When we had this whole idea, we had 10 in mind, but in hindsight I'm so glad we just stuck to nine."

Loading Instagram content

Sydney traffic, missing helicopter, flight delays

Mr Italiano said he expected Sydney traffic between the city and Penrith to be the worst, and an accident on the M4 caused delays that fulfilled that expectation.

However, after their Penrith show, the pair's journey hit the brakes.

Fathom played as a four-piece band in Canberra and Sydney during the record attempt. (Supplied: Nicole Tabuena)

They had chartered a helicopter to take them over the Blue Mountains and avoid the Victoria Pass closure, but arrived at the base to find no helicopter.

"We needed to board the helicopter by 5:10pm because they wouldn't fly after sunset," Ms Guirguis said.

"But then we got there early and there was no helicopter there.

"Then we got a call back from the lady at head office, and she was saying that they were out extinguishing bushfires in the Blue Mountains, which is a fair enough excuse," Mr Italiano said.

The band were delayed by 30 minutes because their scheduled helicopter was busy assisting with firefighting. (Supplied: Nicole Tabuena)

Half an hour later, the duo got their helicopter ride to Lithgow.

It wouldn't be until their chartered plane leg between Bathurst and Goulburn that they would hit another snag.

"Firstly we went to the wrong terminal," Ms Guirguis said.

"As soon as we were taking off, the right propeller stopped working," Mr Italiano said.

The band used the tour to fundraise for mental health charity Beyond Blue. (Supplied: Nicole Tabuena)

"Our pilot … upgraded us to a jet which was fantastic and a lot safer."

The delay put the band an hour behind schedule, but a blessed run of traffic lights to Canberra helped them get on stage with time to spare.

"We just had green lights all the way to the venue," Ms Guirguis said.

"Cate and I jumped on stage, pumped out a 15-minute set," Mr Italiano said.

" We had a look at the countdown, there was only about 15 seconds. "

Thousands raised for mental health

The band said they fundraised for Beyond Blue as part of the tour, gathering at least $2,200.

"We wanted half of the sale going to Beyond Blue and the other half going to the bands that were supporting us," Mr Italiano said.

"So we actually won't be making any profit from this."

The band travelled in a minibus between most of the venues. (Supplied: Nicole Tabuena)

Mr Italiano said they wanted to support musicians doing it tough, trying to make it amid venue closures and festival cancellations following the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Ever since COVID the music industry definitely took a big hit," Mr Italiano said.

"We found out that musicians are five times more likely to experience depression and anxiety just from the amount of stress that goes into finding work."

Certification under way

To certify the record, the band need to prove there were 10 people at every venue through their ticket links, and at least two witnesses with them at all times.

They also captured video evidence of their attempt, with Mr Italiano wearing a body-worn camera strapped to his chest the entire way.

Ms Guirguis and Mr Italiano will now compile their evidence and submit the claim to Guinness World Records, which they say could take months to verify.

Mr Italiano is no stranger to the process, having previously broken the record for most pull-ups in 24 hours in 2022.

For now, the band plans on resting after releasing their aptly named song Record Breakers on Saturday.

"That'll be our soundtrack for the next few months," Mr Italiano said.

World.title: Donald Trump reiterates support for united Ireland, won't talk about Scotland 'yet'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has caused a stir by stating his support for a unified Ireland.

The comments, made during a weekend trip to the Republic of Ireland, were striking because previous US presidents — even those with Irish roots, like Joe Biden — have avoided commenting directly on the subject of unification.

The issue remains a flashpoint within the UK and Ireland 28 years since the end of The Troubles, a period of civil unrest and violence over the status of Northern Ireland.

Here's what you need to know.

Trump makes his point, three times

On Saturday, local time, Donald Trump had a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, and said they discussed various topics including trade.

Mr Trump afterwards said he backed Irish unity.

"Well, I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," Mr Trump said.

"It's going to happen eventually … I think it would be a fantastic thing.

"Now the UK will have something to say about it … but I think it would be a great thing."

Mr Trump said later on Saturday that there "was no good answer" to the question on Irish unity but repeated that he thought it would be "a very cool thing".

Donald Trump's visit to Ireland combined both politics and golf. (Reuters: Cathal McNaughton)

On Sunday, Mr Trump attended the Irish Open at his golf course in Doonbeg, western Ireland, and repeated his comments.

"You have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland and it would seem to me that one of the 'naturals' of all time is to put them together," Mr Trump said.

Why have the comments sparked controversy?

After centuries of colonial rule, most of Ireland won independence from Britain a century ago in the Irish War of Independence, becoming a self-governing Roman Catholic-majority country.

Under the Anglo-Irish Treaty, the United Kingdom maintained rule over Northern Ireland, which was split between two main communities: nationalists — most of them Catholic — who desired unification with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British.

Protesters with balloons demonstrate against the visit of Donald Trump in Dublin on Saturday. (AP: Kin Cheung)

In the late 1960s, tensions exploded into The Troubles, three decades of violence involving republican and loyalist paramilitary groups as well as British troops and security services .

Over 3,500 people died, many civilians, in a series of bombings in Ireland and the UK, while British troops carried out violent enforcement, including the Bloody Sunday massacre.

Mr Trump's comments come weeks after new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the United Kingdom was "off the table", a position Downing Street on Saturday said remained unchanged.

Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, the accord that largely ended 30 years of conflict, a referendum can be held only at the discretion of the British government.

How have politicians reacted?

Gavin Robinson, the leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, Northern Ireland's largest party advocating continued union with Britain, wrote on X:

"Northern Ireland's constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.

"Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people."

Sinn Féin, a political party that supports the unification of Ireland, said it approved of Mr Trump's comments, although the left-leaning party has little in common with him politically.

Gerry Adams who was Sinn Féin leader when the Good Friday accord was signed, said:

The "remarks by President Trump on the issue of Irish unity are welcome, even though we profoundly differ with him on many other matters."

Andy Burnham's office pointed back to his statement last week that he was "100 per cent" behind the Good Friday accord and that the UK would only consider allowing a referendum "when public opinion has changed to the point where the call has to be considered".

Andy Burnham says a unity referendum is "off the table". (AP: Kin Cheung)

Opposition UK Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said Mr Trump was "shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state".

"This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension."

Donald Trump has repeatedly spoken of plans to make Canada the "51st state" of the US, and angered authorities in Greenland by suggesting he could launch a takeover of the country.

Will Trump weigh in on Scotland next?

Mr Trump was asked on Sunday about independence for Scotland.

"You asked about Scotland. That one I won't talk about yet. I'll save that for another day," he said.

Scotland held a referendum in 2014 in which the population narrowly voted to remain part of Britain. Governments since have ruled out an immediate re-run.

In a separate development, the leaders of the main Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish separatist parties announced in a statement that they were to hold talks in Cardiff on Monday, local time, aiming to advance their campaigns to break away from Britain.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Feeding a crowd or wanting leftovers? Try these five affordable meals
World.content:
I often have anywhere up to eight people to feed during busy weeks, which means meal prepping in our household is essential.

Factor in a few fussy eaters and there needs to be careful consideration of not only what's on the menu but making sure there's enough for everyone.

These five recipes are tasty, affordable and, for me, stretched far enough to feed extra mouths or to have leftovers the next day.

This sausage pasta bake is perfect for easy dinners and freezes well. (ABC News: Lina Jebeile)

This is the kind of dinner that's easy for a weeknight but also perfect for feeding family or friends.

It took very little time to prep and was a real hit with my family. I chose to use regular beef sausages, instead of the Lebanese sausages. We fed eight of us with this dish and still had some left over.

Hetty Lui McKinnon's lentil bolognese ragu. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

The ingredients in this hearty bolognese are pantry (and wallet) friendly, and the lentils pack protein, which make it equally satisfying.

It also went down without a fuss among our kids, despite being a meat-free version of a popular family favourite. This recipe is also freezable, so you can make a huge batch to keep on hand.

Elizabeth Hewson says this recipe delivers the comfort of an "old-fashioned" stew, fast. (Supplied: Nikki To/Murdoch Books)

It was the name of this recipe that drew me to it and it didn't disappoint, eating it feels like a warm hug.

The tasty chicken stew doesn't ask very much of you and that proves that cooking something delicious for the family doesn't have to be complicated.

I bulked it out with a few extra potatoes and added some leftover mushrooms I had too to make it go further.

This recipe makes a big batch to make the most of your time. (ABC News: Tim Grey)

Depending on the size of your family, this tasty cottage pie will give you a second serving to be frozen, or reheated and served for dinner the following night.

The recipe is versatile for using whatever leftover vegetables you might have on hand and the lentils also help bulk it out.

Perfect for busy weeknights, Lina's baked chicken and pesto gnocchi is packed with flavour. (ABC News: Lina Jebeile)

This one-pot chicken and pesto gnocchi is by far the easiest recipe, which I made ahead using 10 minutes of my lunch break.

I used almost 700 grams of chicken to flesh it out as well as slightly more cherry tomatoes from our garden.

World.title: New report lays bare public housing 'failures' in WA's far north
World.content:
Almost seven in 10 public housing tenants in Western Australia's far north are waiting on urgent repairs to their properties, a report by local advocates has found.

The Kimberley Community Legal Service's (KCLS) Broken by Design report surveyed 166 public housing tenants across 22 communities in Western Australia's Kimberley and found the system was badly failing tenants.

Some houses were riddled with a myriad of issues, from structural damage and electrical faults, to plumbing problems, mould and pest infestations.

More than 95 per cent of those surveyed did not consider their homes to be safe or in good condition.

KCLS outlined key recommendations to improve the system, saying changes must be two-pronged, involving immediate maintenance and longer-term investment.

The report found 95 per cent of tenants surveyed did not consider their homes to be safe or in good condition. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

The ABC understands WA Housing Minister John Carey has agreed to meet with KCLS to discuss the report.

'Expensive and dysfunctional'

Tenants, who are not permitted to organise their own repairs, are required to have essential repairs undertaken by a "qualified environmental health representative".

To report a maintenance issue, tenants contact Housing and Works through a call centre or with a local housing officer.

Staff are required to record the request and issue a work order to the head contractor, who arranges a subcontractor to do repairs.

A licensed Kimberley builder, not named in the report for employment security, detailed chronic issues plaguing the remote homes.

"[The] entire shower floor was literally collapsing and falling away, and as soon as I ran the shower the water was pouring out underneath the slab," he said.

" In four years of doing this work in the Kimberley, I've seen standards of repair that simply wouldn't be accepted anywhere else in the building industry. "

In Beagle Bay, a tradesman fixed one tenant's broken shower with a bucket lid. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Over half of Kimberley renters are living in social housing, according to the report, with many tenants describing their homes as unsafe and unreliable and sometimes unliveable.

KLCS chief executive Matt Panayi said while this sounded simple on paper, the process was fragmented and difficult in remote communities.

Matt Panayi says public housing tenants deserve homes that work. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

"The current model is expensive and dysfunctional, that's reflected in the title of our report: Broken by Design," he said.

"All the evidence points to it being systemic problems that arises from how the model itself operates rather than small independent points where things are going wrong."

Another challenge, according to Mr Panayi, was completed maintenance often failed to address the underlying issue, resulting in further delays and additional costs.

Transparency and accountability

The report said 85 per cent of maintenance was reactive, despite evidence suggesting "planned maintenance was more effective and cost-efficient".

Loading...

It said about $250 million had been spent on travel and overhead costs associated with housing maintenance since 2019.

Public housing in the region has been shaped by decades of initial underinvestment, according to Mr Panayi.

"Aboriginal leaders in remote communities have long linked social disruption and health issues with poor public housing and bad conditions," he said.

"The government needs to be accountable for their responsibilities to provide safe and habitable housing for tenants."

A broken timber deck is an ongoing safety hazard at Kalumburu. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

KCLS suggested locally delivered maintenance, a preventative repair structure, accountability and quality assurance in the form of increased inspections.

Long-term, the community legal service wants enforceable minimum housing standards, investment in housing officers and ways to address overcrowding.

The WA government is reviewing housing maintenance arrangements, including the current model of awarding long-term contracts for maintenance and repairs.

The Department of Housing and Works has been contacted for comment.

World.title: World Athletics firm on Russia ban, Coe acknowledges need for solution
World.content:
World Athletics president Sebastian Coe has said the governing body's position on the exclusion of Russian athletes has not changed ahead of an upcoming Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) case, while acknowledging the need for a resolution.

Russian Athletics last month filed a fresh appeal with CAS challenging sanctions imposed by World Athletics, which has barred Russian and Belarusian athletes from international competition since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Our position hasn't changed, and this isn't about politics or passports. It's about the integrity of competition," Coe told reporters on the final day of the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest.

Aussie athletics star shocked at massive pay packet for coming second Australia's Nicola Olyslagers finishes second in the high jump at the new Ultimate Championship competition.

"From the age of 18, I believe that every position I've taken … it's about integrity and it's about competition, and that matters to me."

Coe declined to discuss the federation's legal strategy ahead of the arbitration proceedings but said World Athletics would continue to defend its stance.

"So our position won't change," he said. "And look, yes, this does need to be resolved, and I'm acutely aware of that. (But) I don't think our legal teams would be particularly thankful if I laid out our approach on this."

The comments came a month after Russian Athletics confirmed a new CAS filing, following an initial filing in July, aimed at overturning sanctions it says prevent it from fully representing Russian athletes internationally and participating in World Athletics decision-making processes.

Despite reaffirming the federation's position, Coe said he recognised the importance of ultimately restoring full global participation in the sport.

"We want a full complement of people on a global level competing in our sport, and that has to be our overall objective. Of course, it does."

The Lausanne-based CAS serves as sport's highest arbitration body and is expected to hear Russian Athletics' challenge in the coming months.

World Athletics has maintained one of the toughest positions of any international federation since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, while some sports have gradually reintroduced Russian and Belarusian athletes under neutral status.

The International Skating Union has established a pathway for selected Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete as neutral competitors, although it confirmed earlier this week that Kamila Valieva and three other figure skaters had their neutral status revoked.

Russian state news agency TASS quoted Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev as saying that all the skaters affected by the ruling would appeal to CAS.

Reuters

World.title: Feral pig problem raises bird flu fears in famous wetlands
World.content:
H5 bird flu is yet to reach the Macquarie Marshes, but landholders fear the region's feral pig problem could make an outbreak harder to contain.

The internationally recognised wetlands, near Warren in central north-west NSW, provide habitat for tens of thousands of waterbirds, including many threatened species.

David Duncan from the Macquarie Wetlands Association manages Burrima, a conservation property bordering the nature reserve.

The Macquarie Marshes provide important habitat for tens of thousands of waterbirds. (Supplied: Richard Kingsford)

He said an outbreak of the H5 strain of bird flu in the marshes could be particularly damaging, given the number and diversity of waterbirds that gathered in the wetlands.

"The potential to spread there is quite high and it would be absolutely devastating if it came on the back of a flood or a colonial nesting event," he said.

Mr Duncan said bird flu would add to an existing biosecurity problem in the marshes, with feral pigs, foxes and cats already taking a significant toll on native wildlife.

Introduced predators are estimated to kill millions of native animals across Australia each day, while Mr Duncan said pig numbers around the marshes had surged after several favourable seasons since the 2017–2020 drought.

"The feral pigs and cats and foxes are already creating massive damage, and they are a threat as a potential vector to spread bird flu."

David Duncan says feral animals could make a bird flu outbreak harder to contain. (ABC Western Plains: Kim Goldsmith)

Mr Duncan said controlling pigs required a coordinated approach because they could travel long distances between properties, and the responsibility should not fall solely on individual landholders.

"They move big distances. They might be on your farm one day, but they can be three or four farms away the next night," he said.

"You can't do something on your own. You've got to do something at least at a district level to try and control them. It needs to be vigilant and constant."

Landholders say keeping cattle away from waterways used by wild birds could be difficult. (Supplied: Richard Kingsford)

He said greater attention needed to be paid to biosecurity threats already present in the environment, rather than focusing on only emerging threats.

"Biosecurity is far more than preparing for or reporting the next exotic disease or pest to arrive," he said.

"It must control or eradicate the introduced species and pests that are already here, killing out native wildlife."

Richard Kingsford says a bird flu outbreak could have a devastating impact on already struggling waterbird populations. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

'They're going to take a big hit'

University of NSW conservation biologist Richard Kingsford said waterbirds were particularly vulnerable because they congregated in large numbers at wetlands, allowing the virus to spread through contact, faeces and scavenging birds.

Widespread wetland habitat across western NSW and the Murray-Darling Basin has helped keep birds dispersed, but Professor Kingsford said the risk could increase as conditions become drier.

"They will start to concentrate, particularly in an El Niño year as those inland wetlands start to dry up, and that's a real concern," he said.

"This influenza can kill sometimes half of a population. So that's how devastating it can be for wildlife," Professor Kingsford said.

Landholders fear a bird flu outbreak could have a devastating impact on wildlife in the Macquarie Marshes. (Supplied: Richard Kingsford)

Controlling an outbreak across large and remote wetlands would also be difficult, although Professor Kingsford said some populations could bounce back.

"Over time there's a potential for some of these populations to recover, but they're going to take a big hit," he said.

Professor Kingsford will undertake his annual aerial waterbird survey across eastern Australia in October and November, covering up to 2,000 wetlands.

The Macquarie Marshes are one of the largest remaining semi-permanent wetlands in southern Australia. (Supplied: Richard Kingsford)

But authorities cannot monitor every wetland, meaning landholders, birdwatchers and citizen scientists could play an important role in detecting an outbreak.

"It's essentially the citizen science that is going to tell us what's going on," he said.

Questions over how to respond

On Monday, the NSW government confirmed new H5 bird flu cases in Woy Woy on the Central Coast and Bulli in the Illawarra region, bringing the total number of cases in the state to 32.

There have been no cases detected in inland NSW.

Landholders near the marshes are being advised to avoid grazing livestock in areas heavily populated by waterbirds where possible, particularly if sick or dead birds are present.

A NSW Government spokesperson said H5 bird flu infection or disease had not been reported in beef cattle herds globally.

"Although transmission to livestock is considered low risk, there is a need for vigilance and grazing on or near wetlands like Macquarie Marshes may increase the risk," the spokesperson said.

Kate Milner says landholders have questions about what a bird flu outbreak could mean for the region. (Supplied)

But Macquarie River landholder and RiverSmart Australia chair, Kate Milner, said that could be difficult to implement.

"That sounds great on a piece of paper, but not in practice," she said.

"Cattle need water, and they will graze in the marshes and along the river, which is where birds congregate."

The NSW government has also urged landholders to maintain strong farm biosecurity and keep working and pet dogs away from wild birds and carcasses.

But Ms Milner said landholders still had questions about the potential impacts of an outbreak, including what it could mean for backyard poultry, water supplies and access to the marshes.

"There's quite a lot of talk flying around, but nobody really knows," she said.

A community information session will be held in Warren on Thursday to give landholders more information about preparing for and responding to an outbreak.

People who find sick or dead birds are being urged not to touch them and to report them to authorities.

World.title: Liam Martin celebrated a try with a foul-mouthed spray. Here’s what his mum had to say about it
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Liam Martin celebrated a try with a foul-mouthed spray. Here’s what his mum had to say about it Christian Nicolussi September 14, 2026 — 3:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Liam Martin was unsure what his mother would say to him after he was caught on national TV letting loose a stream of foul language after scoring a try for Penrith against the Roosters on Sunday. So we thought we’d call Mrs Martin herself. Liam Martin had some choice words for Roosters’ winger Billy Smith. Nine “I’m actually having a coffee with Liam now, and I was just talking to him about that incident,” Maxine Martin told this masthead. “I was trying to clarify what he said. He told me he was only saying very nice things to all the Roosters players. I have to believe him.



“I was more excited to see the gorgeous photos of Liam and his son Joey after the game. I love them both.” Martin sprayed Roosters centre Billy Smith with some choice expletives when he scored the first four-pointer during Sunday’s 19-12 qualifying final victory. There was no history with Smith, Martin said – he just happened to be the first person in his line of sight. The Penrith backrower was excellent on Sunday. Getty Images The Penrith back-rower was in the faces of several Roosters players including Smith, Naufahu Whyte and Hugo Savala, who was on the end of another spray after he shanked a penalty kick on half-time – a flashpoint which led to a melee featuring his good mate Spencer Leniu. “We’re good now, we shook hands so we’re alright,” Martin said of Smith. “There’s no history there. It’s just a game of footy. I was bringing that fire, I guess. I feel like it [the combativeness] is something I can bring to the team.



“When you’re out there, it’s that competitive environment, but at the end of the game you shake hands, and you’re mates again. It’s something I enjoy.” Pressed on what his mother might say about the bad language, Martin smiled and said: “My missus [Chelsea], my mum, they’ll tell me I was carrying on like an idiot. It was heat of the moment.” Martin once again proved he is one of the few players in the NRL who consistently stands up in the big games. Few back-rowers would have the athleticism Martin displayed to leap and then plant the ball down for a try off a Nathan Cleary kick. Martin said he had “surprised myself” with how quickly he was able to get his body into the position to score. The significance of reaching yet another preliminary final, bringing the luxury of the week off, was not lost on Martin.



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Cleary cleared for preliminary final, but sweating on foot injury scans “That’s the seventh year in a row [we’ve made a preliminary final], and it’s pretty special,” Martin said. “You never take it for granted. It’s an incredible achievement, but nobody remembers who makes the prelim or wins a prelim. The job isn’t done – there’s plenty we can improve on.” Panthers co-captain Isaah Yeo will be glad of the week off after surviving a second game playing with a ruptured pectoral muscle. He made 22 tackles and did not miss one. As for teams targeting his injured right side, Yeo said: “I’m in the middle, so you’re always going to be making tackles. I don’t know if I’d be making any more than I would normally. It felt fine; I’m really happy.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: A lecturer replaced himself with an AI avatar. His students couldn’t tell the difference
World.content:
NationalVictoriaUniversity A lecturer replaced himself with an AI avatar. His students couldn’t tell the difference Jackson Graham and Nicole Precel September 14, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When university lecturer Luke Rowe decided to replace his recorded online lecture with an AI-generated avatar of himself, he expected his students would notice immediately that something amiss. Instead, most were unable to initially differentiate between the real recording and the avatar. And once they could, students said they preferred the AI version of Rowe to the real thing. “I was eating humble pie, and I was sitting there going, ‘Why is that?’” the senior education researcher at Australian Catholic University said. “Hopefully, my human judgment will exceed that of AI”: ACU education lecturer and researcher Luke Rowe. Simon Schluter One reason was that the avatar had a smoother and deeper sounding voice than Rowe. There were other telltale signs that should have alerted students, but seemingly didn’t, at least not at first – hand gestures that misaligned with speech, and the eyes of the avatar being difficult to read, for example.



Before conducting the experiment with his class, which is itself focused on AI ethics, Rowe had to get approval from the university. Though ACU said it has no plans to replace academics with AI avatars, the experiment was part of its aim to teach students about responsibly using tools they will find in the workforce. Rowe said the avatar had plenty of benefits for personalising learning. Students can change the language it speaks in or speed up the cadence. From a teaching perspective, the AI avatar allows the researcher to edit and update lectures, keeping lessons up to date. “Hopefully, my human judgment will exceed that of AI,” he said of delivering lectures himself. “But if we’re talking of efficiency, no way; AI can absolutely do this more efficiently than I can.”



In recent years, a number of Australian universities have moved away from traditional hour-long lectures towards online mini-lectures. However, educators are yet to understand the effect avatars will have on how students learn online and the trust they have in teachers, Rowe said. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Inside Melbourne universities’ plans to future-proof degrees and jobs “From a human perspective, students can smell a lack of authenticity a mile away,” he said. “And when you’re authentic, and you genuinely care about them, and you ask them how they’re going and care about how much they learn, they will enjoy it and engage more.” Early research also suggests people need to master knowledge and skills with their own brain before they start to complement their thinking with AI.



“The pyramid is built from the bottom up,” Rowe said. University of Melbourne deputy vice chancellor of education Gregor Kennedy said the university was taking a balanced approach to introducing AI. “I don’t think we’re moving towards an AI study buddy situation at the moment, but we’re certainly trialling tools that help students navigate administrative aspects of the university,” he said. “From my point of view, we’ve got to think about not undermining the teacher and student relationship that is fundamental to a good education.” The university currently requires that half of all assessments in many subjects are secure from students offloading their thinking to AI. This can involve oral assessments, where they explain the thinking behind their essays, and timed exams. “Students do the essay, and then you’re in a dialogue with students about what they’ve prepared,” Kennedy said. “It’s useful for the student; it’s useful for the assessor.”



La Trobe University, which labels itself an “AI-first university”, introduced an AI-powered robot last month to help trainee and early career teachers simulate difficult conversations with parents. “We don’t have a central initiative to roll out avatars, but we’ll be following with a very keen interest any innovation in this space,” La Trobe vice chancellor Theo Farrell said. Loading While he can foresee a day when AI assists teachers with marking student work, Farrell stresses decisions such as these will ultimately be up to academic boards to advise on and approve. “When I started teaching decades ago, because of the volume of essays that we had to read, we produced a template … and then there would be a scale of one to 10, and you would tick where it was and provide two lines of comments at the bottom,” Farrell said.



“Now you can imagine quite precise feedback that’s given by an AI agent, where at the end of the day, you’ve read the essay and pushed ideas to the AI tool, but you don’t have to write the actual feedback. It produces the feedback, you review it, and you calibrate it based on your review.” Related Video Video icon 1:53 Tech leaders call for urgent global slowdown on AI He said educators needed to be supported to trial how AI tools could be used to enhance learning. “It could be possible that in five to 10 years’ time we will see a very different learning experience. We’re still stuck in the industrial age in the way that we teach, but AI offers us that hyper-personalised experience.” The sector’s regulator, the Tertiary Education Quality Standards Agency, has standards that all higher-education providers must comply with regardless of whether courses are delivered by academics or supported by AI tools.



“Students should understand how technology is being used in their learning and should not be misled about the nature of the teaching,” a spokesperson for the agency said. “Used appropriately, technology can support innovation, accessibility and new approaches to teaching and learning. Technologies such as avatars in teaching can have legitimate educational applications. “What is important is that the use of technology is intentional, purposeful, educationally sound and appropriately transparent.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Wallabies recall former World Cup star after NFL detour
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Wallabies recall former World Cup star after NFL detour Jonathan Drennan September 14, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wallabies coach Les Kiss has recalled utility back Jordan Petaia after a three-year absence from Test rugby as part of a new-look squad to take on South Africa at Optus Stadium in Perth on Sunday. Petaia left the Queensland Reds in 2024 to pursue a career in the NFL, eventually signing for the Los Angeles Chargers before being waived last August. He subsequently spent a season in France with Perpignan, before signing a long-term deal in Japan with Urayasu D-Rocks. Jordan Petaia signed with the LA Chargers in April, 2025 but was waived by the NFL side later that year. Getty Images Kiss said the training camp ahead of the Springboks Test was the perfect opportunity to integrate Petaia back into the Wallabies squad. The 26-year-old last represented his country in the 2023 World Cup defeat to Wales, starting as centre. “It was just the ideal opportunity to see Jordan; he’s been out of the system for a couple of years now,” Kiss said. “He has played in two World Cups. We just wanted to touch base with him and have him come and work out with us to see how he’s going.



“So it was just a good opportunity to see Jordan back in the environment and him to have a good look at us with the new coaching structure and all those sorts of things.” Petaia played most of his rugby for Perpignan on the wing, with Kiss believing that the former Reds player will likely be trialled in the back three. Jordan Petaia is back in Wallabies contention, after last playing in the 2023 World Cup. Getty “Positionally, we know he’s covered wing, 15 and 13 in the past. Once he hits the ground with us, we’ll have a good look at it, but it’ll be definitely in one of those positions – likely a back-three position.” Force playmaker Harry McLaughlin-Phillips has been named in the squad after Carter Gordon suffered a fractured fibula in Mendoza against Argentina.



Kiss could have picked Japan-based Noah Lolesio or the returning Reds five-eighth Tom Lynagh, but opted for the experience of the “battle-hardened” McLaughlin-Phillips. “It finally landed on the fact that Harry had been recently in [the Wallabies training squad] in the Nations Cup and he impressed immensely in there,” Kiss said. “He’s the most battle-hardened ten of all the options. “I’ve thought about tens outside [Australia] ... there’s a number that were mentioned, including Noah [Lolesio], and we went through the footage that we have available. We did our due diligence, that’s for sure, and it landed that Harry had earned this right.” There is no room in the squad for Brumbies veteran prop James Slipper, with Kiss saying that while the most capped Wallaby in history remains in the picture, he has tried to increase the depth at loosehead by including Aidan Ross and Isaac Kailea to cover Angus Bell.



“We’re keeping in touch with Slips about what his progress is,” Kiss said. “He’s doing a good conditioning block and he’s doing some scrum coaching with the Brumbies, he’s doing everything he can for Australian rugby at this stage where he is. Related Article Opinion

Australian rugby Reality check in the mail for Wallabies with scary Springboks up next Iain Payten Senior Sports Reporter “We’ve certainly got a close eye on Slips and we know that experience can just come straight back in for us whenever we need it.” South Africa underlined their status as the best team in the world by sealing a 3-1 series victory over New Zealand in Baltimore last Saturday. The Springboks will play at Optus Stadium for just the second time, after an 18-point victory over the Wallabies at the venue two years ago. In that Test, the Wallabies lost four front-rowers, forcing them to deploy captain and No.8 Harry Wilson as a makeshift loosehead prop.



Historically, the Wallabies boast a relatively strong record against South Africa in Western Australia: across eight Tests in Perth in the professional era, Australia have won four, drawn one and lost three. The Springboks are due to arrive in Sydney early on Wednesday after flying directly from the United States. South Africa will initially be based on the Central Coast at their training base for next year’s World Cup, before travelling on to Perth.
