World.title: Australian man, children found dead in Bali in suspected double-murder suicide
World.content:
Updated NationalWATragedy Australian man, children found dead in Bali in suspected double-murder suicide Holly Thompson and Heather McNeill Updated September 14, 2026 — 3:25pm ,first published 11:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An Australian man and his two young children have been found dead inside a Bali home in what authorities suspect was a double-murder suicide. The bodies of Perth man Damien John Shaw, 56, and his two children, aged 4 and 6, were discovered by Indonesian police on Sunday morning after the mother of the children asked neighbours to carry out a welfare check at the family’s rental house in Kuta. The bodies of Perth man Damien John Shaw, 56, and his two children, aged 4 and 6, were discovered by Indonesian police on Sunday morning. She was in Jakarta at the time, having left only days prior, and called the neighbour crying, according to local police. A Denpasar Police press release said a neighbour, Nur Khamid, received a phone call from Shaw’s wife, who was in Jakarta.



“In the phone conversation, the witness was asked to help check on the condition of her husband and her two children living in the bungalow, as they were unreachable,” the release said. Shaw’s wife allegedly told Khamid she had spoken to her husband on the phone, and heard one of their children crying. Loading Khamid went to the front of the property and attempted to look through the window, but couldn’t see anything. A second person was called to help and also could not see anyone inside the home, and the local community leader was contacted.



A few minutes later, the leader arrived with several neighbours who were also renting bungalows at the property. They knocked and banged on the door while calling out to the occupants, but received no response and the door was forced open. Shaw and his two children were inside. “Police officers arriving at the scene proceeded to process the location and conduct a preliminary examination alongside the Denpasar City Police identification team,” the Denpasar police release states. “Based on the external examination of the three victims, preliminary findings suggest that the two children died as a result of violent acts.”



Officers are investigating the cause of death for the three people, with autopsies being carried out. The family first rented the property in 2022, and were signed to stay until 2029. 9 News Perth reported the deceased man was from Fremantle. However, it is understood both children were not Australian citizens. The Department of Foreign Affairs is assisting the family.



WA Premier Roger Cook said the news was “horrific”. “A father and children have lost their lives,” he said. “There is a very confronting situation there. This is a very sad, sad situation, and our hearts go out to everyone involved, and we hope that we can get to the bottom of what’s gone on here as soon as possible.” Lifeline: 13 11 14 Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Why the US-Iran peace deal falling apart wasn’t all Trump’s fault
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Why the US-Iran peace deal falling apart wasn’t all Trump’s fault Farnaz Fassihi September 14, 2026 — 3:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was riding high in early July, fresh off the successful negotiation of a peace agreement with the United States, and had travelled to neighbouring Iraq for part of a weeklong funeral spectacle for Iran’s slain supreme leader. Suddenly, he got stunning news. A billboard in Tehran depicting US President Donald Trump. AP Iranian forces had opened fire on three commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, setting ablaze a Qatari tanker and damaging other vessels. Iran was under siege in world opinion. Outraged, Pezeshkian phoned General Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guard, and in a raised voice called the actions reckless and demanded answers, according to five Iranian officials and two Guards members familiar with the events.



Vahidi told the president that he had neither authorised nor had advance knowledge of the strike, the five officials said. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, which plays a critical role in both the war and negotiations, had also been in the dark, he said. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is not only contending with US aggression but also trying to keep tabs on a hardline faction inside the regime. AP In fact, much of the country’s leadership was unaware that a fringe hardline faction had decided to act on its own. Ultimately, those clandestine efforts derailed a push by more moderate pragmatists in Iran to reach an end to hostilities with the United States and repair their nation’s ailing economy. The hardliners succeeded in part because the only figure with the authority to resolve such disputes — the new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei — has been a phantom since taking office in March. He has not been seen, and his voice has not been heard. And the authenticity of written statements and messages attributed to Khamenei has been questioned, including by Pezeshkian, according to three Iranian officials. Pezeshkian immediately returned to Tehran. By the next morning, even as the funeral ceremonies were still under way, the US had retaliated with airstrikes on Iran. The two countries were back at war.



Senior Iranian officials and a Revolutionary Guard member said in interviews that what followed were some of the most volatile political confrontations within Iran’s leadership in memory. Officials engaged in shouting matches. Two senior generals threatened to resign. Accusations of treason and betrayal flew. The reverberations, officials said, contributed to a shake-up at the National Security Council and the supreme leader’s appointment of General Mohsen Rezaei, a seasoned politician and former commander in chief of the Guard, to lead the council, as he was thought to have the skill to mediate among political factions. But divisions persist, and the hardliners who have committed Iran to escalation are in an even stronger position. Last week, Iran and the US traded attacks, with Iran repeatedly targeting US naval vessels for the first time, and the US blowing up at least eight Iranian oil tankers. This account of the inner deliberations of Iran’s leadership is based on interviews with eight Iranian officials, three members of the Revolutionary Guard, four former officials and a review of dozens of speeches and comments by government officials and military generals from June to September published in the Iranian press and social media.



The officials interviewed for this article spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss delicate issues of national security. Influential spymaster Three Iranian officials said inquiries by the government and security forces traced the decision to strike the three commercial ships in July to Hossein Taeb, a cleric and influential spymaster who had opposed the peace deal with the US from the outset. Taeb had been telling the new supreme leader that Iran had made a mistake in ending the war and agreeing to the deal, they said. In a recent speech to military families, Taeb said he was not opposed to talks but that “negotiations that ignore the rights of our people and concede to the excessive demands of the enemy have no place in Iran’s politics”. Khamenei recently appointed Taeb as the head of the Basij militia, which is responsible for quelling domestic dissent. He had previously served for more than 20 years as chief of the Revolutionary Guard’s intelligence agency before the previous supreme leader ousted him in 2022 over failures such as Israeli infiltration of his rank and file, and a foiled plot in Turkey.



Taeb re-emerged after that supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed at the start of the war, and he played a key role in the selection of the son Mojtaba as the successor to his father, officials said at the time. Hossein Taeb remains a central figure inside the regime, although in 2022 he lost his post as head of the intelligence apparatus of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard. AFP “The attack on the ships was orchestrated with the goal to blow up the memorandum of understanding with Trump and to kill the prospects of any future negotiations and deal,” Alireza Namvar Haghighi, an Iran expert and former official who still has close contacts in the government, said in an interview from Canada. When Pezeshkian demanded to know who had struck the three ships, he was told that commanders in the field had acted on their own, in line with an order empowering them to attack any ship violating Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz without waiting for approval from central command, according to the officials with knowledge of these discussions. In one sign of the dispute, the Guard’s Khatam al-Anbiya headquarters never issued a statement claiming responsibility for the July 7 attack, as has been routine in other attacks before and since.



Iranian officials relayed this same account to the US and some of its regional allies in the immediate hours after the attacks, blaming rogue operators, according to US officials who briefed reporters at the time and the three Iranian officials. Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, was dispatched to Oman, a key mediator, to try to defuse tensions with Washington. Related Article Middle East at war ‘Satan fish’: The US drone sub captured by Iran in the Strait of Hormuz On the streets and on state television in Iran, meanwhile, the hardliners openly attacked the negotiating team and its peace deal, and at nightly rallies, crowds chanted for a return to war. The Iranian government has devised an official narrative deflecting blame for the collapse of the agreement, saying Washington violated it first by not stopping Israel’s attacks on the militant group Hezbollah in Lebanon, by withholding Iran’s frozen assets and by sneaking ships through a portion of the Strait of Hormuz not controlled by Iran. But few inside Iran’s political circles are convinced by this version, including Pezeshkian himself, five officials said.



Pezeshkian said publicly last month that every agreement sees violations and that they should be addressed through talks, not confrontation. When he was privately told by generals that Khamenei had approved the July attack on the three ships, the president demanded proof, according to three Iranian officials. Phantom leader Under the Iranian form of government, the supreme leader has ultimate authority to settle internal disputes. But Khamenei’s whereabouts, his physical health and mental acuity, and the extent he is involved in state affairs have become subjects of fevered speculation. “The security situation requires for him to be protected, but I’m asking, how long is this supposed to go on? Six months? One year? Five years? Ten years?” Hojatoleslam Alireza Pirouzmand, a senior cleric and academic at Iran’s National Defence University, said on state television in late July. He added that if “we can’t see our leader, then we will remain in a perpetual state of weakness and decline”. The face of Iran’s new Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, gazes from hundreds of banners on display in Tehran. AP



This month Khamenei’s mother-in-law, Tayebeh Mahrouzadeh, gave a lengthy video interview to a local reporter, describing the extreme security precautions surrounding family members and saying they had no news of the ayatollah and his three children. Her husband, politician Gholam-Ali Haddad Adel, told Iranian news media in July that while Khamenei had no contact with anyone for security reasons, “God willing, he is healthy.” The few comments attributed to the missing leader about the peace deal have added fuel to the dispute. After the agreement was signed, a statement in his name was issued saying he had approved because it had been endorsed by the president and a majority of the National Security Council – but that he was of a different opinion “on principle”. That phrase – “on principle” – has been repeatedly used by hardliners to attack the deal. Related Article Iran Who is Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s new supreme leader? In May, Pezeshkian said he met with the ayatollah but did not say when or where. Two Iranian officials and a former official said the circumstances of the encounter were bizarre. They said an ambulance with blacked-out windows was used to drive Pezeshkian around, while a secure video connection was established. A person who said he was an interlocutor for Khamenei appeared on a monitor and purportedly passed messages between the two men.



Pezeshkian confided to a close ally that he was unsure whether he had actually been communicating with the supreme leader, according to the officials with knowledge of the meeting. Last month, Pezeshkian said he had been granted a second meeting and that it had lasted seven hours. “We spoke about all the issues facing the country,” the president told Iran’s state television, listing them as affordability, unemployment, sanctions, unity and resilience during wartime. He did not describe the circumstances of the meeting or reveal what Khamenei had said. War plan For weeks, the political leaders and generals running Iran have debated two ways to break the stalemate with the United States, officials said.



Under one approach, Iran could seek to return to negotiations. Under the other, it would escalate attacks on US targets, aiming to strike naval vessels, kill US troops and raise global oil prices. Related Article Middle East at war ‘These waters aren’t safe’: New oil supply fears as Houthis seize key island, Saudi pipeline attacked Both would aim to end the US naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports, which has paralysed trade and brought oil sales down to zero, according to officials. Iran’s economy is deteriorating. The currency is plunging daily, inflation is soaring and the government is facing a cash deficit. Hardline generals, including Brigadier General Seyyed Majid Mousavi, who commands the Revolutionary Guard’s Aerospace Force, pressed for confrontation, officials and two Guard members said. The generals told the National Security Council they had devised a detailed war plan in which Iran and allied militias, in particular the Houthis in Yemen and armed Shiite Muslim groups in Iraqi, would intensify attacks, including on regional oil facilities, further widening the scope of the war and raising its costs for the United States and its allies.



Pezeshkian and General Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is the speaker of parliament and the top negotiator with the US, were among the officials who warned that the war plan risked dragging the country into an abyss, with even fiercer US airstrikes and more crippling economic pressure. But by last Saturday, the hardline faction had gained the upper hand. “The war between Iran and the United States,” said Mahdi Mohammadi, the top adviser to Ghalibaf, “has entered the phase of escalation”. This article originally appeared in The New York Times

World.title: ‘The rule is black and white’: Why Old Xavs have been booted from the grand final
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘The rule is black and white’: Why Old Xavs have been booted from the grand final Marc McGowan September 14, 2026 — 3:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Old Xaverians’ under-19s premier men’s team will miss out on playing in Saturday’s grand final after fielding an ineligible player in the preliminary final at the weekend. The Victorian Amateur Football Association announced late on Sunday night that the Old Xavs would receive a $100 fine and forfeit their five-point victory over St Kevin’s for breaking finals eligibility rules. Old Xavs have been booted from the VAFA under-19s premier grand final for fielding an ineligible player. Photo © Ari Hatzis St Kevin’s, not Old Xaverians, will compete in this weekend’s grand final against Old Brighton. This masthead is not suggesting that Old Xavs intended to break VAFA rules. VAFA rules state that under-19s footballers cannot have played more than 12 games in the season in question in the Talent League – the AFL’s premier junior feeder competition – to retain finals eligibility.



The player in question, who was on Oakleigh Chargers’ list and in Greater Western Sydney’s academy this season, exceeded that tally, but met other eligibility criteria, which required him to play at least five games for Old Xavs, including a minimum of two after June 30. This masthead contacted Old Xaverians president Michael Logan, general manager James Woods and under-19 coach Matthew Handley. St Kevin’s president Patrick Mount told this masthead it was an “unfortunate situation”, but that people at his club flagged the player’s ineligibility with the league once they noticed he played in the game. “There have been people saying we knew about it and kept it deliberately quiet, but team sheets can be changed until the last minute, and you don’t know if a player is actually going to play until you see them on the field,” Mount said.



“I didn’t know who he was personally, but we had a number of people on our side who flagged it, and every player’s profile on play HQ is publicly accessible and clearly showed he played 16 games in the Talent League. “The rule is black and white – you can’t play more than 12 [Talent League] games. “We have great respect for them as a football club, they have very good people in charge, and I don’t think this was anything more than an administrative oversight. I don’t think it was a deliberately sinister ploy to seek an unfair advantage.” In a statement, the VAFA said it had investigated and confirmed that Old Xaverians under-19 men’s team fielded an ineligible player against St Kevin’s on Saturday. “In accordance with VAFA rule 50, ‘A club which includes a player who is not eligible in a team by which it is represented in a premiership match shall be fined as prescribed in schedule of fines contained in rule 129 ($100) and shall forfeit all matches in which such player played … each such match shall be awarded to the opposing club...’,” the statement read.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Monday. Steven Siewert

World.title: Liam Martin celebrated a try with a foul-mouthed spray. Here’s what his mum had to say about it
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Liam Martin celebrated a try with a foul-mouthed spray. Here’s what his mum had to say about it Christian Nicolussi September 14, 2026 — 3:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Liam Martin was unsure what his mother would say to him after he was caught on national TV letting loose a stream of foul language after scoring a try for Penrith against the Roosters on Sunday. So we thought we’d call Mrs Martin herself. Liam Martin had some choice words for Roosters’ winger Billy Smith. Nine “I’m actually having a coffee with Liam now, and I was just talking to him about that incident,” Maxine Martin told this masthead. “I was trying to clarify what he said. He told me he was only saying very nice things to all the Roosters players. I have to believe him.



“I was more excited to see the gorgeous photos of Liam and his son Joey after the game. I love them both.” Martin sprayed Roosters centre Billy Smith with some choice expletives when he scored the first four-pointer during Sunday’s 19-12 qualifying final victory. There was no history with Smith, Martin said – he just happened to be the first person in his line of sight. The Penrith backrower was excellent on Sunday. Getty Images The Penrith back-rower was in the faces of several Roosters players including Smith, Naufahu Whyte and Hugo Savala, who was on the end of another spray after he shanked a penalty kick on half-time – a flashpoint which led to a melee featuring his good mate Spencer Leniu. “We’re good now, we shook hands so we’re alright,” Martin said of Smith. “There’s no history there. It’s just a game of footy. I was bringing that fire, I guess. I feel like it [the combativeness] is something I can bring to the team.



“When you’re out there, it’s that competitive environment, but at the end of the game you shake hands, and you’re mates again. It’s something I enjoy.” Pressed on what his mother might say about the bad language, Martin smiled and said: “My missus [Chelsea], my mum, they’ll tell me I was carrying on like an idiot. It was heat of the moment.” Martin once again proved he is one of the few players in the NRL who consistently stands up in the big games. Few back-rowers would have the athleticism Martin displayed to leap and then plant the ball down for a try off a Nathan Cleary kick. Martin said he had “surprised myself” with how quickly he was able to get his body into the position to score. The significance of reaching yet another preliminary final, bringing the luxury of the week off, was not lost on Martin.



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Cleary cleared for preliminary final, but sweating on foot injury scans “That’s the seventh year in a row [we’ve made a preliminary final], and it’s pretty special,” Martin said. “You never take it for granted. It’s an incredible achievement, but nobody remembers who makes the prelim or wins a prelim. The job isn’t done – there’s plenty we can improve on.” Panthers co-captain Isaah Yeo will be glad of the week off after surviving a second game playing with a ruptured pectoral muscle. He made 22 tackles and did not miss one. As for teams targeting his injured right side, Yeo said: “I’m in the middle, so you’re always going to be making tackles. I don’t know if I’d be making any more than I would normally. It felt fine; I’m really happy.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: A lecturer replaced himself with an AI avatar. His students couldn’t tell the difference
World.content:
NationalVictoriaUniversity A lecturer replaced himself with an AI avatar. His students couldn’t tell the difference Jackson Graham and Nicole Precel September 14, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When university lecturer Luke Rowe decided to replace his recorded online lecture with an AI-generated avatar of himself, he expected his students would notice immediately that something amiss. Instead, most were unable to initially differentiate between the real recording and the avatar. And once they could, students said they preferred the AI version of Rowe to the real thing. “I was eating humble pie, and I was sitting there going, ‘Why is that?’” the senior education researcher at Australian Catholic University said. “Hopefully, my human judgment will exceed that of AI”: ACU education lecturer and researcher Luke Rowe. Simon Schluter One reason was that the avatar had a smoother and deeper sounding voice than Rowe. There were other telltale signs that should have alerted students, but seemingly didn’t, at least not at first – hand gestures that misaligned with speech, and the eyes of the avatar being difficult to read, for example.



Before conducting the experiment with his class, which is itself focused on AI ethics, Rowe had to get approval from the university. Though ACU said it has no plans to replace academics with AI avatars, the experiment was part of its aim to teach students about responsibly using tools they will find in the workforce. Rowe said the avatar had plenty of benefits for personalising learning. Students can change the language it speaks in or speed up the cadence. From a teaching perspective, the AI avatar allows the researcher to edit and update lectures, keeping lessons up to date. “Hopefully, my human judgment will exceed that of AI,” he said of delivering lectures himself. “But if we’re talking of efficiency, no way; AI can absolutely do this more efficiently than I can.”



In recent years, a number of Australian universities have moved away from traditional hour-long lectures towards online mini-lectures. However, educators are yet to understand the effect avatars will have on how students learn online and the trust they have in teachers, Rowe said. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Inside Melbourne universities’ plans to future-proof degrees and jobs “From a human perspective, students can smell a lack of authenticity a mile away,” he said. “And when you’re authentic, and you genuinely care about them, and you ask them how they’re going and care about how much they learn, they will enjoy it and engage more.” Early research also suggests people need to master knowledge and skills with their own brain before they start to complement their thinking with AI.



“The pyramid is built from the bottom up,” Rowe said. University of Melbourne deputy vice chancellor of education Gregor Kennedy said the university was taking a balanced approach to introducing AI. “I don’t think we’re moving towards an AI study buddy situation at the moment, but we’re certainly trialling tools that help students navigate administrative aspects of the university,” he said. “From my point of view, we’ve got to think about not undermining the teacher and student relationship that is fundamental to a good education.” The university currently requires that half of all assessments in many subjects are secure from students offloading their thinking to AI. This can involve oral assessments, where they explain the thinking behind their essays, and timed exams. “Students do the essay, and then you’re in a dialogue with students about what they’ve prepared,” Kennedy said. “It’s useful for the student; it’s useful for the assessor.”



La Trobe University, which labels itself an “AI-first university”, introduced an AI-powered robot last month to help trainee and early career teachers simulate difficult conversations with parents. “We don’t have a central initiative to roll out avatars, but we’ll be following with a very keen interest any innovation in this space,” La Trobe vice chancellor Theo Farrell said. Loading While he can foresee a day when AI assists teachers with marking student work, Farrell stresses decisions such as these will ultimately be up to academic boards to advise on and approve. “When I started teaching decades ago, because of the volume of essays that we had to read, we produced a template … and then there would be a scale of one to 10, and you would tick where it was and provide two lines of comments at the bottom,” Farrell said.



“Now you can imagine quite precise feedback that’s given by an AI agent, where at the end of the day, you’ve read the essay and pushed ideas to the AI tool, but you don’t have to write the actual feedback. It produces the feedback, you review it, and you calibrate it based on your review.” Related Video Video icon 1:53 Tech leaders call for urgent global slowdown on AI He said educators needed to be supported to trial how AI tools could be used to enhance learning. “It could be possible that in five to 10 years’ time we will see a very different learning experience. We’re still stuck in the industrial age in the way that we teach, but AI offers us that hyper-personalised experience.” The sector’s regulator, the Tertiary Education Quality Standards Agency, has standards that all higher-education providers must comply with regardless of whether courses are delivered by academics or supported by AI tools.



“Students should understand how technology is being used in their learning and should not be misled about the nature of the teaching,” a spokesperson for the agency said. “Used appropriately, technology can support innovation, accessibility and new approaches to teaching and learning. Technologies such as avatars in teaching can have legitimate educational applications. “What is important is that the use of technology is intentional, purposeful, educationally sound and appropriately transparent.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Wallabies recall former World Cup star after NFL detour
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Wallabies recall former World Cup star after NFL detour Jonathan Drennan September 14, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wallabies coach Les Kiss has recalled utility back Jordan Petaia after a three-year absence from Test rugby as part of a new-look squad to take on South Africa at Optus Stadium in Perth on Sunday. Petaia left the Queensland Reds in 2024 to pursue a career in the NFL, eventually signing for the Los Angeles Chargers before being waived last August. He subsequently spent a season in France with Perpignan, before signing a long-term deal in Japan with Urayasu D-Rocks. Jordan Petaia signed with the LA Chargers in April, 2025 but was waived by the NFL side later that year. Getty Images Kiss said the training camp ahead of the Springboks Test was the perfect opportunity to integrate Petaia back into the Wallabies squad. The 26-year-old last represented his country in the 2023 World Cup defeat to Wales, starting as centre. “It was just the ideal opportunity to see Jordan; he’s been out of the system for a couple of years now,” Kiss said. “He has played in two World Cups. We just wanted to touch base with him and have him come and work out with us to see how he’s going.



“So it was just a good opportunity to see Jordan back in the environment and him to have a good look at us with the new coaching structure and all those sorts of things.” Petaia played most of his rugby for Perpignan on the wing, with Kiss believing that the former Reds player will likely be trialled in the back three. Jordan Petaia is back in Wallabies contention, after last playing in the 2023 World Cup. Getty “Positionally, we know he’s covered wing, 15 and 13 in the past. Once he hits the ground with us, we’ll have a good look at it, but it’ll be definitely in one of those positions – likely a back-three position.” Force playmaker Harry McLaughlin-Phillips has been named in the squad after Carter Gordon suffered a fractured fibula in Mendoza against Argentina.



Kiss could have picked Japan-based Noah Lolesio or the returning Reds five-eighth Tom Lynagh, but opted for the experience of the “battle-hardened” McLaughlin-Phillips. “It finally landed on the fact that Harry had been recently in [the Wallabies training squad] in the Nations Cup and he impressed immensely in there,” Kiss said. “He’s the most battle-hardened ten of all the options. “I’ve thought about tens outside [Australia] ... there’s a number that were mentioned, including Noah [Lolesio], and we went through the footage that we have available. We did our due diligence, that’s for sure, and it landed that Harry had earned this right.” There is no room in the squad for Brumbies veteran prop James Slipper, with Kiss saying that while the most capped Wallaby in history remains in the picture, he has tried to increase the depth at loosehead by including Aidan Ross and Isaac Kailea to cover Angus Bell.



“We’re keeping in touch with Slips about what his progress is,” Kiss said. “He’s doing a good conditioning block and he’s doing some scrum coaching with the Brumbies, he’s doing everything he can for Australian rugby at this stage where he is. Related Article Opinion

Australian rugby Reality check in the mail for Wallabies with scary Springboks up next Iain Payten Senior Sports Reporter “We’ve certainly got a close eye on Slips and we know that experience can just come straight back in for us whenever we need it.” South Africa underlined their status as the best team in the world by sealing a 3-1 series victory over New Zealand in Baltimore last Saturday. The Springboks will play at Optus Stadium for just the second time, after an 18-point victory over the Wallabies at the venue two years ago. In that Test, the Wallabies lost four front-rowers, forcing them to deploy captain and No.8 Harry Wilson as a makeshift loosehead prop.



Historically, the Wallabies boast a relatively strong record against South Africa in Western Australia: across eight Tests in Perth in the professional era, Australia have won four, drawn one and lost three. The Springboks are due to arrive in Sydney early on Wednesday after flying directly from the United States. South Africa will initially be based on the Central Coast at their training base for next year’s World Cup, before travelling on to Perth. World.title: Australian man, children found dead in Bali in suspected double-murder suicide
World.content:
Updated NationalWATragedy Australian man, children found dead in Bali in suspected double-murder suicide Holly Thompson and Heather McNeill Updated September 14, 2026 — 3:25pm ,first published 11:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An Australian man and his two young children have been found dead inside a Bali home in what authorities suspect was a double-murder suicide. The bodies of Perth man Damien John Shaw, 56, and his two children, aged 4 and 6, were discovered by Indonesian police on Sunday morning after the mother of the children asked neighbours to carry out a welfare check at the family’s rental house in Kuta. The bodies of Perth man Damien John Shaw, 56, and his two children, aged 4 and 6, were discovered by Indonesian police on Sunday morning. She was in Jakarta at the time, having left only days prior, and called the neighbour crying, according to local police. A Denpasar Police press release said a neighbour, Nur Khamid, received a phone call from Shaw’s wife, who was in Jakarta.



“In the phone conversation, the witness was asked to help check on the condition of her husband and her two children living in the bungalow, as they were unreachable,” the release said. Shaw’s wife allegedly told Khamid she had spoken to her husband on the phone, and heard one of their children crying. Loading Khamid went to the front of the property and attempted to look through the window, but couldn’t see anything. A second person was called to help and also could not see anyone inside the home, and the local community leader was contacted.



A few minutes later, the leader arrived with several neighbours who were also renting bungalows at the property. They knocked and banged on the door while calling out to the occupants, but received no response and the door was forced open. Shaw and his two children were inside. “Police officers arriving at the scene proceeded to process the location and conduct a preliminary examination alongside the Denpasar City Police identification team,” the Denpasar police release states. “Based on the external examination of the three victims, preliminary findings suggest that the two children died as a result of violent acts.”



Officers are investigating the cause of death for the three people, with autopsies being carried out. The family first rented the property in 2022, and were signed to stay until 2029. 9 News Perth reported the deceased man was from Fremantle. However, it is understood both children were not Australian citizens. The Department of Foreign Affairs is assisting the family.



WA Premier Roger Cook said the news was “horrific”. “A father and children have lost their lives,” he said. “There is a very confronting situation there. This is a very sad, sad situation, and our hearts go out to everyone involved, and we hope that we can get to the bottom of what’s gone on here as soon as possible.” Lifeline: 13 11 14 Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Why the US-Iran peace deal falling apart wasn’t all Trump’s fault
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Why the US-Iran peace deal falling apart wasn’t all Trump’s fault Farnaz Fassihi September 14, 2026 — 3:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was riding high in early July, fresh off the successful negotiation of a peace agreement with the United States, and had travelled to neighbouring Iraq for part of a weeklong funeral spectacle for Iran’s slain supreme leader. Suddenly, he got stunning news. A billboard in Tehran depicting US President Donald Trump. AP Iranian forces had opened fire on three commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, setting ablaze a Qatari tanker and damaging other vessels. Iran was under siege in world opinion. Outraged, Pezeshkian phoned General Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guard, and in a raised voice called the actions reckless and demanded answers, according to five Iranian officials and two Guards members familiar with the events.



Vahidi told the president that he had neither authorised nor had advance knowledge of the strike, the five officials said. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, which plays a critical role in both the war and negotiations, had also been in the dark, he said. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is not only contending with US aggression but also trying to keep tabs on a hardline faction inside the regime. AP In fact, much of the country’s leadership was unaware that a fringe hardline faction had decided to act on its own. Ultimately, those clandestine efforts derailed a push by more moderate pragmatists in Iran to reach an end to hostilities with the United States and repair their nation’s ailing economy. The hardliners succeeded in part because the only figure with the authority to resolve such disputes — the new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei — has been a phantom since taking office in March. He has not been seen, and his voice has not been heard. And the authenticity of written statements and messages attributed to Khamenei has been questioned, including by Pezeshkian, according to three Iranian officials. Pezeshkian immediately returned to Tehran. By the next morning, even as the funeral ceremonies were still under way, the US had retaliated with airstrikes on Iran. The two countries were back at war.



Senior Iranian officials and a Revolutionary Guard member said in interviews that what followed were some of the most volatile political confrontations within Iran’s leadership in memory. Officials engaged in shouting matches. Two senior generals threatened to resign. Accusations of treason and betrayal flew. The reverberations, officials said, contributed to a shake-up at the National Security Council and the supreme leader’s appointment of General Mohsen Rezaei, a seasoned politician and former commander in chief of the Guard, to lead the council, as he was thought to have the skill to mediate among political factions. But divisions persist, and the hardliners who have committed Iran to escalation are in an even stronger position. Last week, Iran and the US traded attacks, with Iran repeatedly targeting US naval vessels for the first time, and the US blowing up at least eight Iranian oil tankers. This account of the inner deliberations of Iran’s leadership is based on interviews with eight Iranian officials, three members of the Revolutionary Guard, four former officials and a review of dozens of speeches and comments by government officials and military generals from June to September published in the Iranian press and social media.



The officials interviewed for this article spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss delicate issues of national security. Influential spymaster Three Iranian officials said inquiries by the government and security forces traced the decision to strike the three commercial ships in July to Hossein Taeb, a cleric and influential spymaster who had opposed the peace deal with the US from the outset. Taeb had been telling the new supreme leader that Iran had made a mistake in ending the war and agreeing to the deal, they said. In a recent speech to military families, Taeb said he was not opposed to talks but that “negotiations that ignore the rights of our people and concede to the excessive demands of the enemy have no place in Iran’s politics”. Khamenei recently appointed Taeb as the head of the Basij militia, which is responsible for quelling domestic dissent. He had previously served for more than 20 years as chief of the Revolutionary Guard’s intelligence agency before the previous supreme leader ousted him in 2022 over failures such as Israeli infiltration of his rank and file, and a foiled plot in Turkey.



Taeb re-emerged after that supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed at the start of the war, and he played a key role in the selection of the son Mojtaba as the successor to his father, officials said at the time. Hossein Taeb remains a central figure inside the regime, although in 2022 he lost his post as head of the intelligence apparatus of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard. AFP “The attack on the ships was orchestrated with the goal to blow up the memorandum of understanding with Trump and to kill the prospects of any future negotiations and deal,” Alireza Namvar Haghighi, an Iran expert and former official who still has close contacts in the government, said in an interview from Canada. When Pezeshkian demanded to know who had struck the three ships, he was told that commanders in the field had acted on their own, in line with an order empowering them to attack any ship violating Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz without waiting for approval from central command, according to the officials with knowledge of these discussions. In one sign of the dispute, the Guard’s Khatam al-Anbiya headquarters never issued a statement claiming responsibility for the July 7 attack, as has been routine in other attacks before and since.



Iranian officials relayed this same account to the US and some of its regional allies in the immediate hours after the attacks, blaming rogue operators, according to US officials who briefed reporters at the time and the three Iranian officials. Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, was dispatched to Oman, a key mediator, to try to defuse tensions with Washington. Related Article Middle East at war ‘Satan fish’: The US drone sub captured by Iran in the Strait of Hormuz On the streets and on state television in Iran, meanwhile, the hardliners openly attacked the negotiating team and its peace deal, and at nightly rallies, crowds chanted for a return to war. The Iranian government has devised an official narrative deflecting blame for the collapse of the agreement, saying Washington violated it first by not stopping Israel’s attacks on the militant group Hezbollah in Lebanon, by withholding Iran’s frozen assets and by sneaking ships through a portion of the Strait of Hormuz not controlled by Iran. But few inside Iran’s political circles are convinced by this version, including Pezeshkian himself, five officials said.



Pezeshkian said publicly last month that every agreement sees violations and that they should be addressed through talks, not confrontation. When he was privately told by generals that Khamenei had approved the July attack on the three ships, the president demanded proof, according to three Iranian officials. Phantom leader Under the Iranian form of government, the supreme leader has ultimate authority to settle internal disputes. But Khamenei’s whereabouts, his physical health and mental acuity, and the extent he is involved in state affairs have become subjects of fevered speculation. “The security situation requires for him to be protected, but I’m asking, how long is this supposed to go on? Six months? One year? Five years? Ten years?” Hojatoleslam Alireza Pirouzmand, a senior cleric and academic at Iran’s National Defence University, said on state television in late July. He added that if “we can’t see our leader, then we will remain in a perpetual state of weakness and decline”. The face of Iran’s new Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, gazes from hundreds of banners on display in Tehran. AP



This month Khamenei’s mother-in-law, Tayebeh Mahrouzadeh, gave a lengthy video interview to a local reporter, describing the extreme security precautions surrounding family members and saying they had no news of the ayatollah and his three children. Her husband, politician Gholam-Ali Haddad Adel, told Iranian news media in July that while Khamenei had no contact with anyone for security reasons, “God willing, he is healthy.” The few comments attributed to the missing leader about the peace deal have added fuel to the dispute. After the agreement was signed, a statement in his name was issued saying he had approved because it had been endorsed by the president and a majority of the National Security Council – but that he was of a different opinion “on principle”. That phrase – “on principle” – has been repeatedly used by hardliners to attack the deal. Related Article Iran Who is Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s new supreme leader? In May, Pezeshkian said he met with the ayatollah but did not say when or where. Two Iranian officials and a former official said the circumstances of the encounter were bizarre. They said an ambulance with blacked-out windows was used to drive Pezeshkian around, while a secure video connection was established. A person who said he was an interlocutor for Khamenei appeared on a monitor and purportedly passed messages between the two men.



Pezeshkian confided to a close ally that he was unsure whether he had actually been communicating with the supreme leader, according to the officials with knowledge of the meeting. Last month, Pezeshkian said he had been granted a second meeting and that it had lasted seven hours. “We spoke about all the issues facing the country,” the president told Iran’s state television, listing them as affordability, unemployment, sanctions, unity and resilience during wartime. He did not describe the circumstances of the meeting or reveal what Khamenei had said. War plan For weeks, the political leaders and generals running Iran have debated two ways to break the stalemate with the United States, officials said.



Under one approach, Iran could seek to return to negotiations. Under the other, it would escalate attacks on US targets, aiming to strike naval vessels, kill US troops and raise global oil prices. Related Article Middle East at war ‘These waters aren’t safe’: New oil supply fears as Houthis seize key island, Saudi pipeline attacked Both would aim to end the US naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports, which has paralysed trade and brought oil sales down to zero, according to officials. Iran’s economy is deteriorating. The currency is plunging daily, inflation is soaring and the government is facing a cash deficit. Hardline generals, including Brigadier General Seyyed Majid Mousavi, who commands the Revolutionary Guard’s Aerospace Force, pressed for confrontation, officials and two Guard members said. The generals told the National Security Council they had devised a detailed war plan in which Iran and allied militias, in particular the Houthis in Yemen and armed Shiite Muslim groups in Iraqi, would intensify attacks, including on regional oil facilities, further widening the scope of the war and raising its costs for the United States and its allies.



Pezeshkian and General Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is the speaker of parliament and the top negotiator with the US, were among the officials who warned that the war plan risked dragging the country into an abyss, with even fiercer US airstrikes and more crippling economic pressure. But by last Saturday, the hardline faction had gained the upper hand. “The war between Iran and the United States,” said Mahdi Mohammadi, the top adviser to Ghalibaf, “has entered the phase of escalation”. This article originally appeared in The New York Times

World.title: ‘The rule is black and white’: Why Old Xavs have been booted from the grand final
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘The rule is black and white’: Why Old Xavs have been booted from the grand final Marc McGowan September 14, 2026 — 3:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Old Xaverians’ under-19s premier men’s team will miss out on playing in Saturday’s grand final after fielding an ineligible player in the preliminary final at the weekend. The Victorian Amateur Football Association announced late on Sunday night that the Old Xavs would receive a $100 fine and forfeit their five-point victory over St Kevin’s for breaking finals eligibility rules. Old Xavs have been booted from the VAFA under-19s premier grand final for fielding an ineligible player. Photo © Ari Hatzis St Kevin’s, not Old Xaverians, will compete in this weekend’s grand final against Old Brighton. This masthead is not suggesting that Old Xavs intended to break VAFA rules. VAFA rules state that under-19s footballers cannot have played more than 12 games in the season in question in the Talent League – the AFL’s premier junior feeder competition – to retain finals eligibility.



The player in question, who was on Oakleigh Chargers’ list and in Greater Western Sydney’s academy this season, exceeded that tally, but met other eligibility criteria, which required him to play at least five games for Old Xavs, including a minimum of two after June 30. This masthead contacted Old Xaverians president Michael Logan, general manager James Woods and under-19 coach Matthew Handley. St Kevin’s president Patrick Mount told this masthead it was an “unfortunate situation”, but that people at his club flagged the player’s ineligibility with the league once they noticed he played in the game. “There have been people saying we knew about it and kept it deliberately quiet, but team sheets can be changed until the last minute, and you don’t know if a player is actually going to play until you see them on the field,” Mount said.



“I didn’t know who he was personally, but we had a number of people on our side who flagged it, and every player’s profile on play HQ is publicly accessible and clearly showed he played 16 games in the Talent League. “The rule is black and white – you can’t play more than 12 [Talent League] games. “We have great respect for them as a football club, they have very good people in charge, and I don’t think this was anything more than an administrative oversight. I don’t think it was a deliberately sinister ploy to seek an unfair advantage.” In a statement, the VAFA said it had investigated and confirmed that Old Xaverians under-19 men’s team fielded an ineligible player against St Kevin’s on Saturday. “In accordance with VAFA rule 50, ‘A club which includes a player who is not eligible in a team by which it is represented in a premiership match shall be fined as prescribed in schedule of fines contained in rule 129 ($100) and shall forfeit all matches in which such player played … each such match shall be awarded to the opposing club...’,” the statement read.

World.title: Wellington City Council apologises for library website overspend
World.content:
Wellington City Council has apologised for spending over $600,000 on a website to draw visitors to the newly reopened City Library.

An independent review found shortcomings in the oversight, procurement process and the value for money offered by the site.

Chief operating officer James Roberts - the senior responsible officer for the whole Te Ngākau Civic Square upgrade, including the library - said he took "full accountability" for the expense.

"It is clear from the review there are lessons we need to take from this and I've already started making changes to ensure it doesn't happen again.

"Managing projects of this size, scale and complexity - such as earthquake strengthening on reclaimed land - is enormously challenging. I accept that one of the implications of this is that I didn't pay enough attention to this element of the project," Roberts said.

In June, Wellington's deputy mayor Ben McNulty said he became aware of the bill for the website the day after the Council Grants Committee had been forced to decline $3m in community funding due to a record volume of applications.

McNulty said the fee was "an atrocious amount of money to be spent on this type of website".

Wellington's deputy mayor Ben McNulty RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Author of the review Colin MacDonald found an ambitious project scope, a rushed tender process and a lack of oversight - beyond the board overseeing the Te Ngākau Civic Square redevelopment - combined to see the website's reach up to half a million dollars more than would typically be spent on a comparable Government website.

MacDonald said typical government website costs ranged from $100,000 to $350,000 in comparison.

He said scope of the redevelopment Te Ngākau Civic Square informed the project leading to the decision to create a highly polished, stand alone site designed to attract visitors to the newly reopened library.

"The project team operated under a strong, high-level mandate approved in 2020 and 2021 by Council to drive the regeneration of Civic Square.

"They considered that the biggest risk facing them was that not enough people would turn up and use the new facilities and the regeneration outcome would not be achieved. This may have given tacit permission to always go for the best. I could find little evidence of wider perspectives (e.g. from the executive leadership team) being brought to bear on the project and its decisions," MacDonald said.

RNZ / Mark Papalii

The report said a rapid "procurement in-a-day" tender process - which used a closed panel to assess proposals across a single day - undermined the market competition for the contract.

The tender - which went to market on May 2025 and was scheduled for implementation four months later - saw only two applications from six service providers approached.

The successful applicant was determined on the basis of their pitch for the first phase of the project which amounted to an initial expense $75,000 - rather than the likely full project cost.

The vendor was then retained for the remaining phases of the project.

The report said website's cost represented less that 0.1 percent of the $614M Te Ngākau Civic Precinct programme - which the library redevelopment was a part of - and meant the cost of the site did not trigger further scrutiny beyond the board overseeing the project.

"Because website spending was within delegated authority and represented a small share of the overall budget, it was never discussed at the programme board, limiting oversight. The programme continued to be guided by its original 2020 and 2021 foundational documents," the report said.

MacDonald said the project was allowed to make decisions that had implications for other parts of the council without sufficient consultation.

He said - while project leaders believed they had "consulted widely" with other parts of the council - perceptions from outside were that it had become increasingly difficult to influence decisions relating to the project.

"Some subject matter experts felt side-lined. This became particularly relevant as the website development and implementation progressed," MacDonald said.

MacDonald said a council commission value for money appraisal pointing out the cost of the site was "in the premium price bracket" and could have been "an opportunity to pause and reconsider the scope and specification".

"A more moderated approach by the project could have delivered a less expensive site that was still fit for purpose in supporting the relaunch of the building, its facilities and services, and the wider Te Ngākau precinct," MacDonald wrote.

The report made eight recommendations including developing a Council web strategy, procurement planning based of "whole-of-life" costs for projects, creating a formal value for money framework, appointing independent chairs for major programme governance boards and updating project mandates when council priorities change.

Mayor Andrew Little said the council would work towards implementing the recommendations and improving council practises to provide better transparency of costs and value for money for ratepayers.

"I've been clear that under my mayoralty - when the Council organisation makes mistakes - we front up to the public, we fix those mistakes and we learn from them. That's why I asked for this review, and that's what is happening now.

World.title: Vanuatu ferry disaster exposes gap between warnings and action
World.content:
The Vanuatu ferry disaster has exposed a critical gap in how weather warnings are turned into action across the Pacific, according to the country's top meteorologist.

MV Matui, Vanuatu's inter-island ferry sank in rough seas off the coast of Vanuatu over the weekend, leaving one person confirmed dead and more than 30 people missing.

Vanuatu Meteorology and Geo-Hazards Department (VMGD) director Levu Antfalo said his office could forecast dangerous conditions and warn the public, but it had no authority to stop vessels from putting to sea.

His comments come as meteorological leaders from across the Pacific meet in Tonga for the 8th Pacific Meteorological Council Meeting to discuss how to strengthen weather and climate services and make warnings more effective in protecting lives.

Antfalo said Vanuatu's warnings about the conditions were issued days before the MV Matui sank last Friday.

"The warnings came out earlier, so we pushed out the warnings on Tuesday. So there was good lead time for them to see the message and act upon it. But this is how much we can do," he said.

"We can only put out the information. To stop the vessels going out, that's not our mandate."

The Vanuatu Meteorology and Geo-Hazards Department also issued a marine strong wind warning at 5am on Friday, warning of dangerous conditions across all coastal waters.

It forecast southeast winds of 26 to 30 knots and very rough seas of up to three metres in northern waters.

Elsewhere, southeast winds of 21 to 25 knots and rough seas of up to 2.5 metres were forecast.

The warning urged sea travellers and mariners to take safety action, specifically noting that the conditions could be hazardous to small boats and vessels.

Antfalo said the warnings provided information that vessel operators can use to assess whether their particular boat is capable of handling the conditions.

A larger vessel may be able to withstand conditions that could be dangerous for a much smaller boat, he said.

The problem, he said, was that the final decision currently rests with the vessel operators and relevant authorities.

He believed the disaster should prompt a rethink of that system.

Rather than leaving captains to interpret general weather warnings themselves, Antfalo says warnings could be tied directly to different categories of vessels, with regulations determining which boats can safely operate under particular conditions.

"And if that can be done and can stop vessels that go out that would put danger to the ship and lives, then that's what I see now is putting harsher regulations to stop people going out when we put out warnings," he said.

He said that would require stronger cooperation between the meteorological service, the Vanuatu Maritime Safety Office, the National Disaster Management Office and search-and-rescue agencies.

The issue is particularly painful for Antfalo as a Ni-Vanuatu.

He said hearing that dozens of people were missing was devastating, particularly reports involving twin four-year-olds and concerns about the availability of life jackets.

He also said one of the people involved in the response was connected to one of the VMGD's projects.

From accounts shared from Vanuatu, Antfalo explained, the vessel appeared to have capsized suddenly.

That, he said, reinforced why marine warnings need to be taken seriously even when conditions at sea can change.

"When there's a warning, there's uncertainty in terms of wave height changes, as you call it. So, if there's a warning, I would prefer for those marine vessels to take heed of those warnings," he said.

Meteorological services can only provide the scientific assessment of conditions, including wind strength and wave heights, the director noted.

"But that could change when you're out in the sea," Antfalo said.

MV Matui, Vanuatu's inter-island ferry, sank in rough seas off the coast of Vanuatu over the weekend. Supplied / Tui's Shipping / Facebook

The Matui disaster has therefore become an important issue for the Pacific meteorological community's meeting in Tonga.

The regional meeting is considering how Pacific meteorological services can strengthen forecasting, warnings and communication with communities and the agencies responsible for acting on that information.

For Antfalo, the Vanuatu tragedy demonstrates why that work cannot stop with the meteorological service issuing a warning.

He said there needed to be greater responsibility across the chain, from the people producing the forecast to those regulating vessels and the people deciding whether to travel.

"At times, probably, yes, it may be on our side. But for this case, it's on the other side, where our people do not take heed," he said.

Antfalo said a national investigation would be needed to determine what happened and identify any lessons for Vanuatu.

But he believes the wider regional discussions should also consider how meteorological warnings can be connected more effectively to decisions made by other agencies and stakeholders.

He expected the issue could be raised at the Pacific Ministerial Meeting on Meteorology, which follows the current technical meeting in Tonga.

He said improving safety is a shared responsibility.

"I would agree that this meeting, and even the PMM ministerial meeting, probably it would be raised so that how we can do better, not just on our side, but on our stakeholders as well, and how we can work together to continue to promote safety, I'd say."

PM unhappy with Maritime Authority's performance

As Vanuatu takes stock of this maritime tragedy, the prime minister has transferred responsibility for the country's Maritime Safety Authority to his Office

Jotham Napat has withdrawn responsibility for the VMSA from the Ministry of Fisheries, Ocean and Maritime Affairs and moved it directly to the Ministry of the Prime Minister.

It's understood that Napat is unhappy with the performance of the Authority, in light of the MV Matui tragedy.

World.title: Are oil price hikes putting a pre-election OCR increase back in play?
World.content:
Recent spikes in global oil prices and bond yields appear to be increasing the possibility the Reserve Bank will need to hike the Official Cash Rate again in October.

While the Bank hiked the OCR earlier this month by 0.25 percent, to 2.75 percent, financial markets interpreted the commentary associated with the increase as dovish, with a pause in hikes in October looking likely.

The Reserve Bank is due to review the OCR again on October 28, just over a week before the election on November 7.

But the BNZ Economics team said in a research update today that the outlook has shifted.

"Things can change very quickly in this zany world that we now live in. The last few days have been a case in point with oil prices soaring, bond yields rising aggressively, central banks looking increasingly likely to push rates higher, the New Zealand dollar falling and, as a wee counterpoint to the unfortunate developments, New Zealand growth aggregates showing remarkable resilience," BNZ said.

Oil prices surged back over US$100 (NZ$172) a barrel last week on renewed fighting between Iran and the US and growing concern about the disruption to the Red Sea oil route from Houthi rebels.

The research note went on to say that a few days back, markets were pricing in little chance of a rate hike in October and almost no chance of two before the end of the year.

"Now, there's a near two-thirds chance of a hike priced for the first meeting and around an even chance of two rate hikes," BNZ said.

BNZ said it thinks the market assessment is entirely apt, pointing out that when the Reserve Bank put together its September Monetary Policy Statement it assumed the Dubai crude oil price would average US$83.70 (NZ$144.66) across the September quarter, falling to US$78.40 (NZ$135.50) in a year's time.

The economists note that the crude price is almost 17 percent higher than had been assumed for the next quarter and, in addition, the NZD on the trade-weighted index is currently sitting at 65.4 compared with a 66.9 estimate.

They say this not only puts further upward pressure on domestic fuel prices, but also on imported inflation generally.

BNZ said the full impact of the recently elevated oil prices will be a big shock to the fourth-quarter inflation reading.

World.title: Doctor at medical centre which allegedly refused use of defibrillator for dying man was 'unaware' of situation
World.content:
The only doctor at an Auckland medical centre which was criticised by the public for allegedly refusing to help a man who lay dying on the footpath nearby says he was "unaware" of what was happening.

A man died on New North Rd in Mt Albert on Thursday afternoon, just metres away from the Mt Albert Medical Centre.

Do you know more? Email melanie.earley@rnz.co.nz

Leoni Mcinroe, one of a number of members of the public who tried to save the man, said the medical centre refused to let members of the public use a defibrillator, take a pillow and blanket or offer any help in the 15 or so minutes she was on-site before emergency services arrived.

"I saw someone on the ground and ran down there. I asked if an ambulance was called and a lady told me yes, and I asked if anyone had been into the medical centre to ask for help and a young couple told me they had and the receptionist told them he wasn't their patient so they couldn't help."

On Monday, in a statement sent to media, the centre's only doctor, Dr Kiran Patel, acknowledged the distress and grief the community was feeling. He said he had been with a patient as the incident unfolded.

"I am saddened and shocked by the events that unfolded outside my practice, Mt Albert Medical Centre. At the time of the incident, I, along with our nurse, was in surgery with a patient, and unaware of the emergency situation."

The centre was a one doctor practice with only one nurse, he said.

Patel said a full review was being undertaken with his team and relevant authorities to understand the events leading up to the man's death.

"At this stage, we believe there was a misunderstanding around what was being requested and what was happening outside at that time.

"What I can confirm is that once our team became aware that there was a situation happening outside the practice, they called an ambulance and tried to help by providing any assistance required.

"I have been a proud member of the Mt Albert community for several years and also served as a doctor in East Tamaki for a number of years. We care deeply about our community and the privileged role we carry in healthcare. "

While the review was carried out, Patel said he couldn't say more but he wanted to make it clear that the centre was always willing to help anyone in an emergency situation.
